en: We pay homage to Prajāpati— the singular bliss, the immortal, the unborn, consciousness, the imperishable, who is both non-universal and universal, and who is fearless.
Learned scholars disagree regarding the Vedāntas:
some consider them to lack authority, arguing that if the Self is established by other means of valid cognition, the Vedāntas would merely be restatements (anuvādaka).
Because [the meaning] is unestablished due to the non-apprehension of its relation;
because it is not the object of a sentence since it is not the meaning of a word; and because it would lack human purpose if it did not instruct one toward engagement or withdrawal.
Others, however, under the guise of the authority of the duty to practice, declare that it is actually non-authoritative.

Still others, because of the contradiction with ritual injunctions and the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, consider the literal meaning to be figurative when the scriptural sense is accepted.
To refute that, it is said: "Bliss."
And he honors the Supreme Deity with praise characterized by the expression of its qualities and with prostration characterized by the humbleness of body, speech, and mind;

and he introduces the subject matter of the treatise— namely, the demonstration of the authority of the Vedāntas regarding such a reality by means of the refutation of misconceptions— for this too constitutes the purpose of the treatise.
On this point, some [object]:
"If Brahman consists of bliss, then the seeker of liberation would engage in practice out of passion for that bliss."
Furthermore, activity rooted in passion is the seed of saṃsāra; thus, it would not lead to liberation.
It is said that one who is tranquil and self-controlled perceives the Self;
however, one who acts out of attachment to bliss does not become tranquil.

Therefore, one who is weary of sufferings and free from passion for pleasures, proceeding toward the reality of Brahman which transcends all suffering, is liberated. Furthermore, the scriptural passages concerning bliss (ānanda) refer precisely to the transcendence of all suffering;
for the word "bliss" is observed to be used when the suffering of hunger and the like has ceased.
And others maintain that this very [pleasure] is happiness;
nor does this entail the undesirable consequence [of happiness] in the case of stones and the like,
because it is only when pleasure is experienced as having an inward orientation that it is recognized as happiness.
Or [it is so] because of the perception of a self characterized by that.
In response to those [objections], he says: "Bliss" (*ānanda*).
It is not merely the cessation of suffering that constitutes happiness.
Because pleasure and pain are seen to occur simultaneously in one who is suffering from heat while half of his body is submerged in a cool lake;

for if pleasure were defined as the absence of the other [pain], then even though there is pain in the half of the body not submerged, it would follow that he experiences pleasure because of the absence of the other [pain].
Consequently, it would absurdly follow that one being cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell is happy, simply because of the absence of the pains of other hells.
Furthermore, because there is an absence of suffering through the gateway of other faculties within the suffering of a single faculty;
and for this reason as well: even for that which is not [inherently] suffering, a pleasurable sensation arises from contact with a particular object.
Even in a case where there is the cessation of suffering, [pleasure arises].
Even in that case, it is not merely that [the food and drink] itself is pleasure; rather,
it is because pleasure is achieved through those specific foods and drinks by means of which the removal of suffering is accomplished.
And that [pleasure] is not possessed of distinctions such that a specific means for it would have to be required for the sake of those distinctions;
however, because pleasure possesses degrees of excellence, its dependence on superior means is logical.
Furthermore, they think:
"Even if no other suffering is to be removed, nevertheless, because desire is of the nature of suffering, the cessation of that [desire] constitutes happiness."
Even in that case, one who is without desire would not experience happiness in the enjoyment of a particular object;
yet, even one who is indifferent becomes gladdened upon contact with a delightful object.
This might be argued:
Only that object which is desired brings pleasure, and no other;
therefore, it is solely through the cessation of desire that objects become sources of happiness.
Otherwise, whatever is pleasant for one person would have to be pleasant for everyone.
If pleasure were defined by the cessation of desire, then it would be logical that whatever one desires or takes pleasure in is itself one's pleasure;
in that case, even for one who lacks such desire, the enjoyment of a particular object might manifest that desire, and upon its cessation, one would experience pleasure from that very thing.
But this too is insubstantial.
For the enjoyment of sense objects does not necessarily lead to the destruction of desire;
indeed, it has been said: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects. Likewise: "Passions increase in accordance with the repeated practice of enjoyment."
And there is skill regarding the sense faculties;
furthermore, the cessation of desire arises from seeing the defects in sense objects,
wherein the pleasure would be equivalent to that of actual enjoyment.
And if the attainment of the desired object were the same [for all], there would be no difference in their joy, because the cessation of desire would be indistinguishable.
This might be argued:
[The opponent claims: "In the case of excessive desire, there is the conceit of an excellence of pleasure upon its cessation, whereas in other cases it is otherwise.
But that is not so.
An object attained through excessive exertion does not please as much as one that was sought after but arrived without effort. For instance:

One does not rejoice as much in [pleasure] obtained through affliction as one does in that which arrives unexpectedly and was not anticipated. Furthermore, if pleasure consisted merely in the absence of desire, then the states preceding and following the enjoyment of an undesired object would not differ from the state of actual enjoyment.
Alternatively, the transcendent state (*parāvasthā*) would not differ from the state of the destruction of desire (*kāmapradhvaṃsa*).

If you argue that in the state of enjoyment (*bhogāvasthā*) one is simply someone for whom desire has been awakened and subsequently destroyed, then it would follow—contrary to experience—that one is happy in both the preceding and succeeding states, while being miserable in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, an object that has not been attained but is present in memory serves as the awakener of desire.
That which has been attained is what brings about cessation;
if it were merely the awakening of what has already been attained, there would be no cessation from that.
Furthermore, where there is desire, there is no happiness.
For even when something is sought after through hundreds of desires, one observes that someone may still suffer upon its enjoyment;
whereas desire is preceded by pleasure, since such [desire] is observed to exist when that [pleasure] has been previously experienced.
Furthermore, whatever sexual inclination there may be toward those possessing a particular species, even in the absence of prior experience, that too is based on experiences from a previous life.

Just as the desire of a certain person for a certain object arises due to causes such as the difference in species, so too does a certain pleasure arise for someone; thus, there is no lack of systematic order.
Moreover, some even suffer because of the cessation of desire, since in its absence there is no capacity for the enjoyment of sense objects; therefore,
they are not seekers of cessation.
They desire to turn away from sense objects because those objects have become unenjoyable due to some cause;
why, then, are they distressed?
Because they have not attained the pleasure of that birth which was previously experienced,
just as those whose sense faculties are impaired by bile and other humors desire to abstain from superior food and drink, so too do they suffer through their renunciation of sensual desires.
In this regard, there is no other cause for the cessation of the joy arising from that experienced birth than [the absence of such experience];
therefore, the rejection of pleasure that is to be personally realized is improper.
We see, however, that it was described by your honors merely to entice those who are attached to pleasure.
Thus, happiness is nothing other than the cessation of suffering;
and that is the primary meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda).
Furthermore, when verbal testimony is the means of valid cognition, it is proper to understand things exactly as they are expressed by the words.
Furthermore, activity therein is not based on passion (*rāga*).
For mere desire is not passion;
rather, they call passion that attachment to unreal qualities which is projected by ignorance (*avidyā*).

However, due to the purity resulting from the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), the clarity, inclination, and desire of the mind toward reality are not established as belonging to the side of passion (*rāga*). This is just as the lack of agitation produced by the vision of the unreality of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) does not belong to the side of hatred (*dveṣa*). Otherwise, even though reality transcends all suffering, if there were activity based on hatred toward it, there would be a continuous bondage to cyclic existence.
Moreover, even for those who are attached to the perceived excellence of others, mastery over the senses is taught as a means consisting in the renunciation of desire and so forth;
likewise, it shall be so here as well. And how, in that case, is there a prohibition against attachment to objects other than those desired?
Because one observes a lack of engagement when everything is negated;
likewise, there is desistance even from other [objects] due to attachment to supreme pleasure that has arisen.
And so it has been said:
"Selfishness is not praised, nor indeed is desirelessness found here [in this world].
It might be argued:
if bliss is to be experienced within Brahman, [then...]
If the agent were other than the action, it would entail the consequence of duality;
moreover, the relationship between agent and object does not exist without an action and an instrument. Therefore, [the text says]: "Brahman is bliss."
And thus, it would not be so;

for if it were designated by way of possessing that [quality], the term "without a second" would be untenable. If there is no cognition, then even if it exists, it is as if non-existent; therefore, its mention is useless.
For its mention is for the sake of human purpose (puruṣārtha);
yet how can that which is not cognizable be a human purpose? It is said:
this should be viewed as being like [the mention of] a result and like [the mention of] an agent.
For instance, all investigators maintain and recognize that the fruit of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is either distinct from it or non-distinct; and yet,
that fruit is not unperceived.
For if that [consciousness] were itself unperceivable, it would follow that everything is unperceivable,
since the perceivability of entities is produced by it;
yet it is not perceivable.
Because no other fruit [of cognition] is perceived, and because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress;
therefore, it is self-cognizable, owing to its being self-luminous.
And it would be imperceptible, because, like an object, it would lack the status of being an action;
furthermore, if the agent— the self— were imperceptible, consciousness itself could not exist.
For at that time, it does not occur to one thus: "This has been known by me."
For a self that is not self-cognized cannot be connected to the fruit or to the object;
and if there is no such connection, what distinction is there between that which is cognized by oneself and that which is cognized by another?
Nor, indeed, is it [the self] cognized.
Because if it were an object (*karma*), it would follow that the agent (*kartṛ*) is distinct from it, and it would follow that it is not the self (*anātmatva*).
Therefore, its being cognized consists precisely in its being the self-luminous nature of the self.
Likewise, for Brahman, which is the self-luminous light, its nature as bliss is not something to be cognized [as an external object].
Because it lacks the status of being an object;
yet it is not imperceptible,
because it is self-luminous.
"By what means could one see whom?"— this negation as well has action as its object;
for it is said that [the state of the Self] is caused precisely by the complete subsiding of all actions.
"When for him everything has become the Self alone"— regarding this,
others think that dharmas are of two kinds.
They are both of the nature of existence and of the nature of non-existence.
Among these, those of the nature of non-existence do not obstruct non-duality, as for example:
"One, immortal, unborn."
For the cessation of difference, arising, and passing away is not some entity that would bring about duality;
and if bliss were an entity, [it would likewise entail duality].
If that [consciousness] is the subject (dharmin), then cognition (vijñāna) would be its property (dharma); or, if cognition is the form of the subject,
then bliss (ānanda) is the property.

For it is not logical for one thing to have two forms, because that would involve a contradiction. In that case, regarding the statement "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," since bliss and Brahman— which are positive entities— are related as attribute and substrate, their difference would result in the destruction of non-duality (advaita).

It might be argued as follows: even a property (dharma) is not distinct from its substratum (dharmin), because if they were distinct, the relationship of property and substratum would be untenable, as in the case of a cow and a horse.
That is incorrect, because even if there were non-difference, that [distinction] would be untenable, just as it is with the nature of the substratum (*dharmī*).
Therefore, the property (*dharma*) is in some way different.
And thus, there is the scriptural teaching on the absence of absolute difference.
The statement "one only, without a second" would not be tenable;
likewise for one who perceives two forms in a single thing.

Therefore, the word "bliss" (ānanda) is merely a limiting adjunct (upādhi) for the absence of suffering in Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness; just as words such as "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short," etc., have as their limiting adjuncts the absence of grossness and so forth.
Nor is there identity between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), because the employment of two distinct words would otherwise be redundant.
Furthermore, how could there be identity between that which is denoted by non-synonymous terms?
Therefore, the meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda) in reference to Brahman is simply the cessation of suffering. To this it is replied:
there is no fault, because the two words convey a specific light whose nature is exhilaration, just as in the case of moonlight.
And as it is said:
"The sun is supreme light."
Furthermore, the words "excellence" (*prakṛṣṭa*) and "light" (*prakāśa*) are not synonyms;
nevertheless, by means of these two, a single specific object—a particular kind of light—is conveyed.
For in the case of the sun, excellence is not something other than the nature of its light.
Nor is it of the nature of light through excellence; rather, a distinction within light is perceived by means of two words.
Likewise [in the case of]: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss."
Thus, by means of the two words "bliss" (*ānanda*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), the nature of Brahman is understood as being either a variety of bliss or a variety of consciousness.
Some maintain that this [nature] is supreme because it lacks the state of suffering characterized by dependence on external means and characterized by perishability.
However, others do not accept even that, since one must understand things according to the words [of scripture], and the object is established solely through the authority of scripture.
For when transcendence cannot exist by way of its own nature, it is not logical for that [transcendence] to be merely figurative based on the absence of contact with a contradictory [attribute].
Therefore, it is correct that Brahman has as its very essence the nature of the Self, which is the supreme manifestation of the Self.
And in this way, it is appropriate that worldly bliss is but a measure of this [supreme bliss].
Because of limitation;
however, this is difficult to establish in the case of the cessation of suffering.
For this reason as well, the self has bliss as its intrinsic nature.
Because it is the locus of supreme love;
for its being the locus of supreme love is indeed heard in scripture: "This is dearer than a son."
And it is indeed perceived;
for instance,
this desire for self-preservation belongs to everyone, even to a worm.
"May I not cease to be; may I come to be"—
this [wish] is possible only with respect to something dear.
And affection (premā) is directed toward that which has the nature of happiness; it is not directed toward suffering, nor toward that which is devoid of both [happiness and suffering],
because of aversion and indifference [respectively].
Others, however, on the basis of the retrospective reflection, "I slept happily," assert that there is an experience of pleasure within the self during deep sleep.

For if there were no experience, neither such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) nor the admission of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) would be possible; nor, if the experience were otherwise, could there be a reflective awareness that "it was pleasant."
And there, nothing other than the self remains to be experienced;
likewise, it is heard in scripture that one attains the world of Brahmā day after day.
Regarding this, others say:
Even from the cessation of suffering, the establishment of happiness is not absolute, because [the notion of] "clinging" (parāmarśa) is still established;
regarding them, they say:
it is logical that the word "happiness" is used as having the cessation of suffering as its cause when a change [from that state] is understood.
Otherwise, it would be more appropriate to take it in its primary sense.
Regarding this, they say:
since both types of designation are observed and both are logically consistent, the meaning cannot be established by mere designation alone; enough of this excessive detail.
On this point, some [object]:
"Because of the established order of experience, and because the distinction between the liberated and those in saṃsāra is logically possible," [there must be a Lord].
Because the power of vision possesses purposefulness, because it is contradictory for it to act upon itself,
because the seer is inferred from the seen,
and because the seen is perceived as divided into sound and so forth, just as pleasure, pain, and delusion are distinct.
They consider the scriptural statement regarding oneness to be based on a metaphorical application (upacāra) caused by the absence of distinctions of genus, place, and time;
and the statement "All this is indeed the Self" is likewise due to a metaphorical application based on the fact that everything has the Self as its ultimate purpose.
To them it is replied: "One," as in:
"Indra, through his magical powers, moves in many forms."
Thus, it has been clearly demonstrated that the perception of various forms is based on *māyā*.
In that case, how can it be said that "oneness" is merely figurative?
Likewise, the negation of plurality is manifest.
"There is nothing whatsoever manifold here"; and there is the censure of the perception of manifoldness:
"He goes from death to death."
And there is the absence of the perception of difference—
as if the vision of difference were due to delusion— expressed as: "He who sees here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity."

Thus, what is indicated by the word "as if" (iva) is not possible if [the identity] were merely figurative. Granted that identity might exist through metaphorical usage, there would still be no cessation of actual plurality.
If it is argued that even this is spoken of only by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), we say no;
for there is no purpose [for such a designation].
Metaphorical designation occurs only when there is a basis (*nimitta*) and a purpose (*prayojana*).
Furthermore, we do not perceive any purpose for employing the metaphorical designation of the cessation of diversity;
on the contrary,
it would be for the sake of higher rebirth or the supreme good that the cessation of diversity would be metaphorically designated.
For that [knowledge], by negating the distinction between the goal and the means and by manifesting the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) everywhere, would be in contradiction with it;
for it is an undisputed fact that the highest good belongs to one who has desisted from everything.

Likewise, from the restrictive phrase "one only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*) and from the repeated mention of that same meaning through the words "only" and "without a second," it is indicated that the purpose of the Śruti is the cessation of difference in every respect.
For in the case of repetition, there is an intensification of the meaning, as in: "Oh, how beautiful she is! [repeated].
"Ah, how beautiful!"—
even this does not constitute a deficiency;
it is merely figurative from afar.
As for the argument that "it is because of the establishment of experience," it is replied:
this is worthless, since the establishment of experience is proven even by means of an imagined distinction.
For instance—

even with respect to a single self that is omnipresent, or of the size of the body, or of atomic size— a distinction in experience is observed based on imagined differences, such as: "There is pain in my foot."
"I have a pain in my head"—
for there is no actual connection between the foot and the pain in the head, because [the foot] lacks cognition.

Even for those who maintain that the self is co-extensive with the body, it is not merely the bodily parts that experience sensation, because that would entail the consequence that the self is devoid of sensation.
This might be argued:
If there were a single self, then, just as in that case, there would be a recollection of experiences in other bodies;
but this is another matter altogether.
For now, there certainly exists a fixed order regarding experience.
Moreover, even in that case, one part does not connect with the sensation of another part;
likewise here as well, the soul (jīva) does not connect with the sensation of another soul—thus it is the same.

Furthermore, in the case of gems, swords, mirrors, and so forth, the distinct arrangement of colors, shapes, and other qualities is perceived despite the absence of any actual division [in the object].
And in this way, the distinction between those liberated and those still transmigrating is also logically established.
For instance, even though the self is one, when it is joined with pleasure, pain, and so forth in certain locations, it is understood as if bound there and as if liberated elsewhere.
Just as a face appears soiled on a soiled mirror surface and pure on a pure one, yet when perceived without a mirror it is not affected by the defects of those conditions;
this might be argued:
conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a property of the cognizer’s cognition and is not capable of establishing the actual nature of the object.
Indeed, things do not change in accordance with the cognition of the perceiver;
nor does an effect arise from that which is merely metaphorical,
for a youth who is metaphorically called "fire" does not burn.
The established rule has indeed been stated;
that is true,
for it is a delusion.
Even in this case, the status of being an error is not precluded by a staff;
for even an imagined snake-bite leads to the effect of death,
and a reflected image serves the function of illumination.
As for the claim that there is a distinction between the seer and the seen because the seer is inferred through the very existence of the seen,
and that the seen is manifold because various distinctions such as pleasure and so forth are perceived—
that too is incorrect.
It has been stated that as long as the seer is not manifest, there can be no establishment of the object seen; furthermore,
it will be explained that there is no perception of distinctions among objects seen, because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lacks the capacity for delimitation.
The capacity for vision possesses purposefulness because it serves its own self;
nor is there a contradiction in its activity directed toward itself,
as has been stated by way of the analogy of a lamp and the analogy of the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Moreover, this relationship of seer and seen is only conceivable if there is identity; for it arises from the conscious self (cidātman) as the seer undergoing such and such transformations or manifestations (vivarta).
But if there were plurality—that is, if the two were distinct by nature, with unmixed and mutually unrelated essences—what kind of relationship of seer and seen could possibly exist?
For it is not logical that what is not in contact with consciousness (citi) could be cognized.

If it is argued that a connection certainly exists when there is a complete transfer [of the object] into the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), we say no; because consciousness is pure, immutable, and incapable of transferring [into another].

If it is argued that the intellect (buddhi), being an object of perception, undergoes transformation through the reflection (chāyā) of consciousness due to its proximity to consciousness, then what is this "reflection"?
It is the appearance of that which is not of the nature of something else as being that thing.
In that case, the visible object is not seen from the perspective of ultimate reality;
and since it is not seen from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is difficult to maintain that there exists anything distinct from the seer.
As for the one who thinks:
The object of sight is established as such solely by its being seen,
not by a [real] relation;
and as for the act of seeing—
"This" refers to an object that has an external form;
he should be told:
"True, it refers to an object that has an external form."
This occurs because of the transformation or the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the single Self in such and such ways, as in the case of one’s own reflection in the surface of a mirror.
For instance, one perceives the self situated in the mirror-surface as if it were distinct from oneself;
however, it is difficult to understand how consciousness could perceive itself as something distinct and unconnected with it.
And thus, the non-difference of the object of vision from the seer is recorded in scripture:
"When the Self is known, all this becomes known.
Therefore, it is rightly said that [the Self] is one.

However, those who maintain that the self consists of momentary cognitions assert that the attainment of Brahman is characterized precisely by the cessation of cognition through the total eradication of the afflictions along with their latent impressions (*savāsanakleśa*).
And thus it is heard in scripture:
"After passing away, there is no consciousness."

Others, however, [hold it to be] characterized by the arising of pure knowledge in which the disturbances of objective forms have been shaken off due to the total eradication of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

For if [the self] were without beginning or end, there would be nothing whatsoever to be removed or added; consequently, the treatises intended for that purpose and the activities directed toward that end would be rendered useless.
To explain: if its nature were that of pure knowledge (*vidyā*),...
Nothing whatsoever would need to be abandoned or attained,
because of the absence of ignorance and the presence of knowledge.
If [the self] were of the nature of ignorance, [then this would follow].
If that [ignorance] were eternal, it would follow that it must either abandon its prior nature or undergo the acquisition of a different nature;
likewise, even if ignorance possessed both natures, since knowledge would already have been attained and ignorance would be impossible to eradicate,
he says this in response to them:
"It is the immortal, the unborn.
Nor is there any futility in the scriptures or in the activities aimed at liberation, because ignorance is that which is to be removed.
In all philosophical systems, even beginningless ignorance is accepted as being destructible;
we do not say that there is no destruction of what is beginningless, but rather [we deny it] in the case of the eternal nature of Brahman.
[KKS_9] Now, if ignorance is not the intrinsic nature of Brahman, it would follow that it is something other than Brahman;
or else, it might not exist at all—in that case, what is there to be removed? Suppose this view is held:
Ignorance is non-apprehension;
how could it be a distinct entity?
Nor is it something that cannot be removed.
Because all operations of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their purpose the cessation of non-apprehension;
that too is incorrect, for [non-apprehension] is what is removed by ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists in the non-apprehension of reality (*tattva*).
And that [ignorance] is eternal with respect to Brahman;
nor is there anyone other than Brahman for whom the non-apprehension of reality regarding Brahman would be removed by knowledge obtained through effort.
But in the case of Brahman, simultaneous apprehension and non-apprehension are contradictory;
or, if they were not contradictory, ignorance would never be removed.
However, for one for whom ignorance is the apprehension of the contrary, [this is not the case].
If that nature belongs to Brahman, how could it be revoked if it is eternal?
If it does not belong to its nature, then it would become something else;
and it must be stated to what [else] that [nature] would belong.
Because there is no other than Brahman;
if it is argued that it is Brahman itself [that acts], there is a contradiction.
Because it is of the very nature of knowledge;
or, if there is no contradiction, by what could its cessation be brought about?
To this it is replied:
Ignorance is not the intrinsic nature of Brahman, nor is it something other than it;
it is neither absolutely non-existent, nor is it existent.
In this very way, this ignorance is called illusion (*māyā*) and false appearance (*mithyāvabhāsa*).
If it were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of anything— whether different or non-different from it— it would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) itself, and thus not ignorance.
If it were absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower, it would not be a factor in conventional discourse; therefore, it is indeterminable. All proponents of philosophical views must accept this.
For instance: according to the proponent of emptiness, the vision of things as they truly are regarding existence is not ignorance;
however, if [existence] were equivalent to a sky-flower, it would not be a constituent of conventional discourse.
Even for the proponent of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*), there is no denial of the object as long as cognition exists in accordance with its appearance;
for the forms of the objects of knowledge, such as blue and yellow, which appear externally, cannot be denied,
since it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to appear externally.
Like a flower in the sky:

even for those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), if the appearances of permanence and so forth regarding impermanent things, as well as errors such as [the perception of] silver, were to possess a real existence in their manifested form, they could not be classified as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor, if they were absolutely non-existent, could there be any worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) based upon them.
This might be the case:
let it be that the form appearing does not exist, but the appearance itself certainly exists.
And that [unreal appearance] is proclaimed to be ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is not the essence [of the matter];
for when that which appears does not exist, its very manifestation cannot be established as real.
There would be a mere appearance;
even the notion "that is its appearance" is nothing but an error.
Therefore, ignorance does not exist as a reality.
Nor is it non-existent;
for this very reason, its cessation is of a non-firm nature, because it is merely an illusion.

How could there be a change in that which is firmly established in a different intrinsic nature? For that would entail the loss of its own nature; moreover, in the case of emptiness, it has ceased of its own accord.
And thus, there is neither the loss of non-duality nor the absence of that which is to be removed;
as for the question of whose ignorance it is—
We say it is "of the individual souls" (jīvānām).
But surely the individual souls do not differ from Brahman?
For thus it is said:
"Having entered with this living self (jīva)";
this is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha),
yet they appear distinct through conceptual construction (kalpanā).
Of what, then, is conceptualization the differentiator?
It cannot be of Brahman, for that which consists of knowledge is devoid of conceptualization.
Nor does it belong to the individual souls (jīvas),
because those souls do not exist prior to conceptual construction (kalpanā), which would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence:
for the differentiation of individual souls is dependent upon conceptual construction.
Regarding the statement "the conceptual construction has the living being as its locus," some here say:
"The fault lies precisely in the establishment of a real entity."
A non-established entity is not capable of producing another entity,
nor is it [capable] in mere illusion;
for indeed, there is no logical impossibility within illusion.
For illusion (*māyā*) consists precisely in having an object that cannot be established;
if its object were established, it would not be an illusion because it would exist as it appears.
However, others [argue as follows]:

They explain that because both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the living being (*jīva*) are beginningless—like the continuum of seed and sprout—there is no mutual dependence that would result in a logical inconsistency.
Thus it has been stated by those who maintain that ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna*): "Ignorance is beginningless and purposeless."

In that regard, because it is beginningless, there is no fault of mutual dependence; and because it is purposeless, there is no occasion for questioning the purpose of the creation of the manifold diversity of distinctions.
As for what some question—
"Even a fool does not act without having a purpose in mind";
therefore, the purpose for the Supreme Brahman in creating the phenomenal world must be stated.
It cannot be the favoring of others.
Because there were no beings to be favored prior to creation, and because creation is characterized by subsequent suffering,
[the Lord's activity] is not for his own sake, nor for sport and the like.
"Because its desires have been fulfilled"—
if that [creation] were based on ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be no occasion for it;
for ignorance does not proceed by depending upon a purpose.
For illusions such as a city of the Gandharvas do not possess the aforementioned purpose;
likewise, the statement "there can be no impure modification of the pure Puruṣa" is also applied to the division of creation which is based upon ignorance (avidyā).
Moreover, it is only for those who have accomplished their purpose and whose desires are fulfilled that engagement in play and the like arises from a sense of exuberance;
however, for those whose minds are dragged down by longing and who are devoid of delight, such play is simply undesirable.
Furthermore, there is no fault of partiality or cruelty.
For there is no distinction of passion or aversion in a magician who displays various elaborations according to the division of their parts being complete or incomplete;
nor is there any such distinction in those who create various paintings from clay, wood, and so forth, according to the difference between them being finished or unfinished;
nor is there any inequality or cruelty in children playing with various figurines made of clay and other materials.
The teachers maintain that there is no fault in [the Lord] ordaining diversity in accordance with the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*);
nor is there the fault of [the Lord] not being the Sovereign (*anīśvara*).
For a Master who bestows different fruits in accordance with the differences in service does not thereby cease to be the Master.
Likewise, even for that which is pure, there is an impure modification;
for there is no absolute lack of distinction between the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*),
otherwise the very relationship of primal nature and modification would not exist.

Just as the solid transformation of water, such as hailstones and the like, arises from its liquid state, so too should one contemplate the manifold diversity between material cause (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), such as the conscious scorpion arising from the unconscious cow dung; enough of this digression.
[Objection: But surely, since they are non-different from the reality of Brahman, living beings (*jīva*) must also be pure by nature.
How, then, can there be room for ignorance regarding these [reflections]? This is a trivial matter; for the reflection in swords and the like is not at all distinct from the bright original object.
And yet, in that case, impurities such as blackness find an opportunity;
if you argue that this is an illusion (*vibhrama*), then it is the same for living beings (*jīva*)— their impurity is likewise an illusion.
Otherwise, it has been stated that purity would indeed be difficult to attain.
This might be argued:
"Swords and the like are causes of error regarding the face; [but this is not the case here]."
Likewise, here too, a cause for the delusion must be stated; however, since the delusion is beginningless, it is as if searching for a cause is inappropriate.
And thus [it is asked]: "The activity of ignorance, like that in dreams and so forth—by what is it produced?"
Thus it was replied.
But surely, if innate ignorance is beginningless and without cause, how could it be destroyed?
All treatises indeed set out for the eradication of innate ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, the natural blackness of atoms of earth is superseded by color produced through baking (*pākaja*).
Now, one might object: "Let even something innate be removed through the encounter with some extraordinary cause."
But for the proponent of monism (*aikātmyavādin*), since that [object] does not exist as something adventitious, how could there be its cessation? Indeed,
knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot be the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), because if it were, there would be no opposition between it and ignorance (*avidyā*), as they would coexist.
Alternatively, if there were a contradiction [between ignorance and knowledge], the world would be eternally liberated due to the constant cessation [of ignorance];
nor can another adventitious knowledge serve as a contradictory remover,
because in the doctrine of non-dualism (aikātmyavāda), such a separate entity is impossible.
Furthermore, it is impossible for that which is adventitious to possess the nature of Brahman.
As it has been said:
"No one is able to eradicate innate ignorance."
For if there were an occurrence of a different characteristic, the inherent nature would perish in some cases.
"But there is no distinct cause for those who accept the doctrine of a single self.
To this, it is replied:
This has been stated: that living beings are defiled by ignorance, but not Brahman;
for the latter is eternally pure, of constant luminosity, and its nature is not adventitious.

Otherwise, even for one who has attained the state of Brahman, ignorance would not cease; in that case, there would be no liberation. Now, if it were the case that Brahman itself transmigrates and Brahman itself is liberated, [then this fault would follow].
If one were liberated, it would follow that everyone is liberated;
for it is Brahman itself that transmigrates through the perception of difference and is liberated through the perception of non-difference.
And for those whose minds are defiled by innate ignorance (*avidyā*), the cessation of that ignorance occurs through the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) as a distinct causal condition;
for there is no innate knowledge in individual souls (*jīva*s),
since it is indeed innate ignorance alone that exists.

There is the dissolution of that adventitious ignorance. Furthermore, although the individual souls (*jīvas*) are non-different from Brahman, the distinction between knowledge and ignorance is explained as being like that of an original object and its reflection.
By what means, then, is ignorance removed?

By means of the various practices taught in the scriptures— such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*), along with celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other such means— how so?

It is this very practice of meditation preceded by hearing and reflection directed toward the Self, regarding which it is said, "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*), wherein the entire manifold of difference has been negated.
That [knowledge] clearly sublates the perception of difference, which is its counter-correlate;
and while it dissolves the perception of difference by means of generality, it is itself dissolved as well.

Furthermore, hearing and the other [means of knowledge] do not have the cessation of other distinctions as their object by way of abandoning the distinction between the hearer, the hearing, and the object to be heard.
Rather, it is by way of generality;
and when even that has dissolved, his self shines forth, clear and perfectly pure.

Just as water turbid from contact with dust, when a powder of a specific substance is added, gathers up other particles of dust while being itself gathered up, thereby attaining its own state of clarity.

In the same way, when the perception of difference is dissolved through hearing and other means, the individual soul (jīva) abides in its own pure and perfectly cleansed nature, because of the absence of distinctions and because the difference residing therein has vanished.
Indeed, it is only through ignorance (avidyā) that the soul is divided from Brahman.
Upon the cessation of that [limitation], one becomes the very nature of Brahman;
just as when the distinctions such as a jar are removed, the space within them becomes the pure, supreme space itself.
This might be so—
How is differentiation itself withdrawn by means of differentiation?
Because it serves as the antidote to differentiation, just as dust [is removed] by dust.
Thus it has been said.

It is quite evident that even when there is a lingering connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), the repeated practice of hearing, reflection, and meditation serves as the antidote to the perception of duality within Brahman, which is itself beyond all differentiation.
Just as milk digests other milk while digesting itself as well.
And just as one poison neutralizes another poison and itself subsides,
as it has been said:
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together..."
"Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge."
This is what is meant:
both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are conjoined because they stand in the relationship of means and end;
there is no arising of knowledge without ignorance.
If it is then argued that [the relationship] must be established,
and thus impermanence follows from the state of being produced, he says in response:
"By means of ignorance, death..."
This is the meaning:
ignorance is not the means for attaining knowledge;
rather, it is through ignorance—characterized by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—that ignorance itself is brought to cessation.
Death is said to be ignorance itself.

When that [ignorance] has ceased, one attains immortality—which is characterized by the nature of knowledge—and abides in one's own true form, just as a crystal gem, through the removal of the coloring caused by its dependence on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), remains in its own nature without requiring any further effort.
Thus, one abides in the very essence of knowledge.
The meaning is this: ignorance does not exist as something merely devoid of knowledge.
For it is thus:
Even the perception of difference is not devoid of manifestation;
in its absence, difference would not be manifest.
Therefore, it is the Supreme Manifestation itself that manifests in such and such ways.
As it has been said:
"Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
However, [the individual soul] is bound by ignorance (avidyā).
As it has been said:
"The internal person (puruṣa) conceives of all perception—which is non-deficient and free from conceptual construction—as if it were conceptually constructed.
Likewise, knowledge characterized by the hearing of the identity [of the self] and so forth does not exist without ignorance (avidyā).
Because it is bound up with the distinctions of the hearer, the hearing, and so forth;

therein, by means of ignorance alone—which is proximate to knowledge—there is the perception of distinction. Having crossed over that ignorance, one abides in the eternal true nature characterized by knowledge, just as water turbidified by a reflection becomes clear upon the cessation of that [reflection].
It might be argued as follows:
since division is unreal within the context of a single self (aikātmya),
how could hearing and the other [means of knowledge], which are based upon that [division], lead to any result for anyone?
Furthermore, the apprehension of the real from the unreal is itself false,
just as [the apprehension of] smoke is [false] when it is mistakenly perceived as such from vapor. To this, it is replied:
This is not an absolute rule—
that what is unreal cannot serve any purpose;
for illusion (māyā) indeed becomes the cause of both pleasure and fear.
And the unreal is the means for the realization of the real,
just as a line-drawn cow or written letters [are the means for understanding the actual cow or the meaning].
This might be so—
This [world] is real by its own nature and not empty;
however, for the proponents of monism (aikātmyavādins), even the means [of knowledge] are unreal by their own nature.
It is said in reply:
Let things be real by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*);
however, that form in which they are presented [to cognition] is unreal.
The reality of intrinsic nature, when devoid of utility for a purpose (*kārya*), is useless.
Moreover, even the means for perceiving non-difference are not false in their own nature,
because Brahman alone is their true nature.
In that regard, Brahman itself, when bound by ignorance, serves as the means for attaining Brahman.
Just as lines and the like indicate letters and so forth by means of a form that does not actually exist— such as "this is the letter *ka*" or "this is a *gavaya*";
this is also the view of one who thinks:
A line-drawn cow is not the cause for the cognition of other [real] gavayas by way of their being gavayas, nor is a line [the cause for the cognition of letters] by way of their being letters;
rather, it is through similarity.
"A gavaya is like this," and [the convention regarding] the line:
"Upon seeing such a line, this letter is to be remembered."
This contradicts common worldly experience;
for instance,
in the world, children are indeed taught that lines are themselves letters, and they are designated as such without making a distinction between them.
This refers to the one who explains, "This is a gavaya," and the one who understands,
"This gavaya has been seen by me."
Likewise, the inference of an unseen cause of a reflection—situated in a specific location—from that unreal reflection is not false.
Furthermore, the comprehension of distinct objects from an eternal sound, which lacks divisions such as long and short, is not erroneous.
Similarly, a false snake-bite is a cause of death.
Consequently, the inference of death, fainting, and so forth [from a snakebite] is not false, just as it would not be from a real snakebite occurring at a different time and place.

However, for one for whom momentary cognition alone is the self, liberation is impossible because there can be no addition or removal [of qualities]; thus, the scriptures on liberation and the activities undertaken for the sake of liberation would be rendered futile.
Because that which is momentary extinguishes by its own inherent nature,
and because no further excellence can be imparted to it;
for in a single moment, there is no distinction between a state of being qualified and unqualified.
Because a moment is indivisible. If it is thought that there exists something to be added to or removed from the continuum, that is incorrect.
The transmigrating being is both the agent and the enjoyer;

nor can the continuum (saṃtati) be the agent or the enjoyer, because it is not a real entity. Furthermore, how could liberation and bondage belong to that which is non-existent? Now, if it is thought:
The continuum is neither absolutely non-existent nor existent;
rather, it exists through conceptual construction.
Therefore, treatises and activities exist for the sake of liberation from that.
If so, it is the imagined [nature] that transmigrates and is liberated;
and both transmigration and liberation, having the imagined as their object, are themselves merely imagined.
Is this which we are saying not acceptable to you? This has been stated:
saṃsāra and liberation have only the imagined as their object, not the supreme ultimate reality.
Moreover, even if one were to admit that consciousness is momentary, liberation and saṃsāra must still be admitted as belonging to a continuum (*saṃtati*) that is indeed without beginning or end.
For thus:
because the continuum is beginningless and because saṃsāra is not a [substantial] entity, there is no [actual] arising.
There is no annihilation, because [the continuum] lacks substantial reality and because a final moment is logically untenable.
For does that final moment initiate some effect or not?
If it initiates one, it is not "final"; thus, due to its absence, there is no annihilation.
In the absence of undertaking (*anārambha*), there is non-existence because it lacks all causal capacity and possesses the characteristic of non-being.
When that [undertaking] is absent, all the members of the continuum (*santānin*) would likewise be non-existent by this very same sequence.
In the absence of those, the continuum itself does not exist.
Of what is there cessation?
Now, if the final [moment] indeed initiates an effect in another continuum that is omniscient,
then, given the existence of the causal relationship, how can there be a different continuum?
There is nothing other than the relation of cause and effect that establishes a single continuum;
nor is there an establishment of a single continuum based merely on the relation of cause and effect,
but rather on the relation of cause and effect as appropriation (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, the final moment of an omniscient one's cognition is not its material cause (*upādāna*);
for that [final moment] is an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
whereas the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the material cause.
And omniscient knowledge is produced by an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) that has fallen within one's own continuum;
its objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is the final moment.
If the material cause (upādāna) is of a similar nature, [then it follows...]
There is no similarity of kind between the liberated mind and omniscient gnosis;
even for one who thinks that the cessation of the continuum occurs when the effect is of a different character, [this is not so].

In the case of a continuous stream of cognition of form, there would be the undesirable consequence of nirvāṇa due to the cognition of another object. How could there be no nirvāṇa when the mind is uniform? Enough of this excessive elaboration.
However, some—

Desiring the reality of the Self to possess the quality of consciousness while having non-consciousness as its intrinsic nature, they assert that its abiding in a state where all specific qualities have been uprooted is the attainment of Brahman.
For that state of his, being unconditioned by limiting adjuncts such as the body and senses, is vast and is thus celebrated as "Brahman.

Furthermore, if its nature were consciousness, then since it is omnipresent, independent of the body and senses, eternal, and of the very essence of knowledge, the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) would become even vaster due to the presence of various distinct objects of cognition.
If, on the other hand, it does not cognize anything at all, then it is not of the nature of cognition;
for the meaning of the verb "to know" is transitive and is not logically applicable when there is no connection with an object.
He replies to them:
"Consciousness.
Why? For it is heard [in scripture]:
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; "consciousness and bliss," and so forth.
Nor is the aforementioned defect present.
Just as fire, though it is a burner, burns only that combustible object which is brought near to it, and not that which is not brought near or that which is not combustible;
and just as crystal, mirrors, and the like, though clear and luminous by nature, display only that which is placed before them and is suitable for reflection, by means of the falling of its shadow.

Thus, this person, residing in a body which is the locus of experience, enjoys sounds and other objects presented by the sense organs—the instruments of experience—even though his consciousness is eternal; this occurs through the reflection of those objects [upon it]. And for this reason, there is no consequence of everyone being omniscient.
Furthermore, there is no enjoyment of external objects in liberation.
It might be argued: "Since [the soul] is omnipresent, everything exists as its object."
In this regard, what is to be brought forward? It is said:

even for that ignorant person for whom cognition of the self is produced by the conjunction of the mind [with the self], how can there be a restriction of experience, given that all minds are in conjunction with all selves?
For all objects exist as objects for this [consciousness] through the medium of its connection with the mind.
Now, since experience is bound by karma, the established order based on karma applies even to one who maintains that the self is of the nature of pure consciousness; it cannot be warded off.

Moreover, through the perfection of the vision of non-duality, when everything has become one's own self-nature (*ātman*), there is no seeing precisely because of the absence of an object to be seen. Even though its nature is that of a seer, it does not see, just as fire does not burn for lack of fuel;
nor does it possess the quality of illumination, just as light does not illuminate for lack of an object to be illuminated.
As it has been said:
"For there is no loss of the vision of the seer,
because of its imperishability.
But there is no second thing existing there, distinct and separate from it."
[The scriptures state] such things as "what one might see" and "but where for him everything has become the Self alone.
Furthermore, liberation, characterized by the cessation of specific qualities such as consciousness and so forth, does not differ from the position of annihilation;
for the absolute non-perception of even an existing thing is not distinguished from non-existence itself.
And who would desire the non-existence of the Self, which is dearer than anything else? Thus, liberation would be something that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).
This might be argued:
because it brings about the cessation of manifold sufferings, even the annihilation of the Self is desired by a person.
For indeed, those seized by severe diseases and evil are seen striving for their own destruction;
it is true that they bear a form as if composed of suffering, with all happiness uprooted by the growth of their ailments.
But this is not the case for those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), who partake in the various and manifold joys of gods and other beings.

In that regard, just as there is the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because of the cessation of various sufferings, so too there would be the status of not being a human goal because of the cessation of various pleasures.

However, for one who possesses the state of experiencing supreme bliss from which all attachment to suffering has been wiped away, that alone constitutes the absolute human goal; enough of this digression.
By the word "syllable" (akṣara), he expresses its nature as sound, because a particular [term] characterizes the general; or else, it denotes its state of being unchanging.

Because, upon transformation, there is the cessation of the previous dharma and the existence of a momentary state, how can there be the nature of sound by excluding that [momentariness]? How so? [KKS_17] First, regarding its being of the nature of sound:
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The syllable Om is the higher and the lower Brahman," and so forth;
nor does this depend upon a denoted object, since a word ending in the suffix -kāra refers to the very form of the word itself.
The suffix *kāra* is also observed following a group of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) even when preceded by a non-vowel (*avarṇa*), as in:
"What is the purpose of the word *evakāra*?
and "What is the purpose of the letter *ca*? (*cakāra*)?
But do they not explain this quite differently—as follows:
since Brahman, which transcends all particularities, cannot be an object of meditation, this is an instruction regarding a symbol (*pratīka*);
one should meditate upon Brahman by means of this support (*ālambana*).
Just as because direct worship of a deity is impossible, one performs the rite of worship upon its emblem— whether in wood or stone— with the thought that it is the deity itself,
so too the meditator thinks, "That deity is pleased by this. Or rather, by this designation, that which is to be meditated upon [is indicated].
Because the *praṇava* is the designation for that [Self].
It is said:
"Meditate upon the Self as 'Om'."
The rule "one should apply oneself with 'Om'" applies only where the status of being a limb of yoga (*yogāṅgatā*) is explicitly heard;
however, where such [an injunction] as "one should apply oneself" is not heard, the sentence culminates in identity itself, and there it is not thus.
As it is said: "Om is Brahman; Om is all this.

For here, by showing that the syllable Om is the essence of speech through its pervasion of all speech and its non-abandonment thereof, and because the manifold of forms does not abandon the nature of speech—

He concludes with the statement, "The syllable Om is indeed all this. Even where there is the scriptural hearing, "By means of this very [syllable], one should meditate upon the Supreme Person," [the same applies].
Furthermore, that [attainment] is preceded by the realization of the state of being the self of all;
nor is it logical to claim that this state of being the self of all is merely figurative for the sake of praise,
since there is no contradiction even if it is taken in its primary sense.
For it is not contradictory that this nature, which is not ascertainable through perception and other means, is accessible through scripture;
indeed, the non-comprehension [of an object] by one means of knowledge does not deprive another means of knowledge of its object.
Therefore, "the wise person."
Thus, this instruction on meditation is intended solely for one who knows the Self as all;
it is not for anyone else.
Therefore, the sentence reaches its conclusion immediately after that point.
Then, for one who has realized that universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*), there is the instruction on meditation (*dhyāna*).
Alternatively, in such passages as "Speech alone gave birth to all worlds; speech alone enjoyed this; speech spoke," the universal selfhood of Speech is heard in scripture.
Likewise, in the *Vāk-sūkta*, the fact that speech is the self of all and the ruler of all is demonstrated by speech itself: "I move with the Rudras and the Vasus."
Just as by Vāmadeva, who was awakened with respect to the Self, it was said: "I became Manu and Sūrya";
moreover, modifications are endowed with the form of their material cause.
And the world is endowed with the nature of speech;
therefore, it is understood as either a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of speech.
How is its conformity [to speech] established?
Because it is to be experienced as a cognition colored by that [object].

For indeed, everyone clearly perceives the difference between the comprehension of an object from a word and the cognition "there is fire here because of smoke," due to their having different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatā*).
Furthermore, it is so for this reason as well:
As for the relationship of qualifier and qualified that is perceived between two words, as in "a blue lotus," that belongs solely to the objects.
Otherwise,
just as in the case of "it is a post because it is a place where crows perch," there would be a cognition of a distinct object through two meanings that are mutually exclusive;
furthermore, just as with smoke, there would be no certainty of the word's identity when it serves as a cause for comprehension.
Furthermore, the certainty regarding fire derived from smoke or from another means of valid cognition does not conform to the form of smoke;
rather, certainty regarding objects derived even from another means of valid cognition conforms to the reflection of the form of the word.
Therefore, when there is comprehension from a word as well, the comprehension occurs in that same manner.
We do not conclude that this error is caused by an immediate antecedent condition;
for even in the case of infants, this activity directed toward the breast and so forth— avoiding other things—
could not occur unless they were determining "this is it."

When a post or a person has not been ascertained, no activity based on either one occurs; nor is ascertainment devoid of the coloring of speech. Thus, even for those who possess the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of speech from previous births, their cognition is ascertained as being colored by the very form of speech.
And so, we understand that the world, which is grasped through that form, is its transformation (*vivarta*).
Moreover, there are conventional objects whose reality is nothing other than a transformation of words;
by analogy with those, others as well should be understood in the same way.
Just as "one should act" and "one should not act" constitute injunctions and prohibitions, so too is the meaning of a sentence [established].
A collection [is one thing],
while non-existent things such as a circle of firebrands and the horns of a hare are another;
in that regard, injunctions and prohibitions do not pertain to past occurrences of engagement or withdrawal.
Nor does it exist in the present or in the two future times,
because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between "he cooked," "he cooks," and "he will cook."
If it is argued that [the object] is an effect (*kārya*), we say no; for "effect-ness" cannot be established apart from the three times.
Therefore, injunction and prohibition must be mere appearances (*pratibhāmātra*) without a real substrate (*avastuka*), conforming to engagement and withdrawal.
Furthermore, it is not logical that a manifestation (pratibhā) could be devoid of an objective support (anālambana), because its very nature is that of cognition;
nor is it devoid of the conceptual determination (parāmarśa) of the form of words.
Therefore, it is correct to conclude that the reality of speech (śabdatattva) itself appears in various ways in accordance with the inclination toward engagement or withdrawal.
Such is the meaning of the sentence:
a relation (*saṃsarga*) is nothing other than the relata (*saṃsargin*); it does not exist as something distinct from the nature of the related and unrelated entities.

Knowledge is not empty of the object of knowledge, nor is it a conceptual cognition devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of the form of speech; rather, it is logical that the reality of speech itself manifests in various such ways.
This same principle should be applied to collections such as forests and the like, as well as to non-existent things such as a whirling firebrand.

Moreover, although there is knowledge of the notes such as ṣaḍja and of things such as cows prior to the word, it is not of the same kind as that which occurs at a later time following the application of the word.
For prior comprehension is indeed undiscriminating, whereas later it becomes much clearer and possessed of discrimination;
likewise, cowherds, shepherds, and others establish designations for the sake of achieving discriminative knowledge.

Thus, because an excellence of understanding is observed regarding an object upon contact with sound, and because even things that have been mentally perceived become as if unperceived when that [sound] is obstructed— just as grass and such are disregarded by one walking on a path—
the state of being conscious for consciousness depends solely upon the form of speech; or rather, consciousness itself is simply the power of speech.
Some maintain that even when that [manifestation] is withdrawn, there remains a subtle power of speech (*vāk-śakti*).

In any case, since the cognition of the knowable depends upon the form of speech, it is understood that every object of knowledge is permeated by the form of speech; thus, the knowable is either a modification (*vikāra*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of that [speech], just as jars and other objects are of clay.
It is like the moon reflected in the waves of water.
Others, however, on account of the observation of examples such as clay and so forth, consider Brahman to be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
That is refuted by the word "imperishable" (akṣara).
Why? Because [the text says] "constant" (dhruvaḥ).
For it is heard in various places in the scriptures that [the Self] is eternal.
Now, if it is thought: "Even though there is transformation, its eternity is not contradicted because its true nature (tattva) remains unimpaired."
As it has been said:
"That which, even when undergoing modification, does not lose its essential nature—that too is eternal.
This is true.
Nevertheless, if that which is the pure nature of the Self were to undergo transformation in its entirety, it would follow that it is impermanent;
if it were to transform only in part, then because it would possess parts, its permanence and unity would be contradicted.
This very purity, permanence, and unity are possible only in Brahman, which is like space.
Even when there is a limitation imposed by conceptual construction, space remains indeed unlimited, even in its non-conceptualized aspect.
Furthermore, since the transformation of a single part that is conceptually constructed occurs through conceptualization alone, it is well said:
"the imperishable" (*akṣara*).
Some, based on such scriptural passages as "He who is all-fragrance, all-taste," have arrived at the conclusion that Brahman is the Self of all;
and thus, since the enjoyment of objects is possible, it is logical that objects belong to the Self whose nature is luminosity.
If they were to manifest themselves;
for otherwise, the manifestation of insentient things would be impossible.
To those [who hold such a view], he says: [KKS_20]—
"It is not the whole.
Why? Because of the negation of all limiting attributes (*uparāga*) through the statement, "It is neither gross, nor subtle, nor short."
Furthermore, because it is inseparable from all distinctions, there would be no liberation;
for it is impossible to separate a thing from its own nature, just as fire cannot be separated from heat.

Moreover, even if it were somehow separated [from its attributes], since the continuity of the manifold of difference would not be severed and thus separation would be impossible, there would be eternal transmigratoriness.
In every respect, this Self has the manifold of hunger, thirst, and so forth as its very nature.
Furthermore, the cessation of its conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is not admitted.
In that regard, for the proponent of a single self (ekātmyavādin), there is no liberation;

however, for the proponent of distinct selves (ātmabhedavādin), there is a distinction between the liberated and those in saṃsāra, such that for one the [proliferation] is severed while for another it is not.
Therefore, Brahman does not consist of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*); it is established that the phenomenal world is merely the play of ignorance (*avidyā*).
If, then, the phenomenal world is indeed the play of ignorance, [what follows?]
In that case, the emptiness of conceptual proliferation (prapañca-śūnyatā) is the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Let that alone be Brahman,
because it is the ultimate reality.
And thus, its very nature is made known precisely through the negation of all phenomenal elaborations (prapañca), as in: "This is that— 'not this,
not this'," and "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short."
Regarding this, he says: "all.
This is what is meant:
Brahman does not possess the nature of being the self of all; rather, everything has Brahman as its self,
being possessed of form by way of the form of Brahman.

But it is not emptiness alone [that is the self], because that would entail the consequence of its being eternally liberated, which in turn entails the consequence of the futility of engaging in the teaching of that goal.
If it is argued that even if it were eternally liberated, saṃsāra would still be based on ignorance (avidyā):
If non-apprehension is ignorance, how then can cyclic existence be based upon it?
For that [non-apprehension] would be equally present even in liberation.
In that very case, nothing at all would be manifest.
Alternatively, if ignorance is the apprehension of things as they are not,
then there is no universal emptiness.
Because of the Vedic scripture, "By that Person all this is filled," and because of the teaching of the Self in everything, "The Self alone is all this."
Furthermore, because emptiness itself is denied in the statement, "How could that which is non-existent arise?
for an entity indeed appears as something superimposed with a non-existent form when it does not manifest according to its true nature.
But if it were empty, where could there be superimposition, and what could be manifested? Thus, there would be a total absence of causal seed.
[The Upanishad says: "Consciousness is bliss."
Thus, because of this teaching regarding form (*rūpa*), Brahman is not merely the non-existence of everything,
but rather the Self of all. However,
some maintain that since pure happiness is never observed and is invariably accompanied by suffering, there is no state free from contact with suffering.
For no living being is perceived as being exclusively happy, nor exclusively suffering;
rather, it is only for one who possesses suffering that pleasure remains established as pleasure.
The touch of sandalwood is pleasant only to one who is suffering from heat;
regarding this, he says:
"Fearlessness."
For the state of Brahma is entirely free from all fear,
and not even the slightest affliction exists therein,
since one has heard repeatedly that it is without fear.
"Brahman is indeed fearlessness," and so forth.
For indeed, fear does not belong to Brahman by its very nature, because that would contradict its nature as bliss.
That which is adventitious cannot possess a cause, because of the absence of a second [entity];
as it has been said: "Verily, from a second [entity] fear arises."
Furthermore, pleasure is not of the nature of the cessation of suffering, such that pleasure would remain as pleasure only for one who is suffering; this has already been explained at length above.
There is another way:
In this regard, some maintain that even those considered liberated are subject to the fear of returning;
for here, the conscious selves (vijñānātman) must be either distinct from Brahman or non-distinct.
They might be divided either by Brahman itself— for the sake of enjoyment, for the sake of sport, for the sake of manifesting its power, or from its own nature—
or else this division is based upon ignorance; or rather,
it is the cognitional selves themselves that are denoted by the word "Brahman."
Brahman is not something other than these;
for them, saṃsāra is bound by karma and ignorance, or else it is bound by the mutual compatibility between the seer and the seen.

In that case, if [the manifestation] is based on fitness (*yogyatā*), then because fitness is never lost, the fear of recurrence (*punarāvṛtti*) remains unabated. Alternatively, if there is no recurrence because the task has already been accomplished,
then once sound and so forth have been perceived once, they would not be perceived again.
Now, if primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which possesses infinite modifications, ceases to be perceived in its entirety upon the realization [of the Self],
yet continues to function for the sake of perceiving other unmodified forms,

then— precisely because of its infinity— it would be impossible to perceive it in its entirety; consequently, even for one who possesses the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*), a return to worldly existence might be possible.

Even if [the cycle] is bound by karma preceded by ignorance, because karma is infinite in this beginningless saṃsāra and because its time of fruition is not fixed, the fear of relapse does not cease even in the state of liberation, just as it did during the state of cosmic dissolution (pratisarga). Furthermore, even if it is bound by ignorance, since that ignorance is itself causeless and its activity is purposeless, who can prevent its repeated recurrence in exactly the same way?

And likewise, a return from the attainment of Brahman is observed in deep sleep. However, in the case of an independent Brahman, it is not possible for the differentiated individual souls—whether they were previously separated or united—to undergo differentiation again through causes such as bodily enjoyments;
for an independent Lord, like a worldly ruler, might bind them again either for sport, to manifest His sovereignty, or by His very nature.
Now, if this [bondage] depends upon karma, he has no independence over karma;

nevertheless, because karma is infinite and because there is no fixed rule for the time of its ripening, it is possible that even after the passing of hundreds of eons, one may again be bound by those karmas whose time for ripening has arrived.
Since the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) does not pertain to only one single birth— for its manifestation is not caused by death alone, but also by place, time, and other factors—
it is as follows:

Even in a single body, the enjoyment of the fruits of karma is observed to occur sequentially; for it is impossible for karmas that cause the experience of contradictory births to arise and cease simultaneously,
and because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of liberation for those who die in the womb without having performed any karma.
[Regarding] the consequence of liberation—
this is stated therein: "fearlessness."
For this attainment of peace is heard to be supreme;
in it there is no longer any fear of saṃsāra.
Indeed, rebirth in saṃsāra is no longer caused by karma.
For even infinite karmas whose fruits have not yet been experienced are exhausted by knowledge, just as they are by expiatory rites.
Indeed, it has been said:
"The fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes in that same way."
Likewise, it is said: "And his karmas are exhausted.
Alternatively, when ignorance is removed by knowledge, the distinction between agent, action, and fruit is indeed dissolved;
how then could such a distinction possibly arise for him?
Nor is it caused by ignorance, because there is no cause for its arising;
for ignorance is indeed beginningless.
Precisely because it is beginningless, it does not depend upon a cause;
for the operation of a cause occurs with respect to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*),
and if prior non-existence were absent, when would the cause ever operate?
For there is no causal function for that which already exists;
however, ignorance, having been severed [from its cause] though previously non-existent, as it now proceeds, cannot proceed without a cause.
In deep sleep, however, only the state of distraction has ceased.
The impressions of that [state] and the non-perception [of objects] do not cease once [the state] has ended;
otherwise, it would not differ from the fourth [turīya].
However, the designation "attainment of Brahman" is used because of the mere absence of distraction.
Therefore, it is well said:
"fearless. By what means of valid cognition, moreover, is this meaning fully realized?
It cannot be established by perception, because that has as its object a difference contrary to this;
nor can it be established by inference.
Because it is preceded by that;
nor by comparison (upamāna),
because its object is similarity.
And because that [difference] is the locus of differentiation;
whereas presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) applies to the contrary case,
since no linguistic convention whatsoever is possible without difference.
For non-difference is difficult to comprehend without the distinction between the knower and so forth;
nor is non-existence sufficient for the comprehension of the reality that is the nature of existence,
nor even for the comprehension of the non-existence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
Since that [self] is impossible while perception and the other means of knowledge exist,

scripture (*āgama*)— as long as it is composed by a trustworthy author (*āpta*)— does not apply here either, because its scope consists of objects already apprehended by other means of valid cognition.
Nor is it independent,
because it consists of affirmation and negation,
and those two are impossible when reality is established.
Nor is validity established solely with respect to an already existing object independent of that [scripture],
because if it were a mere restatement of what has occurred, it would depend on other means of knowledge;
