furthermore, the comprehension of a word's expressive power comes from common usage in the world.
In that regard, words are employed with reference to objects connected to an action solely for the sake of that action, because they possess meaning only in that way;
for there is no purpose whatsoever in speech devoid of engagement or withdrawal.
Moreover, the comprehension of the relationship of a word does not arise from the mere restatement of what has already occurred,
but rather from that which prompts action;
for it is through activity that one infers the cognition of the object, and thereby perceives the word's capacity [to denote it].
And thus, the capacity of words is not perceived with respect to objects that are devoid of a connection to activity.
This being so, how could words whose efficacy is uncomprehended convey that [past] object?
Furthermore, if that object were already determined by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [then the word would be redundant].
In that case, verbal testimony has no authority; if it is not established, then even less so,
because if it is not the meaning of a word, it is impossible for it to be the object of a sentence.
For it is the word-meaning (*padārtha*) itself that becomes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) by virtue of being qualified.

However, that which is absolutely unperceived and not understood from the word cannot, whether as a subordinate or a primary factor, enter into the sentence-meaning, which consists of the relation between word-meanings. Moreover, a reality in which all limitations have dissolved is simply beyond the scope of cognition.
For every practice proceeds by means of exclusion, [determining] "it is thus" or "it is not thus."
Otherwise, no one would have attained realization.
To the question, "But how can there be realization when all specific distinctions have vanished? he says:
"The poets declare that its establishment is through sacred tradition (āmnāya) and common renown."
And its definition is by way of the dissolution of the proliferation of distinctions.
It will be explained later that even though it speaks of things as they truly are, that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) is not dependent [on anything else].
Furthermore, not all utterances in the world have as their ultimate aim only what is to be done (kārya); for instance, there are also pleasant reports.
"By good fortune you prosper;
a son has been born to you"—
this [statement] leads neither to engagement nor to withdrawal.
Furthermore, purposes for the production of happiness are observed;
yet, one does not find an injunction such as "become happy" regarding them,
because since that [happiness] is established through the very power of the thing itself, no such instruction is required.
Now, it might be thought: there is indeed a specific activity directed toward that [object], and the verbal expression has its purport (tātparya) therein.
True;
the intentionality pertains to the production [of the cognition], not to its apprehension.
Practice, however, must be grounded solely in the true nature of reality (*bhūtārtha*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to postulate that the operation of a word—which culminates in the true nature of reality—has its limit of application in mere activity (*pravṛtti*), even when that word possesses a purpose.
Moreover, a person who has not yet engaged with the means (*upāya*) is urged to engage with it.
Alternatively, because the means were unknown, he had not previously applied himself toward the goal; [the teaching] is directed toward that goal by way of making known the means.
In this case, it is first of all not directed toward the means—the birth of a son—because that has already been accomplished.
Nor is there pleasure therein, because there is no other activity directed toward that purpose.
Likewise, the words of wicked people— unpleasant reports intended to cause despondency— do not instruct one toward either engagement or withdrawal, according to the same principle as before.

Likewise, in the case of one who is coiled by a rope but considers himself to be coiled by a snake, the communication of the truth is seen for the purpose of removing his fear; however, in that situation, there is no injunction such as "Do not be afraid."

For an injunction (*niyoga*) exists only where, having understood the purpose of the injunction, a person subsequently engages or desists through conscious deliberation, either by the force of the injunction or by desire.
In this case, however, fear ceases for that person simply from the realization of reality; because he does not depend on the desire for an injunction, there is no other cause [for his cessation].
Furthermore, once fear has ceased, a person who has spontaneously engaged [in activity] for the sake of that human goal is not one to be enjoined;
nor is he to be enjoined regarding the means to that [cessation], namely, the realization of reality, as in the case of [knowing] "it is a rope."

This is because that [cognition] arises from the word itself—as in "It is not a snake"—and because any subsequent operation following the comprehension of the word's meaning is dependent upon an injunction.

Likewise, reports of events occurring in distant places, intended for those who ask out of curiosity, culminate in the description of facts as they actually are; they do not serve for rejection or acquisition.
Furthermore, even in a case where there is the possibility of rejection or acceptance upon the comprehension of the actual state of affairs—
as in the thought, "This path is beset by obstacles"—
"This plot of land contains a treasure-trove";
even there, it is the word that functions in the acts of rejection and acquisition, because the actual object itself is imperceptible.

Having understood from a word an object that has come into being, and having recollected its status as a cause of benefit or a cause of harm as apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one engages out of desire or desists out of aversion.
Now, the speaker, acting with prior deliberation, employs speech for the sake of inducing the listener’s engagement or desistance;
thus, it culminates precisely in engagement and desistance.
For this [reason] must be applied there, yet it is not applied; likewise, "one should not go by this path. Thus:
"Take this treasure from here"—
this [example] is not essential [to the point].

For even a statement that culminates in a factual matter (bhūtārtha) does not have its status as an auxiliary to engagement or withdrawal obstructed, by way of making that factual matter known, just as is the case with perception and other means of knowledge.

Perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whose functions are fully occupied with the apprehension of real objects (*bhūtārtha*), do not abandon their status as factors for engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), even if they do not make these engagements and withdrawals their direct objects to any significant degree;
the same applies to verbal testimony (*śabda*). Thus, nothing is impaired.
If it is argued that engagement and withdrawal are intended by the speaker (*prayoktṛ*), [then we reply:]...
The meaning of a word does not derive from the intention of the speaker, but rather from its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Otherwise, even the attainment of various human goals through the discovery of a hidden treasure would be the meaning of that word, since it too was intended by him.
And when something is sought to be known through perception and other means with a view toward either engagement or withdrawal, [it is understood through the word's capacity].
Even when directed toward those [objects], activity and cessation do not have as their objects of cognition (*prameya*) things such as direct perception;
even when directed toward those, activity and cessation do not have as their objects the meaning of words.
And for this reason also, it is so: [itaścaitadevam (itaśca tadevam—edition)].
If sound were the meaning, then everyone would have the cognition of grasping it,
whereas for another there might be indifference;
however, if sound were the meaning, there would indeed be only the cognition of grasping it for all.
Nor is the comprehension of the relationship derived solely from the linguistic usage of injunctive sentences, such that it would be understood as being dependent exclusively upon activity;
for it is observed to be otherwise as well.

When one who has not yet mastered the meaning of the word *kāṣṭha* (wood), but has mastered the meanings of the other words, and has mastered the meaning of the case-ending, perceives that which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the action of cooking in the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood," he then understands that [wood] to be the meaning of the nominal stem *kāṣṭha*.
Likewise, mastery [of meaning] arises regarding the causes of joy, grief, and relief from statements that report reality, through the experience of joy and so forth.
For just as, from the observation of a specific activity, a cognition of that specific activity or a cognition of its cause is inferred—
and since no other cause exists and it follows immediately after the word, the capacity of the word to produce it is postulated—
so too, from the perception of joy and so forth, there is an inference of a cognition of the cause of that joy and so forth.
Furthermore, because the word follows immediately after [the event], one infers the capacity of the word for that purpose;

and since the cause of joy— the birth of a son— has been understood through another means of knowledge and no other [cause] exists, one concludes that this sentence, "A son has been born to you," was uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) with reference to that birth of a son.
Furthermore, he determines that from this very sentence, the birth of a son has been understood by him;

thus, through both the application [of the word] and the cognition [it produces], he perceives the capacity of the sentence for this meaning. Or, let it be that in common worldly usage all speech possesses the quality of being an instigator [of action].
And from that, the comprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] arises.
Nevertheless, this must be investigated: do words other than the injunctive term have as their sole purpose their own individual meanings, or...
Is it rather intent upon the connection between the purpose and the object, or intent upon the connection between word-meanings alone?
In that regard, if there were a finality in the mere word-meaning itself, there would be an absence of cognition of the sentence-meaning and the employment [of the sentence] would be rendered futile.
Therefore, the intention is merely the connection with another object.
Since the application and the cognition are established by that much alone, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a connection with a specific [object].
For whoever imagines a connection with a specific [object], [does so without basis].
He imagines a connection with another object;
and thus, even in the absence of an actual effect, the cognition of a specific real object is established through the mutual association of word-meanings.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way.

Otherwise, since in the world the connection between word-meanings is subordinate to the speaker's intention, in the absence of such intention, there would be no comprehension of the Vedic meaning in the Veda. Moreover, if all words were connected only with the "thing-to-be-done" (kārya), there would be no mutual relationship between the word-meanings themselves.
In that case, the injunction (niyoga) would not be understood as having a qualified object;
it would instead have to be accomplished by a single word-meaning alone. Alternatively, the injunction would not be directed toward the application (viniyoga).
Because it has a specific object;
therefore, first there is the application (viniyoga), and afterwards the injunction (niyoga).

What follows from this? Even when there is a connection between word-meanings that exceeds the scope of the mandate (niyoga), the word possesses the capacity for such connection independently of the mandate, because there is a connection with the mandate [only] after the meanings have been mutually connected.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the relation [between word-meanings] is not based on a requirement for the mandate.

Even that which has not been apprehended by another means of knowledge, and whose relation [to its denotation] has not been previously apprehended, can be defined by its own word through the negation of specific particulars;
for the connection of specific words and the negative particle with their respective objects is already known.
And thus it is taught in this very manner:
The phrase "not gross" indicates that which transcends all particularities;
it expresses this by means of the dissolution of the manifold of differentiation.
And this will be explained;
it has another meaning,
as it was said:
If it is argued that reality, in which all particularities have subsided, is not an object of cognition at all,
it is replied:
by the very cessation of particularities, that [reality] is established in the intellect by means of words.
It is like the reality of gold.
For the reality of gold is not seen apart from the obscuration of various differences in shape, such as a lump or a bracelet;
nor are those [shapes] themselves the reality of gold.
Even when that [specific configuration] is abandoned, because it exists in another configuration, and furthermore,

even though the distinction from the superimposition of unseen differences in configuration is not perceived by the senses, it is itself cognized by the intellect through the exclusion of difference and is communicated to another.
This very sequence of practice has been shown by the Śruti itself in the passage: "He is 'not this, not this'";
likewise by others.
"Truth is that which remains at the end when the collection of forms is withdrawn";
likewise by others:
"The world of manifoldness, though free from manifoldness, is explained through superimposition and negation."
This is now being investigated:
does the entire sacred tradition (āmnāya) define Brahman by way of dissolving the manifold of difference, or is it only a certain portion thereof?
Regarding this, some say:
In every part of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the dissolution of some particular distinction is perceived in certain places,
as for example, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
Thus ends the dissolution of the identification with the body.
For here, the qualified candidate is understood to be one capable of experiencing heaven as distinct from the body;
therefore, there is a dissolution of the identification of the self with the body.

Likewise, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel," there is a dissolution of the distinction between different eligible persons due to the qualification of those already authorized.
Similarly, even in the injunctions of prescriptions and prohibitions, there is a dissolution of natural activities rooted in passion and the like;
this occurs directly in the case of prohibitions.
In ritual injunctions, [the agent is directed] by means of an internal mandate (*niyoga*) within the engagement with the rite;
even in the world, there is either a direct prevention from an undesired path, or [prevention] by means of instruction regarding another, beneficial path.

And thus, by means of dissolving the various natural tendencies rooted in passion and the like through the very [performance of] visible rites, the injunctions of action become useful for the qualification for self-knowledge.
For it is taught that the vision of the Self belongs to one who is tranquil, self-controlled, and composed.
And it is possible;
for one who is being dragged away by sense objects, with their mind intent on engaging in the means to obtain them, is unable to concentrate upon the self.
But one who has desisted from natural inclinations and possesses a restrained mind is qualified for the vision of the self.
By implication,
others think as follows:
one whose desires are unfulfilled and whose mind is afflicted by desire is not fit for the vision of supreme non-duality.
But by means of ritual actions performed for a thousand years that destroy all desires, one attains the supreme non-duality, the Self, which is beyond the station of Prajāpati.
In both of these views, the entire sacred tradition culminates solely in the knowledge of the Self. This is the perspective of others:
Indeed, ritual injunctions, while having distinct purposes of their own, lead a person to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self,
because one who has not discharged the three debts lacks that qualification—
as it is said: "Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation."

Others, however, maintain that through the principle of "separateness-in-union" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*), all ritual actions indeed enter into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, based on the scriptural texts: "They desire to know [Brahman] by means of sacrifice," and "By whatever [means] one may sacrifice— even with a mere ladle-oblation— one becomes one whose mind is unimpaired."
Others, however, describe actions as being for the purpose of human refinement (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), insofar as they touch upon the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-adhikāra*),

citing such passages as: "By the great sacrifices and by the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman (*brāhmī kriyate tanuḥ*)," and "He who possesses these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the eight qualities of the self."
Others, however, describe this very point in the opposite way,

[claiming] that the knowledge of the Self alone, by way of purifying the agent, enters into the qualification for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*). Still others, however, consider that there is no connection whatsoever between ritual action and the knowledge of the Self, as they are mutually contradictory, having respectively duality and non-duality as their objects.
In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable.
For injunctions concerning ritual action and the like do not require another objective once their own effects, such as heaven, have been understood from their respective sentences.

Nor does the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, which has no further expectancy once its means—such as celibacy and the rest as previously described—are established, depend upon the injunctions for ritual action.
In that case, how can there be a single common subject matter?
If one should think that the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karman*) and so forth have not yet been understood— [that is, they remain unknown]— then [the objection stands].
"Because heaven and so forth are connected as qualities"— with this [reasoning],

one should explain the *svargakāmādhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, if all injunctions and prohibitions were to culminate in liberation through the dissolution of name and form (*nāmarūpa-pravilaya*), then the prosperity and misfortune of living beings would have no cause in their actions and would be accidental.

In that case, liberation would also [be attained through ritual action], and thus the scripture would be rendered useless. Now, if it is argued that the injunctions for ritual action enter into the domain of knowledge by means of effects such as heaven— just as instructions on traveling along a road enter into the instruction for reaching a desired city—
that is incorrect.
It is appropriate that the instruction for reaching an undesired place follows from the attainment of a village on the way;
for in instructions regarding villages along the path, there is no attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Therefore, because it leaves a sense of expectancy, [the teaching] leads to where the human goal is attained.
They enter into that [realm],
yet there is no such lack of attainment of human purpose (puruṣārtha) in the ritual injunctions for action, because heaven and so forth are desired by the person.
And in that case, when there is no further expectancy, how can there be an entry into another [instruction]? Now, if it is thought:

"When one is led by persuasion through the presentation of ever-increasing qualities of villages to a desired destination, then the instructions regarding the previous villages, having achieved their intended purpose, enter into other subsequent instructions."
Even in that case, it is appropriate [to accept the word as a means of knowledge], because the speaker's intention is apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For by means of another *pramāṇa*, this is apprehended there: "When he has reached this place, this desired object of the speaker will be accomplished."
Therefore, this is what he intends to say,
and not merely by following the literal occurrence of the words.
For this reason as well, it is so: [KKS 29] since,

in every village, when there is a correspondence between the meaning and the speaker and the listener, bystanders who are recipients understand those very previous instructions and previous meanings— even though the intention to reach another place has not been apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And [he gave] instruction for others' sake that was focused on his own interest;
although, according to the actual state of things, the meanings of his previous instructions were beneficial to others, nevertheless, that was not the intended purport of his words.

Just as in the case of the injunctions regarding the acquisition of wealth and so forth, [the purpose] here also lies in assisting the meaning of the ritual injunction; for the intended meaning follows the literal function of the words,
since there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition.
Moreover, in the case of instructions regarding a route to a village, one proceeds there and achieves the goal only by determining that those instructions have that [destination] as their purpose.
However, when the purpose is merely the arrival at the foreign region, proceeding by that specific route is not mandatory;
for since the intended meaning is simply the attainment of that place, one may go by any other path as well.

Nor is there a necessary attainment of the meaning [of the injunction], because even the hearing of a purpose in passages intended for something else is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Therefore, in this case, if the injunctions and prohibitions were intent upon other actions, [the result would not follow].
They do not have heaven and so forth as their effects.
Indeed, an effect such as heaven is not equivalent to an effect such as the *prayāja* offerings, such that it would entail another effect.
And how is it to be stated that [the prohibitions] assist the qualification for self-knowledge through the seen [world] alone?
If it is by way of obstructing engagement with seen objects impelled by passion and so forth, then let it be so for the prohibitions themselves.
It must be explained how ritual injunctions (karmavidhi) bring about cessation;
for they are neither enumerative nor restrictive.
Because its object has not been attained at all;
for an injunction whose object has already been attained is understood to have the result of excluding other [alternatives].
And there is no exclusion through contradiction based on having an identical effect.

For activities arising from a formal injunction (*naiyogikya*) have unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*) with their fruits occurring at an indefinite time; whereas activities driven by passion and the like (*rāgādyākṣipta*) are natural (*svābhāvikī*) and have seen results.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the *sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice and service as means to obtaining a village.
Since the scripture has this much extent,
what contradiction is there in one who seeks the stage of the fruit— whether simultaneously or sequentially— practicing both service (*sevā*) and the means of attraction (*sāṅgrahaṇī*)?
Moreover, if all activity directed toward visible goals were prohibited, then even activities grounded in scriptural injunction (*niyoga*) would be obstructed.
Because they are impossible for one who has not acquired wealth and lacks the necessary means;

moreover, even though the means to sensual pleasure are equal in both types of activity—those directed toward visible and those toward invisible ends—there is no distinction in their being impelled by passion and the like. For instance:
The phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*) is a specific injunction made by way of restating an activity prompted by passion and so forth.
And so, since the attachment to the manifold world (*prapañca*) is equal in both cases, by what distinction does one [action] conform to the nature of the Self,
while the other is contrary to it?
For the impulse toward desire is indeed common to the mind.
Now, if one were not to consider it as being merely a means to desire,
then its occurrence would have been described as being without cause.
And the principle that has been stated would be withdrawn;
furthermore, because they are based on the same functional effect, the suspicion of contradiction and so forth regarding their cessation would be cast far away, finding no room to arise.
Alternatively, by the attainment of desires, the injunctions for ritual action dissolve those very desires and thus become conducive to the domain of knowledge (*jñāna*).
As it has been said:
"When all desires that dwell within his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."
Thus [it is said].
That too is incorrect, because the dissolution of desire does not occur through the attainment of desire.
Rather, it is through discernment born from the contemplation of defects.
For even if the mind is touched by desires in the slightest degree, it is surely carried away by those things that captivate;
as it has been said:

"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects," and "Passions increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyment, as do the skillfulness of the senses. For this reason, too, one should turn away from desires because they are not a means [to liberation].
One should take refuge in self-knowledge, which consists in the pacification of all afflictions; yet,
through various means indicated by the ritual injunctions for action, one would instead become attached to those very same worldly enjoyments that captivate the mind,
and feel aversion toward self-knowledge, whose nature is the dissolution of those very things.

For even if bliss has been heard of regarding the Self, if it has not been experienced, it is not capable of even weakening the desire for bliss based on previously experienced objects, much less of uprooting it.
Therefore, *prasaṃkhyāna* alone is the singular means for the destruction of desire.
But ritual procedures are causes of error;
for even though— in every single scripture— there is in some place the dissolution of some particular distinction, [it remains that rituals lead to confusion].
As for the claim that [the injunction] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" implies the dissolution of the body's identity as the self,
that too is incorrect.
Because this [scripture] has another primary purpose;
for this statement does not have as its primary aim the realization of the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body.
If it is argued that even from a statement whose primary purpose is something else, such a meaning is nonetheless determined, [we reply:]...
That too is like the inference of an elephant upon seeing its footprint when the elephant itself has already been seen;
for, having begun with "Not coarse" (*na sthūlam*), the dissolution of the body and the senses is directly shown,
and by implication, the Vedic [teaching] would be the hardness of the knot of desire and so forth.

The second alternative is also untenable, because desires lack the capacity to eliminate desire as previously described, and there is no authoritative evidence for the entry of those who have no further need for their own purpose into another's domain.
If, however, they shared a single office, there would be a conjunction of all ritual acts;
and that is impossible.

[KS_31] Even those who claim, by way of contrast, that knowledge and action share a single locus must also state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the connection between knowledge and action;
it cannot be established merely by analogy with such cases as "one sprinkles the rice grains."

For in that case, the word *vrīhi*—which, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), is intended to indicate the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the ritual action under discussion—indicates its connection with that contextual *apūrva* because it would be purposeless in its own literal sense.
Nor is it like the passage, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood...
For there, even in the absence of a context, the *juhū* indicates the presence of the ritual action because it is invariably connected to such an action.
In that case, the connection is established by the sentence itself;
however, knowledge of the Self is not heard of in this context,
nor is there any inherent connection between the Self and ritual action.
Therefore, its connection with the ritual action is difficult to state.

Likewise, when the fact of being for the sake of another is unknown, the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) does not function as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); thus, there is a separate qualification (*adhikāra*).
Now, if it is thought:
Because it is stated in the present tense and because there is no connection with desire in the phrase "he does not return again," one must modify the fruit and conceive of it as something else.
And that [expectation] exists only when there is a desire for it;

however, when something is already perceived, there is no such desire. Furthermore, the injunction to know the Self has a visible result: namely, the engagement in ritual actions whose fruits are to be experienced in another body.
Therefore, the injunction for the knowledge of the Self is like the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*).

For the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation, having no further requirement once the understanding of the ritual action is achieved through visible means, does not seek a fruit from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*);
likewise, the injunction for the knowledge of the Self is also so, and thus there is no separate qualification (*adhikāra*) for it.
That too is incorrect;
for this person of the Upaniṣads, who is to be investigated in the Vedāntas, is entirely different [from the agent],
and knowledge of him is not a cause for engaging in ritual action.
For it possesses neither agency nor enjoyership;
thus it is said:
"It does not eat anything at all."
"Another, not eating, looks on";
whereas he who is the agent and enjoyer of actions is established as being directly perceived by everyone.
It is not an object of knowledge through verbal testimony.
But is it not the case that there is indeed identity between the individual soul and the Supreme Self?
For thus it has been said:
"By this living self (jīva-ātman)"—
this is true;
however, such is the form of that very jīva, characterized by its connection to ignorance, which is to be apprehended through direct perception.
And that [Self] is the cause for the engagement in action;
yet it does not depend upon words.
However, that which is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions is what one desires to know through words.
And that [knowledge] is opposed to the engagement in action.

How could the engagement in action be the observed purpose of that knowledge? For instance, for one who realizes the Self as the one, non-dual bliss of Brahman, for what purpose or in what manner could there be any engagement?
Is it because of the fulfillment of all desires and the absence of means such as ritual instruments? It might be argued:
"The knowledge of the person of the Upaniṣads itself is enjoined as an auxiliary to ritual action, in accordance with the text:
'Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful.'"

Likewise, beginning with the passage, "O Gārgī, he who offers oblations in this world without knowing this Imperishable," the text demonstrates that the purpose of the knowledge of Brahman is to show the finitude of the fruits of sacrifices and other such acts;
and by the statement, "Knowledge and action both take hold of him," it demonstrates the conjunction of knowledge and action.
First, however, [the meditation] concerns the Udgītha under discussion,
because it begins with the words, "This syllable 'Om' is the Udgītha."
Furthermore, there is praise for the knowledge of syllables through the censure of other ritual acts;
and there is the joint undertaking of both knowledge and ritual, distinguished as follows:
"One takes hold of one who possesses knowledge as 'knowledge,' and one takes hold of one who possesses ritual as 'ritual.'"

Therefore, even in this way, there is no single locus of authority for action and knowledge; and as for those who claim that action and knowledge are entirely unrelated due to their contradiction— action having duality as its object, [while knowledge has non-duality]—
For those who maintain that "knowledge has non-duality as its object," it follows that non-dual knowledge itself cannot arise,
because there is a contradiction between the distinction of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth and the realization of non-duality.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction because the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*) do not occur simultaneously;
indeed, all differentiation dissolves upon the realization of non-duality (*advaita*).
Nor is there any contradiction, nor is it the case that [the means] is not a means.
Because the means (upāya) occurs prior [to the result], and because it has not yet dissolved at that time;
moreover, differentiation itself is the means for the realization of non-differentiation.
In that case, there would be no contradiction even with respect to actions,
precisely because they are means.
This might be so—
Since Brahman is not something to be accomplished, there is no utility for ritual actions;
and it is heard in scripture:
"There is nothing uncreated that can be achieved by what is created."
Nor is there any utility for them in the arising of knowledge,
because knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
nor are actions auxiliary factors to knowledge.
Because knowledge has no other goal to be accomplished;
liberation is not its goal, for that would entail the consequence of it being impermanent.
Now, the severance of the cause of bondage is what is to be accomplished; when that is severed, one is liberated due to the absence of bondage. But what, then, is the cause of bondage?
It is beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā).
In that case, their separation as distinct entities is not what needs to be established, because the very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
This might be argued:
Let it be that the arising of knowledge (*vidyotpāda*) is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is characterized by non-apprehension;
for a positive entity (*bhāva*) itself is the cessation of its absence.
Moreover, the arising of knowledge is not itself the cessation of erroneous cognition (*viparyāsajñāna*).
Indeed, the exclusion of one entity is not another entity;
nor are entities of the nature of mutual non-existence, for that would entail the consequence of their being non-entities.
If one should think that error, caused by the non-apprehension of reality, will cease of its own accord upon the cessation of its cause— that is not so;
for indeed, non-apprehension is not the cause of anything.
Because [otherwise] there would be the unwanted consequence [of ignorance] occurring even in states such as fainting.
What, then, is the cause?
It has been stated: "Ignorance is beginningless and purposeless."
In that case, the inquiry into a [separate] cause would have no scope.
Furthermore, since error (*viparyāsa*) and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are established as being in a reciprocal relationship of cause and effect, there is no fault.

Therefore, since the cessation of erroneous cognition is to be accomplished by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), there would be a requirement for knowledge to depend upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) in that regard.

And this is the correct view: indeed, those who have attained right knowledge regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects after a preceding error do not exert themselves separately for its cessation,
nor do they depend upon any other auxiliary cause.
For the very arising of a contrary state is the destruction of the preceding one, not a void;
otherwise, destruction would not possess a cause. And knowledge is the opposite of erroneous cognition.
Upon the arising of that [knowledge], error is indeed destroyed.
Now, it might be argued: "Karmas are the causes of bondage."
"Their destruction occurs through knowledge that is dependent upon auxiliary factors.
But how could that [destruction] be possible when there arises a pure knowledge in which all particularities have been completely wiped away?
Furthermore, in such a case, actions would be treated as equivalent to errors and doubts.
"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen."
Thus [it is said].

Now, if it is argued that there is a dependence on something else for the sake of purifying consciousness, that too is futile; for doubt and error, which are the impurities of cognition, cannot exist within a consciousness arisen from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, it might be thought:
"A perceptual cognition other than verbal knowledge is also accepted—one that grasps without the apprehension of distinctions and transcends all conceptual constructions;
for Brahman is indeed the object of that [cognition]."
For verbal cognition, which grasps the connection between distinct word-meanings, there is no dependence on ritual action,
meditation, and so forth for its arising.
What, then, is its distinction?
By what means is that sought?
It is the appearance of clarity;
however, that [appearance] has no utility.
For knowledge exists for the purpose of pervading its object;
and when verbal knowledge has arisen, the object is already fully attained.
If it is argued that [the object] is sought because valid cognition culminates in perception and there is a lack of further expectancy therein, [we reply: no.
Once this object of knowledge has been apprehended, what else could be required?
If it is argued that another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required, we say no; for such a requirement exists solely for the sake of establishing the object of knowledge.
If it is argued that [the repetition] is for the sake of further accomplishment, no; for that has already been accomplished repeatedly even previously.
Moreover, once something is accomplished, there is no cause for requiring its accomplishment again.
If there were another means [of cognition], then one would have to depend upon that other means;
however, regarding the object of knowledge, there is simply a state of being free from further expectancy.
If it is a particular kind of joy,
that is established even by a perception arising from a previous means of valid cognition; therefore,
no other means of valid cognition is required for its establishment.
Even that which is perceived directly by others might be sought after for knowledge because it is possible [that it could be otherwise],
since there is no distinction [between them].
Certainty belongs to others as well.
Because it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Direct perception has as its object that which is fit for rejection and so forth, because its object is proximate.
If it is argued that the others [the sense organs] are not [the cause],
then let the cause of contact be considered;
it is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because valid cognition is established,
and there is no such distinction regarding the object of cognition under discussion:
words and the like have universals as their objects.
If it is argued that perception has a specific (particular) as its object, then the object of perception is indeed not already apprehended by the word. Certainly so.
This has been stated:
Brahman is not the object of verbal cognition.
If, then, Brahman is not apprehended through words, [how can it be known?]
How can worship proceed toward that [Brahman]?
For when one thing is being worshipped, another does not become directly manifest.
And for the direct realization of what form is the injunction of sacrifices and other rites prescribed?

The injunctions for sacrifices and other rites are appropriate for the sake of directly realizing the Self, whose nature is Brahman—characterized by unsurpassed bliss, freedom from evil, and so forth—as revealed by the scriptures.

Once that which is of the nature of the human goal, or its opposite, has been made manifest through an authoritative means free from doubt, there remains nothing further to be expected. [Objection: But even when it has been understood...

Regarding the statement "That thou art," it is argued that even when the identity of Brahman and the Self has been established through the words of the scripture, there remains a dependence on other means for the cessation of the perception of transmigratory attributes, just as before.
This is not sound.

How indeed could one who has realized the identity with Brahman as the Self and known the true nature of the Self be joined with those qualities caused by false perception? For it is heard in scripture:
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
And there is no room for those [qualities] in Brahman, who is free from all evil.
Likewise:
"If a person were to know the Self as 'This I am,' desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he suffer with this body?"
Likewise: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless.
The connection with a body is caused by false identification;
when that [identification] ceases through the vision of reality as it is (yāthātathya), there is bodilessness.
In that regard, the non-connection with the pleasant and the unpleasant is explained.
Therefore, one who has realized the state of being the Brahman-Self does not partake in the attributes of transmigratory existence as he did previously.
As for one who is otherwise, [he remains subject to them].
"It is not that he has realized his identity with Brahman.
To this it is replied: Even when reality has been ascertained through a valid means of knowledge, all false appearances everywhere cease.
They may also persist due to a specific cause,

as in the case of the appearance of two moons or the confusion of directions for those who have ascertained the true nature of the directions and the moon through the authoritative word of a reliable person.

Likewise, for one who has understood the reality of the self from a tradition free from doubt, there may still be the persistence of false appearances due to the power of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) strengthened by the long-standing practice of false views since beginningless time.
To bring about that cessation, something else is required;
and that consists of the practice of the vision of reality as established in the world, as well as sacrifices and other rites which have scripture as their authority.
For practice, by strengthening its own latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and obstructing previous impressions, continues its own effect.
Others hold that sacrifices and the like do so through some unseen mode (*adṛṣṭa*), by means of destroying the impurities that stand as obstacles to the highest good (*śreyas*).
Because obligatory rites (nitya-karma) have the purpose of destroying evil (durita).
It might be argued:
"Let these false appearances continue."
Certainty, however, arises from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And worldly activity proceeds according to reality and according to certainty.
Therefore, for one who has realized the true nature of the self, no engagement whatsoever—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is possible.
It is said:
even when the vision of reality has arisen,
if no impression (*saṃskāra*) has been instilled in the cloth.
Furthermore, when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born of false views have become firm, even certainties come to have false objects;

just as for one who is disoriented regarding the directions and has not reflected upon the words of a reliable person, [he acts] just as he did previously, because his behavior is observed to be such.
Likewise, even when a rope has been measured as such, if one does not reflect upon that measurement, fear arises through the delusion that it is a snake.

Therefore, even though reality has been seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they maintain that one must practice the vision of reality in order to overcome or eradicate the extremely firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the long-standing habituation to false perception from beginningless time.
And thus it is said: "It is to be reflected upon; it is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, there is the injunction of the means such as tranquility, self-control, celibacy, and sacrifice.
Otherwise, what would be the purpose of that instruction? This might be the case—
The claim that the knowledge of reality arises solely from the performance of means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) as prescribed by the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is incorrect;
for comprehension arises from the mere word itself.
For the sacred tradition (āmnāya), which aims at the realization of reality, is not non-expressive prior to the specific means of proof,
nor is it non-conclusive, because it eliminates all doubts without exception.
Otherwise, even regarding the means taught by that [teacher], comprehension would be difficult to attain.
Furthermore, even when there is no certainty [that it is real], actors such as Bharata on the stage become causes of grief, fear, and so forth through a false appearance;
and even when the sweetness of molasses is certain, a false appearance of bitterness therein causes pain as if it were real.
Because one would likewise reject and abandon that [Self], even though it is non-false;
therefore, for the sake of its cessation, even one who has ascertained the nature of Brahman as the Self must depend upon means of realization.
Just as, when reality is manifested through valid cognition, liberation is not something produced by action, so too here.
Likewise, even though there is a specific manifestation [of the word] from the means of production,
the Vedic revelations (śrutayaḥ) must either refer to the state of perfection resulting from practice, or depend upon the knowledge of the means for producing the sound,
because the latter is the cause of that [manifestation].
Enough with this excessive detail.
Even though ritual injunctions have distinct purposes, they lead one into the domain of knowledge, because only one who has discharged the three debts has the qualification for that [knowledge].
Even that is not necessarily so, because the Smṛti records an option regarding the stages of life (āśrama):
"Some [teachers] maintain that there is an option of stages of life for him."
For it is heard [in scripture]: "He may subdue that which he desires," and "Or else, in another way, one may go forth from the state of studentship itself."
"Indeed, knowing this, the ancients did not offer the Agnihotra";
likewise:
"What shall we do with offspring?
and likewise, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices?"
Thus, from the observation of the renunciation of action,

[the text] shows that for one who has entered the householder stage, who considers himself to have accomplished all that was to be done through the knowledge of the Self alone, and who is indifferent toward the discharge of his debts, the sin arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties acts as an obstacle to the dawning of knowledge.
"Having discharged the three debts";
however, this is logical—
because of the principle of "separateness of connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva), even for those rites that have no further requirement for other effects.
"The Brahmins seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas and through sacrifice"—
thus, [these acts] constitute auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge;
and that too is for the purpose of the arising [of knowledge].
It is not by way of being employed for a physical action, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth,
because knowledge has no other function;
or rather, it belongs to the category of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), as is the case with memory.
For knowledge arises from the refinement [of the self];
as it has been said:
"And because they are prescribed, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed."
Is it not the case that the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) occurs precisely upon the arising of vision?

In that regard, let the very vision depend upon the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), specifically the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), which destroy mental distraction; for from a concentrated mind, there arises the clarity of knowledge through its manifestation.
But sacrifices and the like are not [the cause],
because that [result] can occur even without them through practice;
this is true.

Likewise, for those in the higher stages of life (*āśramins*) who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), the dawning of pure knowledge is held to occur even without those [external means];
however, there is a distinction made by time.
For through specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), that [knowledge] is manifested quickly, or even more quickly.
In their absence, [the result occurs] after a long time, and even longer than that.
As it has been said:
"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse."
This is the meaning:
from the scriptural statement "by sacrifice and by gift," it follows that ritual actions are required even for knowledge that is obtainable through repeated practice,
just as, although the reaching of a village can be accomplished even without a horse, a horse is nevertheless required for speed or for ease.
Is it not the case that Brahman itself is of the nature of knowledge?
Knowledge is not other than Brahman;
and that [Brahman] is eternal and uncreated.
In that case, how could anything be required? It is said:
just as a crystal gem whose form is concealed by an adjunct requires the removal of that adjunct for the manifestation of its own true nature, so too should it be understood here.
For the original form of the crystal gem has not been destroyed due to the proximity of the adjunct.
Or, when that [homogeneous cause] has ceased, another [moment] has arisen;
for it is not possible for a previous homogeneous moment, which has been separated by many dissimilar moments, to arise without a cause.
Indeed, when fire has vanished, there is no further continuation of the series of wood from the embers.
Therefore, just as the non-actional nature of the crystal depends upon the removal of the substrate, so too does the nature of the self.
It might be argued: "In that case, it is cognition that is dependent."
And that effect is distinct from the crystal;
for in this case, human effort is directed toward knowledge.
But is knowledge itself desired as an end in its own right?
Or is it for the sake of establishing the intrinsic nature of the object?
It cannot be by way of its own form,
because the object exists only through conventional usage.
Conventional discourse is not based on mere consciousness alone, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of it occurring] even through false cognition.
If, however, cognition were sought as having the nature of the object, [then...]
The operation has that object as its purpose; thus, it is "sought" by that object.
Yet, there is no modification whatsoever in the object due to the cognition, because the two are unrelated.
Because a suitable location exists everywhere,
it would follow that all perceivers would know [it];
furthermore, such a thing is impossible in the case of things destroyed or yet to come.

Therefore, just as that which is not concealed appears as if concealed and as if manifested through dependence on effort, so too the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), though unconcealed, appears as if concealed and as if manifested through effort; this is fully established.
Consequently, it has been described as the universal self (sāmānyātman) in which all distinctions have been withdrawn.
In this very way, [the nature of things] is indicated by the dissolution of distinctions such as bracelets and the like.
And since that [Brahman] is defined by way of the cessation of all specific distinctions,
other experts in the knowledge of Brahman have described it in its general form as follows:
"That indeed is the Great, Unborn Self, characterized by pure existence."
Likewise, it is said: "Existence alone is the source of all distinctions; it is the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti).
Just as the essence of gold, when considered by setting aside its specific forms such as bracelets and rings, is understood as their common universal (sāmānya).
To those who assert that non-existence is the case— saying, "That which lacks distinction cannot be a universal, just like a rabbit's horn"— the following is said in reply:
Regarding the phrase "in which all distinctions have been withdrawn":
if you are proving that it is non-common (*asāmānya*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
For in the absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*), of what would that be the commonality (*sāmānya*)?

However, the universal (*sāmānya*) has been described by the exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādibhiḥ*) figuratively (*upacārataḥ*), because it is defined through the negation of particulars (*viśeṣapratyastamukhena*).

Now, if non-existence itself were the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) of this [reason] due to the very particulars, which are themselves devoid of further particulars.
Thus ends the *Brahmakāṇḍa* in the *Brahmasiddhi* composed by the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra.
— [Edition]; originally, the *Brahma-* and *Tarka-kāṇḍas* were combined;
Vācaspati does not recognize this division.

[The Section on Reasoning] Now, since the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities— which are differentiated by perception and other means of knowledge— are apprehended, word is not a valid means of knowledge regarding a single, non-dual reality,
because it would contradict perception and the other means of knowledge.
It is said: "Like the explanatory statements regarding the floating of stones and so forth,
the wise declare that perception is an affirmer, not a negator."
Therefore, the scripture concerning oneness is not contradicted by that perception.
Now, it may be argued that human words, being dependent on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are rightly considered non-authoritative when they contradict such [other means].

But why should the Veda (*āmnāya*), which is independent and functions without requiring other means of valid cognition, be non-authoritative even when it contradicts them? Furthermore, why do perception and the other means of valid cognition not lose their status as valid cognitions simply because they contradict the Veda?
Since the lack of dependence is equal [in both cases], there is no reason for distinction;
therefore, the labor spent in avoiding contradictions with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is futile.
Regarding this, some say:
In the event of a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition, the authority of scripture (*āmnāya*) is weaker because it is dependent;
for indeed, scripture itself depends upon perception and the others even for the sake of establishing its own nature.
And thus, their validity must be accepted,
because if that were subverted, their very nature would remain unestablished;
however, in the case of the Veda, there is no such dependence upon perception and the other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, because verbal testimony is seen to be fallible,
whereas perception is not seen to be fallible;
moreover, between that which has room for error and that which has no room for error, the latter is more powerful.
Furthermore, perception and the other means of knowledge are without scope [for such objects],
whereas verbal testimony has scope through a figurative meaning. For instance:
It is possible to describe the scope of the non-dualistic scriptures as being figurative;
or else, the scope for Vedānta texts whose meaning is not intended to be expressed lies in their utility for recitation (*japa*).
It has been described that the Upaniṣads are the Vedāntas.

Furthermore, because the Vedic tradition (āmnāya) is subject to confusion while perception and the other means of knowledge are not, the injunctions regarding ritual action—which depend on the notion of difference—and the Vedānta texts—which depend on non-difference—are mutually contradictory; thus, even in the absence of contradiction with other means of knowledge, their authority is difficult to establish. How much more so, then, when there is a contradiction with [the Vedāntas], whose authority is unimpeded and firmly established?
Therefore, one should strive for this in order to avoid contradiction;
and because they are primary,
for perception and the other means of knowledge are indeed primary.
For a living being, the traditional teaching (āmnāya) belongs to a later time;

its scope is eclipsed by those [perceptions] whose objects are established, and thus it must either be interpreted as having a figurative meaning or its interpretation of the object must conform to that [established perception].
Moreover, perception and the other means of knowledge possess primacy by virtue of their actual function;
for the determination of the meaning of the Veda depends upon the analysis of words and word-meanings, and that analysis falls within the scope of perception and the rest.
"Therefore, an effort is made to avoid contradiction.
Others think as follows:

"Even if perception and the other means of knowledge are of equal strength with the sacred tradition (āmnāya), since an alternative (vikalpa) regarding a real entity is untenable, there would be doubt in the event of a contradiction."
Thus, non-contradiction is established. There is another view:
the sacred tradition (āmnāya) alone is authoritative when there is a conflict with it.
"In a sequence of preceding and succeeding [elements], the preceding is weaker, as in the case of the original state;
for indeed, the arising of the succeeding is not established without subverting the preceding.
Thus it is said: For instance:
It is said that for everyone, the discernment of distinct objects is innate and based on perception and other means of knowledge.
However, the non-innate realization of non-duality—which depends upon and is preceded by that [innate discernment]—is adventitious for some alone.
Being unable to arise without first submerging the former, it arises as something that sublates it.
Furthermore:
because perception and the other means of knowledge can have various causes for error,
whereas the Veda is free from any suspicion of defects whatsoever.
For defects reside in persons; since a person is absent in the case of the Word (śabda), such defects are impossible there.

Indeed, it is possible to conceive of and ascertain within perception and other means of knowledge an innate predisposition toward ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) as the cause of error—just like the conceit that the body is the self—on the basis of tradition (*āmnāya*) alone.
But in the case of the impersonal Word (*apauruṣeya-śabda*), there is no suspicion of any defect whatsoever.
Or else, [if that were the case], there would be no valid cognition at all.

However, perception and the other means of knowledge possess a conventional validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*), because as long as the impressions of ignorance persist, there is no subversion of worldly transactional activity.
And where there is a contradiction with worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*).
In the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), however, since defects are possible, its validity does not consist in revealing reality (*tattva-avedana*),
nor in the non-contradiction of worldly convention.
Because its object is unperceived (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because it is observed that [cognitions] produced by defects do not correspond to worldly practice (*vyavahāra-visaṃvādi*),
one cannot postulate a defect as the cause of a cognition that does not correspond to worldly practice in the case of perception and the other means of knowledge;
for such a defect could only be postulated on the basis of a failure in worldly practice.
However, because it is the adversary of the vision of reality born from the Vedānta, the beginningless connection with ignorance is postulated as the very cause for the obstruction of that reality.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the persistence of defects and [the existence of] validity;
for verbal testimony, however, being subject to possible defects, its validity would be extremely difficult to attain.
For it is observed that from defects arises the production of a cognition that is non-concordant with practical activity (*vyavahāra*).
In that case, because the non-concordance with practical activity is suspected due to the suspicion of defects, and because there is an obstruction to [the apprehension of] reality,
validity— characterized by the communication of reality— is not present.
It does not have the characteristic of non-contradiction with worldly convention (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it is correct that when the validity of a word is accepted, it possesses greater force even when there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for the argument that [verbal testimony] depends upon perception and the like:
To this it is replied: it is not in the act of valid cognition that the word depends upon perception and the other means of knowledge, but rather in the establishment of its own nature.
Otherwise, it would not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all.
And thus, because it depends [on other factors] for its own effect, it does not fall short of perception and the other means of cognition.
For perception and the others as well are not independent of other things in establishing their own nature.
For dependence regarding the effect diminishes its capacity;
as for the claim that their validity must be inferred, who indeed says otherwise?
However, that [scripture] has the characteristic of being non-contradictory in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), but not the characteristic of revealing ultimate reality (*tattva*).

From the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), which is established as possessing empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) alongside perception and other means of knowledge, the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) is attained.
Due to that contradiction, [subsequent cognition] sublates only the aspect of seeing reality within those [prior cognitions], not the aspect of non-contradiction with worldly practice;
for it is observed that a subsequent cognition possesses greater force than a prior cognition, even when the latter is required as a cause.
Just as, when trees are at a distance, the cognition of trees arises from the cognitions of elephants;
for the cognitions of elephants are required as causes for the clear cognition of trees.
That [cognition of trees] does not arise merely from the contact of the sense organ with its object.
Because it does not exist at the initial moment [of contact],
nor because of a specific location,
since it arises for one who is situated in that very place.

Therefore, it should be understood that when the mind is directed toward trees standing before one, that [cognition] is produced by the contact of the sense organ and other factors, assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) following a previous error.
In this same way, cognitions of twenty and so forth, which arise from the disappearance of cognitions of one and so on, are also to be cited as examples.
And thus, as for what some describe—
The comprehension of the meaning of the Vedānta is itself contradicted [by this view]:
non-difference cannot be ascertained without difference;
for its comprehension is indeed dependent upon difference as its means.
In that case, the contradiction— that non-difference is understood only by implying difference—
is refuted;
for comprehension implies the means [of that comprehension].
The means does not possess ultimate reality,
because the realization of truth can arise even from false knowledge;
moreover, the conventional reality of differentiation is indeed accepted [by us].
The observation of deviation is common to both verbal cognition and perception when they arise from fallacious reasons;
likewise, non-deviation is equal for the other two [valid means of knowledge],
as is the absence of occasion [for doubt].
If, indeed, the meaning of the Vedānta is exclusively one and non-dual, what other scope is there for those [scriptural passages]?
Or, if their oneness is merely figurative, or if their meaning is not intended to be expressed because they are useful only for recitation (*japa*), [then how can they be authoritative]?
In that case, since there is no contradiction at all, the consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) does not even arise.
How then could there be weakness due to having scope (*sāvakāśatva*)?
And how can there be scope for a figurative sense by overstepping the primary meaning?
How is it that, given the subordinate status of the word with respect to its meaning in the case of the *autpattika* [eternal] relation—
given the statements "for its meaning is seen to be the communication of ritual action" and "but the sentence-meaning is not distinct"— there could be a lack of intention to convey that meaning?

If it is argued that this is because of contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), that is trivial; for the validity of a means of valid cognition does not depend upon another means of valid cognition.
For if it were dependent on that [other means of knowledge], it would abandon its own natural inclination when there is a contradiction with it;
rather, it would function in accordance with it.
But for that which is independent, what reason could there be for following another means of knowledge?
However, since worldly words denote their own objects by depending on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that their function follows those [other means].
But if [the Vedic word] is equally independent [of other means], why is there not the reverse?
Or rather, both would be invalid due to mutual contradiction.
Or is there a sublation of the former, as in the case of the cognition of silver, according to the principle that "in a sequence of two [contradictory cognitions], the former is weaker"?
For surely, the cognition of the mother-of-pearl does not have a different object or no object at all simply because it contradicts the cognition of silver.
How then is there figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) in the Veda?
Where it is impossible for the intended meaning to be established through the primary (literal) meanings of the words,
there the attainment of the object of cognition occurs through the second function (lakṣaṇā) of words, since the operation of words is observed even in that manner.
However, where words obtain their object by their own natural power (svārasya), [the primary function prevails].
In that case, they do not turn back due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
for their object is not dependent upon other means of valid cognition such that it would have to be set aside by their force.
Now, if it is thought:
It is postulated in this way precisely for the sake of favoring both;
for in this manner, both verbal testimony and perception and so forth are favored.
Otherwise, perception and the other means of knowledge would be utterly subverted.
[If you say] they would be sublated—
this is not sound.
A certain conceptual construction regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) may arise in accordance with the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

However, when it comes to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no basis for resorting to conceptual construction while abandoning what is established by its own inherent nature (*svarasasiddha*).
Therefore, the arrangements of alternatives (*vikalpa*) and combinations (*samuccaya*) are postulated in accordance with the means of valid cognition, not for the sake of favoring both [theories].
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that neither [of the two] should be assisted.

If it is argued that those very [means of valid cognition] are the proof—namely, if it is thought that a means of valid cognition does not require assistance from another means of valid cognition—then [we reply]: no.

Rather, it is by its very nature; for, precisely because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it establishes the object through that [cognition]. Therefore, the object must be established in exactly the same way that it is understood from that [cognition].
In this way, it becomes supported by that;
otherwise, it would be contradicted. Furthermore, the determination of an object would be without a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇikā*).
For that reason, because there would be no cognition by its own nature,
because there is no other [means], and because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence.

The cognition of another object established by [the primary] validity must be postulated through the impossibility of that validity otherwise being accounted for, and the validity of that cognition [in turn] depends on it; however,
when the object is obtained through its own inherent force, validity arises from the cognition itself, and thus there is no circularity.
Therefore, when there is a contradiction, it is the sublation of the earlier [cognition] alone that conforms to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because it is so perceived;
it is not the case that the later [cognition] assumes a different object.
Indeed, another object is not postulated for the cognition of the mother-of-pearl fragment in order to assist the cognition of silver;
nor is there a lack of scope for perception and the other means of knowledge due to their having no other recourse,
for that which is the recourse for delusions such as [the appearance of] silver is [available].
That [non-existence] applies to those as well;
if their object is metaphorical or imagined, then it is the same for perception and the other means of valid cognition as well.
Now, because that [object] does not exist, perception and the other means of knowledge are likewise without objects—that is, they have non-existent things as their referents.

Therefore, the conclusion that they either do not intend to denote a real object or possess only a figurative meaning is indistinguishable for both [parties]. By this, the following argument is also refuted, which they say:—
In common worldly usage, it is observed that when a word contradicts other means of valid cognition, it possesses either a figurative meaning or its literal sense is not intended.

Therefore, when there is a contradiction with perception and the like, the Vedāntas must likewise be so [figurative or non-literal], because such a phenomenon is seen even in the case of perception and the other means of knowledge.
As for the claim that the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has its scope sublated by objects established through their primary [status], it is for this very reason that it is sublatant,
like the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Nor can it be justified by postulating an object in accordance with that [cognition],
because [the cognition] is independent;
its status as a means of valid cognition does not depend upon that [object].
There is no joint operation by them,
nor is there a state of syntactic unity between the scripture and the means of knowledge such as perception;
for in both cases, the arising of cognition is independent of one another.
In that case, it is logical that the subsequent [rule] is stronger;
as it has been said:
"In that context, let it be understood that the subsequent is indeed stronger than the preceding."
Where there may be the arising of cognitions that are mutually independent;

However, where there is a state of being co-operative through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the primary sense remains established by its own natural function because no contradiction has yet arisen.

Since the subsequent words are unable to achieve that syntactic unity through their first mode of operation—due to the impossibility of providing the meaning required by that primary sense—they convey the meaning required by the preceding word through a second mode of operation, by virtue of the power of syntactic unity; thus, the primary sense is stronger.
As for the argument that it is "due to confusion," to that it is replied:
there may indeed be confusion.
If the injunctions regarding ritual action were intended to establish difference,
they would instead depend upon a difference already established, [stating]: "One should accomplish this by means of that in this manner."
Thus, [these teachings] have as their primary aim the instruction for the benefit of persons.
This may be the case:

if there is no distinction [between the self and others], then because the three factors [of agent, object, and action] would have subsided, how could there be instruction for the benefit [of others]? It is said in reply:
Just as, for instance, in the case of hawks and other such [animals],
there is an injunction even when the element of what is to be accomplished has ceased, because of the prohibition: "One must not harm any living beings."
The same applies in all cases, even when every part [of the definition] has been refuted.
For instance,
how could violence— which is established as having undesirable consequences— be something that ought to be accomplished?

Now, it may happen that for someone whose mind is overcome by intense anger, whose discriminative consciousness is obscured by a surging darkness, and who perceives even what is harmful as beneficial, one transcends the instruction of the Teacher; likewise, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites, there are three components presented by innate ignorance to those who are unawakened, and it is with reference to these that their instruction is given.
However, those who have awakened are not instructed by means of ritual injunctions for action,
just as those who have overcome the enemies of anger are not instructed by injunctions such as the Śyena sacrifice.
Thus, although there is a perception of difference regarding the ritual injunctions for action which rely on distinctions established through conventional usage, [KKS 44]...

Nevertheless, because those [other parts of the Veda] do not have that as their primary purpose, they possess no authority there, just as the words of an *arthavāda* have no authority regarding historical accounts.
And so, how could there be a contradiction of the Vedāntas by them,
or of them by the Vedāntas?
Moreover, contradiction is observed within perception and the other means of knowledge themselves,
due to the observation of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in cognitions such as those of silver and a fragment of mother-of-pearl,
and because of the cognition of both difference and non-difference everywhere.

Thus, even though the Veda possesses such authority, there may be one of dull intellect who, observing that worldly speech often has figurative meanings when it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, concludes that the operation of words in the Veda is like that in the world;
or there may be one who, due to the dense and deep-rooted darkness of the perception of duality, considers perception and the other means of knowledge alone to be authoritative,
because he observes that worldly speech is sublated by them.
To awaken him to that truth, the contradiction is refuted;
for it is not the case that one who is bitten by a scorpion with mild venom and dies is not treated with medicine.
In that regard, there are three possibilities for perception:
it may be a positive prescription of the thing's own nature, the exclusion of another thing,
or both.
In both cases, there is also a threefold division: simultaneity,
affirmation preceded by exclusion, and [negation].
Regarding the statement "exclusion is preceded by a positive injunction":

in that case, if there is an exclusion of another entity, or if both [the positive injunction and the exclusion] are present, then difference (*bheda*) falls within the scope of perception, which results in a contradiction.

However, in the case of a mere positive injunction of its own nature (*svarūpa*), devoid of the exclusion of anything else, difference is not the objective referent of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For indeed, without exclusion (vyavaccheda), the establishment of difference is not possible;
and perception has the function of mere affirmation (vidhi).
Therefore, how is it that there is no contradiction? It is explained as follows:
When something has acquired a certain form in some respect, it is that very same thing which is negated;
therefore, without a positive affirmation, the occurrence of a negation is impossible.
The operation of perception is not merely exclusion,
nor is it both [exclusion and affirmation] simultaneously,
nor is it affirmation preceded by exclusion.
For when an object is already established, it is only in its established form that it is negated— as in "this is not here" or "this is not that"— where,
on an established ground, an established jar is negated.
Or as [one says], "a horse in a cow.
A negation is not possible without both that which is to be negated and the object of the negation.
How, then, is there a negation of things that are absolutely non-existent, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or a sky-flower?
For there is no negation of it anywhere, at any time,
because it is absolute;
nor is there any establishment of it from anything whatsoever.
Because of their absolute non-existence.
Regarding this, some say:
first, in the case of things such as "sky-flowers," once the sky and so forth are established, flowers of that same kind are negated within them.
