By the statement "the Pradhāna does not exist," properties such as being the cause of the world and consisting of the differentiated effects of pleasure, pain, and delusion are negated with respect to the primal cause.
Others, however, explain that this is a negation of external objects which have acquired form within the intellect due to some cause.
Otherwise, if [the object] is already precluded by fate (*daiva*), what further negation could there be for that which has not yet attained its form?
Or, if it has already attained its form, how can there be an absolute negation?
Moreover, if exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) were a negation of an object that is not even expected, then emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would be the referent of valid cognition (*pramāṇārtha*).
There is no distinction,
because everything is negated everywhere without exception;
however, that exclusion which serves to differentiate depends upon the established existence of the two things being differentiated.
And since that [negation] does not exist apart from a positive injunction, an injunction must be sought beforehand;
for it is accepted that negation is preceded by a positive injunction. Nor is exclusion preceded by a positive injunction, because—
The sequence of the action of a single cognition is not logically consistent;
for that [cognition] arises from what is present and does not involve the apprehension of anything else.
Indeed, it is not logical for affirmation and exclusion, as the two operations of a single means of valid cognition, to exist sequentially; because of momentariness,
if the operations were sequential, the latter would not be an operation of that [cognition].
Because there is an intervention;

moreover, the very arising of cognition— which consists in the apprehension of an object— is its operation, and if that [cognition] arises in the form of a determination, [it is not an operation distinct from itself].
The operation belongs to the injunction itself,
because simultaneity is prohibited and because that which has already arisen cannot arise again.
Moreover, perception (pratyakṣa), which has a proximate object as its objective support, cannot manifest an object that is not proximate;
nor is it capable of delimiting a form that is not being manifested,
for if that which is to be delimited were not being manifested, there would be mere negation (vyavacchedamātra).
Exclusion would belong either to nothing at all or to everything;
therefore, there can be no exclusion when that which is to be excluded does not appear.
Furthermore, it is not logical for perception, which has a proximate object as its support, to manifest that which is not proximate. How, then, can there be subverting perception?
For in that case, within a single cognition, the affirmation of another [object] is admitted to be preceded by the negation of the previous object.
And there is the appearance of a negandum that is not present;
therefore, this rule does not hold, namely, that the negation must be prior.
Furthermore, there would be a succession in the operation of a single cognition,
and there would be the manifestation of an object not present [to the senses] by means of perception;
this is not sound.
In that case as well, regarding silver and so forth established by a prior cognition,
the negation "this is not [silver]" with respect to the general category of the present object is preceded by an affirmation.
The procedure for the positive injunction (*vidhi*) is stated as being preceded by the negation of its opposite; and while it is said that the negation is invariably preceded by the injunction,
it is not denied that the injunction itself may be preceded by a negation.
Furthermore, in that case, there is no successive operation of a single cognition, because it arises with both forms simultaneously;
nor is there any impossibility regarding the exclusion of the object, since both have already been established by the preceding cognition.
Furthermore, since the exclusion operates upon the object to be excluded as it was illuminated by the preceding cognition, there is no consequence of the non-proximity of the object being manifested;
for that [subsequent cognition] arises in dependence upon the former. And precisely through that dependence on the former, it arises possessing two forms.
Otherwise, only a single form would be presented.
Furthermore, for one who does not exclude all exclusions, what exclusion is intended,
by means of which one might be countered?
If it is argued that "that world is established," then why is this not also established by the world—
that a horse is not a cow, and a cow is not a horse?
As for the view that the exclusion of others is nothing other than the prescription of one thing—
namely, as follows:
Just as perception, by virtue of having that form, produces that very form,
so too [it is] because of its restriction to that single form.
"That alone," [it is said].
The phrase "not other" excludes what is other;
and the conceptual constructions "this" and "not this," which are brought forth by the power of that exclusion, set in motion the conventional usage of existence and non-existence.
For there is no exclusion of one thing from another that is distinct from a cognition restricted to a single form and not associated with anything else.
To this it is replied:
"The affirmation of one thing itself is the exclusion of others; it does not have something else as its object."
Let there be no lack of distinction, nor let there be no unity among those who share a single consciousness.
A specific restriction [of one thing] is not the cause for the ascertainment of the absence of others,
because it would follow that there is no distinction between that which meets the conditions for perception and its opposite, leading to the undesirable consequence of excluding everything else;
for such a specific restriction is indeed the non-connection with anything other than that.

And likewise, if there were exclusion due to non-connection, then because there would be no distinction between that [object] and both the perceptible and the imperceptible, there would be an exclusion of both.
Now, if it is thought:
"It indeed occurs; for instance—"
It removes [the misconception] by means of a specific insight into all those non-selves that belong to it, through the restriction to that very self;
and thus it has no other selves, though there may be [other selves] belonging to its space and time.
Because there is no contradiction, as in the case of form and so forth;
in that context, the qualification "attaining the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is intended to determine the exclusion of other places and times,
for it is possible that even if the self is not perceived, its absence in a particular place and time may still be established through the perception of something else.
It is as in other cases;
otherwise, there would not be an equal capacity for apprehension.
True, this distinction exists.
But the capacity for the restriction of perception does not exist at present;
for instance, even though perception occurs with respect to a specific place, time, and form, since that perception is exhausted merely by establishing those forms, it does not exclude taste.
Likewise, the restriction of perceiving a portion of ground, because its operation consists merely in establishing that portion of ground, would not exclude the visibility of a jar either.
Or else, if there were exclusion [of one], there would be the exclusion of everything.
Therefore, even when there is the exclusion of the perceptible, another logical reason (hetu) must be employed,
and not merely the restriction to perception itself.
And likewise, the exclusion of other selves is not established by that [perception].
Granted, since an affirmation consists in the exclusion of the non-existence of the object to be affirmed, its absence might be excluded;
however, the existence of another self is not [excluded].
If it is argued that, as with place and time,
there is no existence of multiple selves for a single [entity],
then the exclusion [of such multiplicity] must arise from contradiction with something else.
It is not so, because there is no restriction regarding perception.
And if there is no exclusion, how can there be multiplicity,
or contradiction, or mutual dependence?
Therefore, the prescription of one thing is not the exclusion of another.

Furthermore, if the exclusion of others were based on the restriction to one [thing], then in the case of a variegated [object] such as a painting, the difference between blue and other colors—which are perceived as part of a single perception—would not be established;
for there would be no restriction of the cognition to a single [color] due to its connection with multiple cognitions within that one [perception].
But surely, entities are distinct by their very nature; it is the cognition itself, by producing those various forms, that differentiates them from one another,
for differentiation is not something other than that which possesses differentiation.
In that regard, even in the case of a positive injunction involving exclusion, that [exclusion] is indeed enjoined; for whatever entity is the nature of a thing must be enjoined by that very nature,
otherwise there would be no injunction of it.
Furthermore, since entities with mutually exclusive natures appear in their respective perceptions,
they are established as being exactly so.

Even in this case, because the appearances are unmingled, if the natures are unmingled, then— given that there is no distinction between the two objects of perception— the exclusion [of one from the other] remains just as it was before.
Moreover,
difference is not the nature of a real entity, because that would entail the non-existence of the entity;
and it is not possible for a real entity to possess difference through a formless [difference].
Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a real entity (*vastu*); for it is indeed postulated and recognized as residing in one or many substrates.
And thus, if that single exclusion, which resides in many, were the intrinsic nature of a real entity, there would be no distinction even among entities.

It is not logical for that which is different to have a non-different nature from a single [entity], just as in the previous case. Now, if one were to adopt the view that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is indeed a distinct entity so that this fault does not occur,
even then, because exclusion lacks any form, entities would not be excluded by way of their own nature.
Another interpretation:
difference is the nature of being mutually non-identical;
if that is the nature of the entity, [then it is not a property distinct from the entity].
There would be the consequence of the non-existence of all things, because of the thesis that they consist of non-existence. Another way [of explaining it]: [KKS_48]—
If difference were the intrinsic nature of an entity, then no entity whatsoever would be one,
because oneness is incompatible with difference.
Even an atom, because it consists of parts, is manifold in nature and thus not a unity. Likewise, its nature as a composite of many parts is also untenable.
Since neither unity nor multiplicity is possible therein, and since a third mode is impossible, it follows that the entity would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
Another explanation of the second half [of the verse]:
it objects to the dilemma of whether [the effect] is different or non-different [from the cause],
stating that this distinction pertains to the nature of things (*vastu*).
Identity with that nature and otherness— these two do not find a foothold in a non-entity whose body is constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For instance:
Inexpressible in terms of identity or difference, its form is manifested by conceptualization which has the latencies of beginningless conceptual construction as its material cause;
[it appears as] "this is different from that" or "this is the difference between these two."
Thus he employs conventional usage;
there is no such thing as "difference" that could be investigated as being either identical to or different from something else.
In this regard, the following further arises: "The distinctness of a real entity cannot be conceived by means of a formless [difference].
If, then, difference is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature—"
For it does not exist according to the actual state of things;
it is merely presented by conceptual constructions.
In that case, there is no difference in the thing itself.
Because there is no difference [between them] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
possession of that [quality] by means of an imagined intrinsic nature (*kalpitasvabhāva*) is not tenable;
it would itself be merely imagined.
Why do you not agree with this which we are saying?
We too say this very thing:
there is no difference in reality.
"This is the manifestation of beginningless ignorance," as it has been said:
"If a thing were of the nature of difference, there would be an absence of any single entity."
"Because of the existence of that [one], there is also the non-existence of the other"—this refers to the non-existence of a thing. Regarding this, they say:
we maintain that the distinct nature (*bhedasvabhāva*) of a thing is dependent upon another, not dependent upon itself.
If it were by way of contradiction that there would be an absence of a single entity,
whereas in its own nature a single entity is distinct in relation to another, then it is said in reply:
Furthermore, dependence on a person does not follow from the nature of the thing itself;
for so-called "dependence" is not some property of a thing by which things could be established [as real].

Indeed, it is not logical for entities that have arisen through their own causes and are established by their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to depend upon other entities for the sake of maintaining that intrinsic nature;
in this regard, this is a property dependent on a person (puruṣapratyayadharma).
Furthermore, entities do not conform to the conditions of a person.

Because things are established in their own intrinsic natures by virtue of their respective causes, the nature of a real entity is not established in accordance with those [mental constructs]. Rather,
it is only logical that its establishment follows the established nature of the real entity itself.
Because it is preceded by that;
and because, if there were mutual dependence regarding the establishment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, it would result in the fallacy of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśraya*).
Alternatively, as it was said:
"Because there is no distinction from a single difference, it follows that there is an absence of difference in the entity"; regarding this, they say:
"Difference is not one, because of the contradiction in its nature."
And if there were identity, the objects themselves would have identity as their cause; therefore, difference is distinguished for each individual object.
How then can there be dependence upon multiple substrata?
Because it is relative; for its very nature is established as dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Thus, all entities are differentiated by their respective inherent differences which depend upon counter-correlates. To this, it is replied:
Regarding the term "human" (*pauruṣeyī*): for a person, having grasped one object, depends upon another for the sake of an action;
but what need for dependence on other objects could there be for entities whose natures have been obtained from their own causes in an unimpaired state?
But surely, for the sake of establishing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
there are indeed various kinds of intrinsic natures of entities; among these, some are established within the reality of things only in dependence upon a counterpart.
If this very distinction [is what constitutes the entity],
then the entity does not acquire its complete nature from its causes,
because the form called "distinction" is dependent upon a counter-correlate.
Furthermore, because it arises from a different cause that serves as its counter-correlate, the subsequent difference could not be its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This might be argued:
"An entity is produced from causes in its very complete form."
In that regard, the form called "differentiation" (bheda) is dependent upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin);
it is never independent, because its nature is such that it arises only together with that very [counter-correlate] of its kind. Thus, there is no manifestation of an incomplete form.
To this, it is replied:
Granted that such an entity may appear;
however, its purposeful dependence must be explained, for when something depends upon another in any respect, [it is dependent].
It is said that "it depends on that," and no other distinction is discerned to establish the difference between the dependent and the independent.
In this regard, first of all, origination does not depend upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
Because it arises from its own causes as something non-deficient,
there is no causal efficiency [in the absence of those causes], since its causal efficiency is observed even when they are not present.
If it is argued that [difference is relative]—
for instance, because difference is not perceived without depending upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—
then it follows that the nature of difference itself is not dependent.
When that [object] has already been established, the subsequent cognition—which arises after the actual state of the thing—requires a distinct counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

For example, although form and other [sensory objects] possess a nature that is independent once they are established, they are not said to possess a dependent nature merely because they require the eye and other [faculties] for their cognition.
Furthermore, due to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), even cognition cannot be conceived as being mutually reliant.
Nor can difference be established from the mere thing itself when its difference has not been apprehended, because that consequence would apply even to a single entity.
Therefore, when there is dependence on human agency, it does not follow the nature of the thing.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a real entity (*vastu*).
Another explanation is as follows: difference (*bheda*) is not the form (*rūpa*) of a real entity.
For [the nature of things] is understood as relative;
yet, in the case of relativity, a real entity does not conform to a person's subjective cognition,
because it is preceded by an established reality.
How, then, are [beings such as] fathers and so forth [established]?
For they do not exist without dependence [on causes],
yet they are not equivalent to things like sky-flowers or cities of the Gandharvas.
Because it is established in the world as a factor for non-contradictory worldly practice, it is said:
why is difference (*bheda*) not likewise established in the world? Moreover:
Expectation regarding one's father and others is conditioned by such factors as the act of procreation.
Through a single specific action, there is a mutual dependence between the short and the long vowels;
for the denotata of the words "father" and "son" have their generative and generated capacities already established,
yet they both pertain to the domain of a common act of procreation.
Because of the difference in intrinsic nature;
therefore, there is dependence upon that by which similarity [is established].
This is what is meant:
in that case, it is the word-meaning that is dependent, not the actual entity (*vastu*).
And the cause for such dependence exists there in the form of a common action, even between two entities that are otherwise fixed.
However, this investigation concerning the true nature of things applies only when there is a difference in their actual state (*bhāva*);
nor is any cause for such dependence perceived.
This should be understood in the same way regarding short and long [measurements]: even within an action of the same kind, there is a relative deficiency or excess in the pervasion of space.
If, then, dependence [of difference] is established even from the difference of effects, then— alas!—

the mutual difference of entities will be established solely from the difference in their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, since difference is established through perception even when [causal efficiency] is absent, we infer the difference of causes from the difference of effects alone, because [perception] functions solely through affirmation (*vidhi*).
If there were identity [between cause and effect], a distinction among effects could not be conceived,
because the distinction among effects depends upon the intrinsic nature of the cause.
If this [cause] produces that [effect]...
Intrinsic nature does not produce anything else;
therefore, the production of another effect must arise from something other [than that nature].
Thus, this attempt to establish difference by means of difference itself is not very clever.
Moreover:
"Even when there is a difference produced by causal efficiency, no difference in form is perceived."
Fire does not possess internal differentiation by way of the distinction between burning and cooking;
nor is a difference in the nature of entities perceived through a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is mutually dependent, nor can such a difference be inferred.
There would be merely a difference in designation, since even in a single fire, a diversity of effects such as burning and cooking is observed.
Now, if it is thought:
Fire is a collection of form and other qualities;
therein, from form comes illumination,
and from touch comes burning.
Granted that burning and cooking result from contact alone;
yet these two are distinct perceptions in the world, even though there is a commonality in the modification of the substance undergoing conjunction.
Furthermore, action is the single cause of conjunction, disjunction, and latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*).

One should consider that the self is the [cause] of desire and so forth; that existence and so forth are [the causes] of lightness, luminosity, and so forth, each being non-different from them; and that color-form and so forth are [the causes] of specific cognitions and of their homogeneous moments.
But surely we do not assert a difference based merely on a difference in causal efficiency;
rather, it is based on the non-occurrence there of that which is impossible there and has not been observed.

For example, even when the eye is present, the auditory faculty is distinct because of the absence there of the cognition of sound, which is impossible for it and has not been observed in the deaf person.
Furthermore, entities generally possess effects that are mutually incompatible,
since the effect of one thing is not observed elsewhere.
Now, how is this impossibility of a common effect to be understood?
But was it not said that [the effect is not seen there] because of its non-perception?
In that case, it is not impossible.
For one for whom the world is non-dual, how can there be non-perception when the entire collection of effects is seen in one place alone?

In that case, since the difference must first be established for there to be non-perception therein, and since the establishment of the difference depends on that non-perception, the inference of difference is untenable due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Now, it might be thought:
"Because of seeing what was not seen before"—
that is incorrect, because we observe successive effects even from a single cause.
It might be argued as follows:
If there were absolute non-difference, the observation and non-observation of effects would not be tenable,
because there would be no distinction [between them]. Therefore, the difference in effects does not subvert non-difference.
Without subverting that [perception], there would be an inference of a mere particularity;
and we do not at all disregard that as being within the domain of conceptual construction,
because it is impossible for it to exist as a real entity.
Because identity and difference are both impossible.

For one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and does not admit that the particular has any identity [with its cause], how could there be the production of an effect possessing a nature identical [to its cause] when there is no difference in the nature of the cause?
Now, even for those things that perish without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśa*), the effect is identical because it is non-different from its object of conceptual construction (*kalpanāviṣaya*).
Alas! In that case, since the difference in effects is established precisely through the difference in their objects of conceptual construction, the postulation of a difference in causes is futile.
Or, if there is no difference in the effect... [or: if there is no difference in the effect by means of the non-difference of the effect—according to the edition].
If one were to require that there be no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the causes,
this would contradict the fact that a single effect arises from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that possess distinct intrinsic natures,
just as visual consciousness arises from the eye and other factors [or, according to Ms A, the cognition of form and so forth].
[Objection: Just as, then,
for the non-difference of the nature of the effect, the non-difference of the nature of the cause is not required, so too, for its difference, the difference of the cause should also not be required.
Moreover, even in the case of a single effect produced by multiple causes, the distinction among the objects of the causal operations has been described by that very [author],
as in the case of the cognition of color: the eye has the restriction of grasping only color.
The nature of apprehension arises immediately from cognition,
while the form of that [cognition] arises from the object;
and if the similarity between effects were not produced by the sameness of their causes, [the inference would be fallacious].
Inference of a cause from its effect would not be possible, because it is possible for things of a different genus to produce effects of the same genus;
and if there were no difference in the cause, then the absence of difference in the effect would be superfluous.
Who could prevent the arising of something of a different class from that which is of the same class?

In this regard, just as there is no difference in the effect due to the practical non-difference [of the cause], so too there is no difference in the effect due to the practical difference; thus, there is no distinction.
This might be argued:
If difference were imagined, it would not be capable of producing a difference in effects;
for there is no characteristic other than causal efficacy that defines what is ultimately real.
This is equally applicable even in the case of non-difference.
For one might also think: "The cognition of difference arises from the observation of contradictory causal activities occurring simultaneously."
For instance—
the universe is perceived at one time as endowed with various contradictory properties, such as birth and death, increase and decrease, staying and moving, sorrow and joy; therefore,
it is understood that it possesses differentiation.
To this as well, the same answer applies by way of repetition: "by means of burning, cooking, and disintegration.
How so? First, he should be asked this:
What is the meaning of "contradictory"?
If it means impossibility in one and the same place, that is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Or if it means having mutually exclusive natures, [that too is not established].
Furthermore, since birth and the other states consist in the cessation of one another's forms,
difference is not established from this;
for even in a single fire, both the capacity to burn and the capacity to cook are observed.
For there is no plurality of phenomena without their mutual exclusion;
therefore, if there were such difference, nothing could be a single entity possessing multiple properties.
Now, contradiction consists precisely in the nature of mutual non-existence— that in a single thing, it both exists and does not exist.
From that, there is the determination of difference;
that is incorrect, for it is not the case that these two are merely properties (dharma).
How, then, could there be an understanding of difference from their opposition?
Furthermore, in the case of things such as a sky-flower, since both [opposition and non-opposition] are absent, both [the aforementioned faults] would follow.
Now, if you say that opposition is the relationship between the victim and the slayer—
Joy destroys sorrow, and sorrow destroys it;
the same applies to the others as well.
Even in that case, one that has not yet arisen does not destroy the other.
It does not have a different substratum;
therefore, it must be stated that it causes destruction while existing in the same substratum.
And thus, because those two are observed to share a single substratum, the inference of a difference in substrata based on their observation is not non-erroneous.
Now, properties (dharmas) that consist of both a positive form and its exclusion are contradictory—
such as permanence and impermanence, or corporeality and incorporeality.
From their connection, the cognition of difference arises.
That too is not the case, because it is not necessarily true that whatever exists in a certain place [must arise from it].
It pervades that [space];
for chariots and the like, or their conjunctions and so forth, do not pervade space,
nor do they pervade other conjoined things such as earth and the rest.
Because they are delimited.
Thus, although delimited phenomena depend upon an undelimited and infinite object, they do not pervade it.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence even within a single thing.
But one might think:
"The distinction between objects consists in the difference in their causal efficiency;
from that [difference] comes the cognition of distinction."
For if there were identity, no distinction would be tenable;
and thus oil would arise from milk, and curd from sesame seeds.
Likewise, when one thing is born, everything would be born.
It perishes and would perish;
otherwise, it would merely be a difference expressed by another word.
As it has been said:
"If [the cause] were to perish simultaneously with its arising, then everything would be applicable everywhere"; to this objection, the same answer applies:
"by means of the distinction between burning and cooking."

If the distinction between sesame seeds and milk is not established by the diversity of their effects, then how can one understand the difference between them? Furthermore, if it is argued that curd is produced from milk...
The restriction "not otherwise" means that what is intended to be known through an established restriction cannot enter into that definition [of difference],
for that would entail the consequence of the restriction itself being unestablished.
Therefore, the capacity to produce curd and its absence constitute the distinction;
from that, there is difference.
For it is not logical for a single entity to possess both capacity and incapacity with respect to the same object.

Furthermore, this conjunction with contradictory properties, which was the cause for [postulating] difference, has just been refuted. For just as long-lasting entities, when conjoined with properties of limited duration, do not become subjects of contradiction— whether they possess those properties or do not— likewise, infinite entities are not contradicted by those occupying limited space.
If it is asked how a finite phenomenon can belong to the infinite,
there is no room for doubt whether they are distinct or inexpressible;
even if they are not distinct, [the finite] is like a limited duration within a long duration.
Furthermore, for one who does not understand the point regarding the long duration of time, this should be recited again:
"by way of the distinction between burning and cooking.
Even though fire is a single entity, it burns some things and cooks others.
And thus, the burner and the non-burner are not distinct;
likewise, it does not produce other burnings or other cookings upon that very same object to be burned or cooked.
Similarly, although seeds and so forth are individually capable, they do not produce other sprouts.
Nor is it the causal complex (*sāmagrī*);
thus, there would be both the state of being a producer and the state of not being a producer.
Alternatively, if the power to produce resides in the single [entity] itself, [then...]
Why does it not produce another [effect], whether past or future?
Or rather, their capacity lies only in that [specific instance], and not elsewhere, even in something of the same kind.
Why? Because that [capacity] itself arises, and because capacity is to be understood through its effect;
thus, there is no contradiction between being capable and being incapable.
In that case, even if there is no difference [between the substances], there is no contradiction in the fact that curd is not produced from sesame seeds when it is produced from milk.
For instance,
that curd which has its origin in milk does not have its non-origination from sesame seeds.
By which [reason] would there be a distinction due to the contradiction between capacity and incapacity?
Why? Because sesame seeds are not distinct from milk.
Or, if it is argued that there is a contradiction because another curd does not arise [from them].
And that is not the case, because [the cause] lacks capacity elsewhere and possesses capacity only there, as is the case with seeds and the like.
For it is not the case that every capable cause produces everything of the same class,
since that would entail the absurd consequence that all effects of the same class would arise from a single cause.
Now, it might be thought: we determine difference because of the distinct application [of things] to purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*);
for indeed, milk is applied to the production of curd.
"It is not sand"—
this too is inconclusive,
because even when there is oneness, we observe its application through differentiation.
That very same objective entity is employed when accompanied by auxiliary factors, not when it is alone.
Now, if it is thought that [the entity] is indeed different [in each case]:
This is due to the distinction of limiting conditions (upādhi) arising from the proximity of auxiliary factors (sahakārin).
In that case, then, this difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika), residing only in its conceptual representation (pratyaya), and not in an ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ).
And such a distinction of entities is indeed admitted;
for even one who asserts a distinction based on momentariness, since that distinction is the same [in all cases], everything would be applicable everywhere.
Or rather, nothing exists anywhere at all, because its causal capacity has never been observed.
If it is argued that its existence is established because it is non-different from the object of conceptual construction, [we reply:]...
It has been stated that there is no distinction [between the two views], because for the opponent as well, [the object] is distinguished from such [a thing].
Furthermore, there is one who asserts both difference and non-difference regarding a single [entity].

Therefore, for one who accepts the intrusion of contradictory properties even in a single entity, it is impossible to distinguish between sesame seeds and milk on the basis of their being respectively the producer and non-producer of curd.
Thus,
this very [single entity] possesses a power that is incapable of bringing about differentiation.
When the conceptualization of a distinction between states is like that of fire, then it is futile;
for a distinction in action is perceived in a single entity, and the impossibility [of such a distinction] is unproven.
Furthermore, that which has not yet been perceived lacks the capacity to sublate non-difference,

because it serves merely as the cause of a particularity, and because such a thing— which is indefinable in terms of being either identical to or different from reality— is merely a basis for conceptual construction; moreover, just as non-difference arises from such a cause, so too does difference arise from a cause of that same kind.
Furthermore, because contradiction is either inconclusive or unestablished,
and because the systematic arrangement [of the Vedas] is inconclusive regarding a difference in application,
since that [difference] is established through an imagined difference just as through non-difference.

Furthermore, if both difference and non-difference were to coexist in a single substrate, and if both capacity and incapacity, as well as application and non-application, could likewise coexist in one and the same thing, then this would be some inconceivable excellence of power belonging to that very entity, capable of producing the entire manifold of distinctions— just as fire possesses the distinct causes for cooking and burning. When such a case is possible, the postulation of difference is groundless.
"Because that [result] is established even from a single one"— this is the previous conclusion.
This very point has been restated in a verse:
"Such is his greatness";
this is the extent of his power— that even though he is one, he is "thousand-headed."
Thus,

regarding the statement "that which has been and that which is to be," how can there be a basis for the conventional usage of various contradictory qualities and effects as previously indicated in the two preceding verses?
Therefore, from that which is considered perceptible,

or from that which is indicated as unseen in the statement "The Person alone is all this," or from the manifestation of the world through the distinction between the divine and human realms in the words "And also of immortality"— the Person is greater than each one and greater than the whole.
Therefore, in that which is infinite, there can be no inclusion of limited things, even those considered contradictory;
he demonstrates that very superiority with the words:
"All beings are but one quarter of Him."
Even the entire manifold of reality (*bhūtaprapañca*) is but a small portion of this; how much more so, then, each individual thing?
For it is thus:
The form that is "three-footed"— meaning immeasurable, infinite, and devoid of the manifold phenomena of death and so forth—
abides "in heaven," that is, in the state of radiance or in the state of supreme bliss.
In the solar disc, or in the celestial station;
for it is there that it is to be worshipped.
For that [cause] is indeed the locus of its perception; thus it is said to be "therein. According to another interpretation:

even if the cause is imagined to be non-different, why would there not be a different effect due to the difference in the state of the causal distinction, such as the difference in the effects themselves?
Or why is there no confusion,
or why is the established order not reversed,
even though there is a difference in the milk?
Oil comes from sesame seeds alone, not from sand; and yet,
even when distinct, the eye, light, and so forth, as well as arrows, horns, and the like, perform a single function.
And even though there is a difference [between the causes and effects], why is it that oil comes from sesame seeds and curd from milk,
but oil does not come from milk and curd does not come from sesame seeds? If you think it is due to the inconceivable potencies of entities—
Because they are inconceivable and non-derivable, the capacities of entities— such as "why?
and "how?"— are established through inference based on the observation of their effects.
From these [causes], there is the distinction and the determination of the effect, and not the reverse.
If this is so, let that excellence of capacity belong to a single entity alone— that which produces multiple effects that are both fixed and non-erroneous.
Since its existence is established by that much alone, the postulation of multiple entities for things is without any basis in valid cognition.
It might be argued:
"Even for fire, the difference in effects is based on a difference in its potencies;
therefore, multiple effects do not arise from a single cause."
In that case, if fire is also a cause,
how is it that multiple effects do not arise from a single [cause]?
Or, perhaps you intend for the potencies alone to be the causes.
To this it is replied:
Just as that which has distinct powers has a single, non-distinct form as its substratum.
Likewise, why is a form that serves as the cause for various actions not accepted?
If it is argued that a distinction in capacities (*śakti*) is postulated because of the contradiction of a single entity being connected to multiple effects,
and if there is a contradiction in one thing having multiple relations, [then the following applies].
How can a single entity be connected with various distinct powers?
In that regard, just as a single nature of an object is joined with various powers,
why is its connection with various effects not likewise admitted?
Now, if contradiction exists when there is a connection with various effects,
but not when there is a connection with various powers,
then a specific reason must be stated.
Moreover, since powers are non-different [from the substance], it is accepted that a single thing possesses a manifold nature.
In that case, its oneness is contradicted by the multiplicity inherent in its own substratum;
however, to say that it is contradicted by the multiplicity residing in other substrata as found in the effects is a fine statement indeed!
Alternatively, if the powers themselves are indeed distinct entities,
then the meaning of the substratum must be stated; or, if it is their conjunction [that constitutes the substratum], [then...]
If there were distinctness, there could be no conjunction characterized by the non-differentiation of forms;
nor could there be contiguity, for in that case, distinctness itself would not exist.
Because it would follow that any other substance conjoined with that power-substance would also possess that power;
for a substance does not become separated from its power immediately after [the power arises].
Indeed, it is not the case that color is not immediate to the substance of the eye immediately after [the eye arises].
Furthermore, because space and the like are all-pervasive, there would follow the consequence that they possess all powers, since there is no obstruction to their capacity for all objects.
Therefore, the substratum [of a power] must exist due to some specific assistance (*upakāra*).
In that regard, just as a single entity, though its powers are distinct, produces distinct forms of assistance through those distinctions, so too does it act.
Why, then, is it not accepted that effects are likewise [non-different]?
Thus, first of all, there is no apprehension of difference through inference, nor through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
But those who think:
"This is true;
perception is not sufficient for the apprehension of difference."
For the difference between entities consists in the aspect of mutual non-existence, and that is not within the range of the senses; indeed,
the sense faculty is capable of conjunction only with the aspect of existence.
And likewise, it is not even cognizable through an inferential mark (liṅga), because its connection [with any such mark] has not been observed;
nor can presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) be the cause for establishing the effect.
Since the establishment of causal efficacy (*kāryavyavasthā*) itself is untenable when difference is unestablished, it is improper [to posit] that [causal efficacy] therein.

Therefore, a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must be employed for non-existence, based on the causes that perceive existence; or rather, it is a distinct means of valid cognition, called "exclusion" (*vyavacchedaka*), which is different from the prescriptive means of valid cognition (*vidhāyaka*).
For it is dependent upon this that the non-confusion of entities—that is, their nature as non-confused—is established.
As it was said:
"And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon the validity of that [cognition]."
To them it is replied:
Because of mutual dependence, difference is not established by another means of valid cognition.
Without a distinction such as "this is not in this" or "this is not that," there is no cognition;
for indeed, that which is excluded and that from which it is excluded [cannot be known apart from such a distinction].
When those two are not apprehended, there is the cognition of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). There is no negation that does not depend upon an object and a thing to be negated;
for if it were existent, it would result in [the object] becoming empty.
It has been stated that there is no difference [between them]. Their words also say:
"Having apprehended the existence of the object and having remembered the counter-positive..."
"Mental knowledge of non-existence arises without depending on the senses."
Furthermore, if there were no cognition of those two as having unmixed intrinsic natures—
rather, because they exist merely as entities, there would be an absence of the distinction between the object to be excluded and the limit of exclusion—
then negation would be impossible, for in the case of a mere object that lacks differentiation, [negation cannot occur].
When something is required as an object, it cannot be that which is to be negated;
when something is required as that which is to be negated, it cannot be a specific object.
In that case, there would be an absolute negation.
And it has been stated that this [subject] is not tenable as either established or unestablished. For, for someone, from something...
If there were an apprehension of difference, there would be an apprehension of difference for everything from everything, because there is no distinction [between them].
Therefore, having apprehended two things as indeed distinct by means of this unmixed intrinsic nature, one negates the object [of the other] in the form: "This is not here."
The exclusion "this is not that" is to be understood through both possibility and necessity.
Nor is there counter-correlativity otherwise; and when a general object is perceived, the absence of a person in a post [is established].
Because there is no person [to perceive it] and because there is no means of apprehension,
the cognition of non-existence— which establishes a mere exclusion by accepting an established object as that which is to be negated— is observed within each individual.
And thus there is mutual dependence: the cognition of non-existence presupposes non-confusion, and from that, the establishment of non-confusion [follows].

Moreover, the cognition of non-existence does not arise from the mere non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because such cognition does not occur during deep sleep and similar states.
Therefore, it is accepted that when the causes for a means of valid cognition are present, the non-arising of that means of valid cognition is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.

Nor is there any difference in its own nature by which it might be a cognizer through an excellence of capacity, like the eye and other sense organs; rather, it is so because of its invariable concomitance.
Without the absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), there is no non-arising of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even when the causes for such means exist;
however, in the case of [the means] being absent, it would occur due to that absence even if the object of cognition were present.
Thus, like a logical mark (*liṅga*), it generates comprehension in dependence upon cognition.
And if that [cognition] is the cognition of another entity,
it cannot be established unless the difference between entities is established;
for the difference among cognitions, which are themselves to be inferred from their objects, is to be inferred from the difference between the objects of cognition.
And thus, since the comprehension of difference arises only preceded by the establishment of the difference between entities, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Furthermore, if it is argued that the self is non-transforming (*apariṇāma*),
that is not a state of stagnation (*stimitāvasthā*).
Because, in the absence of any cognition at all, no non-existence whatsoever could be apprehended;

therefore, even when there is a transformation into the form of the cognition of another object, the absence of that [specific] transformation into the form of its cognition is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.
And this distinction does not establish itself prior to the establishment of the difference between objects; thus, it is precisely the same fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
But as for those who say:
"The distinction between entities is established through perception alone;
for instance—"
While refuting the view that non-conceptual perception has a universal as its object, it was stated:
"That is incorrect, because a distinct form is perceived in each individual substance.
As for the confusion [of universals] arising from conjunction or inherence, [it is as follows]:
The claim that "it is removed by the means of valid cognition known as non-existence" has already been refuted. As for those who also—

They maintain that it is indeed another perception, following the initial determinative perception (*vidhāyaka-pratyakṣa*), which— having arisen through the assistance of the grasping of the object, the recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), and the requisite procedure (*itikartavyatā*)— is the delimiting factor (*vyavacchedaka*);
just as [this occurs] in the case of a determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), which arises subsequent to the grasping of the object and is mediated by the recollection of words.
Nor is it non-sensory, because that [cognition] arises from the sense organ when assisted by a specific mode of operation (*itikartavyatā*);
this is what they mean when they say that even the cognition "it does not exist" is of this nature.
To them, this very point must be said:
"Because of mutual dependence, difference is not established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"; that is to say, it is not established by another perception (pratyakṣa).
The cognition "this is not that" is either perception or another means of valid knowledge;
in any case, negation is impossible without a distinction between the object and that which is to be negated.
Furthermore,
a negation has no scope regarding things that are being measured as having a single form.

Moreover, since "pure being" (sanmātra) is perceived everywhere, there can be no non-arising of a means of valid cognition regarding an object intended as "other" within things whose nature is that [being],
because both [the object and its cognition] have "being" as their nature;
and because the term "non-existent" (asat) applies everywhere only where a means of valid cognition exists.
"Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the cognition of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
[Objection: But surely, there is no single, undifferentiated form among objects.
For that [undifferentiated form] is understood through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). (It would be understood, according to Ms A.)

That [identity] should be understood [as follows]: for one who has perceived a mere object, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in another object that "this is that very same thing," as there is for one who has seen a single cow when seeing another cow.
As for the persistence of the word and cognition "existent" (*sat*), it is based on etymological derivation (*yoga*), like [the case of] "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth.
For that which is the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is said to be "existent";
this [position of yours] is not sound.
If there were no cognition of a non-different form, it would follow that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is devoid of an object;
for there is no cognition of difference without exclusion (vyavaccheda).
There is no exclusion alone, nor is there exclusion accompanied by affirmation;
nor is there the operation of a means of valid cognition subsequent to affirmation.
It has been explained that affirmation itself is not exclusion.
In that case, if even one [element] were not apprehended, there would be a total lack of an object.
Furthermore, if non-recognition were said to arise from the distinctness of the cow, even while there is a persistence of the form of pure existence (*sanmātra*), [the argument fails].
That [recognition] would not occur even with respect to another cow, because of its difference from Devadatta;
for the kind of cognition of oneness that arises upon seeing Devadatta again does not arise in the same way with respect to another cow.
Now, there is indeed a connection between what precedes and what follows in that case,
but not a connection of one existent with another existent. Furthermore, sir, how can there be oneness through such a connection?
For those whose cognition of form is not distinct,
an object that is not distinct in space and time could not be a single entity.
Indeed, it is only when there is a difference in space and time that there can be a synthesis of the prior and the subsequent in the form "this is that."

And even when there is a difference of location, such as between a circle of cows and a circle of buffaloes which have distinct characteristics, the cognition of a single object is held to arise from the very first non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*), because it conforms to an identical form.
Furthermore, since there is no difference in time in that case, there is no reflective judgment (*avamarśa*) of the form "this is that.
As it has been said:
Even in non-conceptual cognition, there is the apprehension of an object that possesses a dual nature; this is what is called its characteristic, yet it is apprehended by the knower in its pure form.

Furthermore, just as one who has seen a water-jar (*maṇika*) does not fail to recognize it when seeing another water-jar, so too, upon seeing a bowl (*śarāva*), one would not deny the presence of the genus "clay" (*mṛjjāti*) there.
If that [genus] is indeed present there,
it is simply not as prominent as it is in another water-jar due to the greater abundance of its general characteristics.
Because it follows from a limited commonality,
it would likewise apply even to other existing things;
and this will be explained in detail further below, so let us refrain from excessive prolixity.
If it is thought that there are two cognitions appearing as distinct and non-distinct, let them be examined: first, these two cognitions— appearing as the recurring and the excluded— do indeed exist.
For in the absence of those two, the linguistic usage of "conformity" and "exclusion" would not be possible.
Nor is there any cause for the determination of objects other than the nature of consciousness itself;
if that [consciousness] were not the cause, even non-difference would not be established.
This is not the essence;
for it is not the case that the mere fact of being "consciousness" establishes the reality of the object.
For that too must be examined: whether it is contradicted by reasoning, and whether it arises from a valid means of knowledge.
Indeed, the determination of the reality of an object does not proceed from cognitions such as those of a firebrand-circle (alātacakra) and the like.
It might be argued:
"Direct perception is not sublated by reasoning."
True;
it has already been explained that the cognition of difference is not indeed perception,
just as, for example, the cognition of a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra) produced by extremely rapid conjunctions with all directions.

Even though that [cognition] exists, because it does not arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it resembles perception but—like the cognition of things seen in a dream or a fire-brand wheel—is not a cause for the comprehension of reality.
Now, one might object: "In the manner already stated, the arising of the cognition of difference is not possible even from anything other than a means of valid cognition.
Who, indeed, has said otherwise?
For there is no comprehension of difference from the perspective of ultimate reality;
if such were to exist, how could difference be denied? Or, if it is denied, how can there be any comprehension of it?
"It is not cognized" and "it is cognized"— this is a contradiction.
What, then, is this?
Ignorance is delusion;
if the object of cognition existed in accordance with its appearance, there would be no delusion,
but rather right knowledge.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a non-existent thing is untenable;
therefore, it is not defined as existent from the perspective of ultimate reality, nor is it defined as non-existent.
It has been stated that [this is] established in the world because it is accepted in all philosophical systems.

Furthermore, regarding these two types of cognition, four conceptualizations are possible: first, that there are two entities due to the distinction between cognition, through the division of the universal and the particular; [and so forth].
As those who advocate for conjunction (saṃsarga) have said:
"Or there is a single entity whose nature consists of both the universal and the particular," as those who advocate for non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) have stated.
Alternatively, only particulars (*viśeṣa*) are real entities.
Because one lacks the capacity to determine their absolute difference, non-difference—which has those [particulars] as its basis and as its object—is the domain of conceptual cognition.
For indeed, the conceptualization of non-difference is observed among things that are distinct, as in the case of the word "forest" (*vana*).
As those who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference have said:
"Alternatively, non-difference is the ultimate reality.

Because that which is undivided and infinite cannot be determined as such, and because ignorance is beginningless, there arise conceptual constructions of difference based upon it [ignorance] and having it as their object."
For indeed, a conceptualization of difference is observed in the moon, which is non-different, due to the diversity of its reflections in waves;
therefore, there can be no determination of reality without investigation.
In that regard, as for the investigation:
First of all, duality [is not established], because the manifestation of a single identity is impossible.

If it is argued that this [cognition] is produced by inherence (samavāya), that is not so, because difference has not been discarded. To begin with, there are not two distinct entities, namely the universal and the particular,
because they appear without distinction.
For these two cognitions arise as being in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa), namely: "the pot is non-existent" and "the cow is healthy";
they do not arise as being in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa), such as the cognitions of blue and yellow.
Nor is it by way of the relation between qualifier and qualified, as in "the staff-bearer Devadatta," because no such relation appears [in consciousness].
Furthermore, even if a relationship exists, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not possible when the objects are distinct entities;
for while the two related things are grasped as qualifier and qualified by either a single cognition or two cognitions, they are not grasped as being identical with one another.
Furthermore, the realization here that they possess a mutual nature is to be personally experienced by each individual;
for otherwise, if there were a difference between the universal and the particular,
they would not disagree [regarding their identity].
And because there is a misconception of perceiving a particular when there is actually the perception of a universal;
otherwise, just as when smoke is seen, there would be a misconception of fire being imperceptible.
It might be argued as follows:
The cognition of difference does not arise from relation in general, but rather from a specific type of relation, namely inherence (samavāya);
for that [inherence] consists in the essential fusion of entities.
That is not so; for even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), the difference in form (*rūpabheda*) between those two is not eliminated, otherwise there would be no distinction and thus no relation.
And thus, manifestation as a single identity is not tenable.
And this [appearance] exists;
therefore, a difference in appearance that is contradicted by it is not capable of establishing a difference in reality,
either because it is itself internally inconsistent, or...
Because [the two] arise as having a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatva*).
[Objection: Even if there is a difference [between substance and quality], inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause for their being perceived as having a mutual identity.
Indeed, this is its extraordinary power.
That by which it conceals the difference of objects that possess difference,
and thus they appear as non-different—
regarding this, it is said:
If it is held that its capacity for differentiation and disappearance exists even when there is a distinction [between the parts], 1.16.
Ah! Why is that not [the case] for a single thing alone, since it appears in such a way?

If you say that the appearance of non-difference between two things that possess difference occurs through the power of inherence (*samavāya*), then, alas, one must accept that the appearance of multiplicity belongs to a single entity itself due to its specific capacity.
The conceptualization of a difference between entities is useless;
for there is no distinction by which the manifestation of non-difference between two distinct things could be possible.
"It is not possible for a single thing to have various appearances.
[Objection: But surely such a capacity of conjunction is observed in cases like fire and iron balls;
since it is seen there, a manifestation of difference among things that are actually non-different can arise from conjunction.
There is no manifold appearance in a single [entity], because it is not observed. It is said in reply: "This property of conjunction is observed even in that which is single. (MBs 1.17)
Just as a single variegated color appears manifold, so too does cognition;
for indeed, even a single thing is seen to have various appearances, such as a multicolored form.

For that [whole] is certainly not merely a collection of blue and so forth; because if no distinct color were admitted in the inherence of those parts, it would follow that the whole is devoid of color,
and yet the whole cannot indeed be devoid of color.
For in the absence of the formative factors of color (rūpa-saṃskāra), it would not be visible to the eye.
Nor does its visibility follow from inherence in a colored substance (rūpi-samavāya), as is the case with number, action, and so forth.
For it has been said thus:
"Perception [of a large object] occurs because of its inherence in multiple substances and because of its color.
If this were so, every such composite whole (*avayavin*) would be devoid of color.
Now, if it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply because a colorless [whole] is never perceived, [we reply:]...
[KKS_62] Even though it is variegated, it is not formless;
and its form consists of the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth.

Likewise, proponents of cognition possessing the forms of objects (viṣayākārajñānavādins) maintain that cognitions of cities, the three worlds, and so on, appear with the forms of various objects even in the absence of external differentiation.
Furthermore, because they are not distinct from the single reality of consciousness (*buddhitattva*), the forms of objects do not differ even from one another, let alone from consciousness itself.
This might be argued:
Even a variegated form appears as such only due to a relation characterized by inherence-in-that-which-inheres-in-the-same-substratum (ekārthasamavetasamavāya) arising from conjunction;
that is incorrect, because:
Nor is the connection between related things a conjunction, because of the intervention [of space].
For conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is indeed contact (*saṃsarga*);
and from that follows the appearance of each other's form.
And that [appearance] is possible when there is no intervention.

But it is not so when there is an intervention by their own respective substrates. Even with the intervention of a single [substrate], there is no conjunction between the forms of the part and the whole; how much more so when there is an intervention by two?
Furthermore,
when all cognition in worldly discourse— which is conditioned by external factors— is unreal,
then the conceptual construction of distinct entities is futile.

For one for whom cognitions such as "the cow is white," which serve as the basis for linguistic usage, are based on the limiting conditions (upādhi) of quality and genus with respect to substances, these [cognitions] do not correspond to the actual state of things.
Because genus, quality, and substance are mutually distinct entities,
linguistic usage is not based on the objective reality itself;
for that which is not presented by the intellect cannot serve as a factor in linguistic usage, whereas that which is presented by the intellect does so.
Thus, since this conventional discourse is both excluded and followed by an object that is merely constructed by conditions, the postulation of a real distinction between entities is useless;
for such a postulated entity is of no use in conventional discourse, whereas the other [the conditionally constructed] is useful.
Indeed, it is for the sake of making conventional cognitions accord with reality that a distinction between real entities is postulated.

And since that [cognition] is conceptualized, because those [appearances] have another as their limiting condition (*upādhi*), there is no avoidance of its being non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*).
It might be argued:

"In the absence of a real difference between things, a conventional cognition (*vyāvahārika-vijñāna*)—which grasps both the inclusive and the exclusive aspects even though it is non-correspondent with reality—cannot possibly arise."
Because there is no seed.
Indeed, errors such as the perception of a person or silver in a tree stump or a fragment of shell are not without a seed,
for they are based upon a commonality.
It is said:
The seed of cognition that does not correspond to reality is not necessarily external alone;
for internal disturbances such as cataracts and desire are also observed [to produce it]. (MBs 1.20)
[63] Incorrect cognition does not arise solely from defects in the object, such as similarity and the like;
rather, it arises also from internal defects such as cataracts, passion, grief, and so forth.

In that regard, even in the absence of a distinction in the external object, the internal defect characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*) is the seed of conventional cognition; thus, there is no need for a distinction in the object itself.
Let it be, then, that one [entity] possesses a dual nature;
for in this way, the mutual apprehension of the essences of the universal and the particular is accounted for,
and one need not postulate an excellence of causal efficiency in the object that contradicts its actual nature.
Conventional discourse is based on real entities; it is not the case that the operation of conventional cognitions is non-correspondent with reality.
This might be argued:
The dual nature of a single entity is contradictory;
it is a logical impossibility for something to be both one and of a dual nature.
Furthermore, a universal is that which follows after other particulars.
Therefore, difference has a nature that is excluded [from identity];
for their oneness is impossible due to contradiction.
This is not sound.
Wherein do we have the conviction that something is "contradictory"?
It is that which functions in opposition to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

But as for that which is understood by a *pramāṇa* exactly as it is, if one were to designate that very thing as "contradictory" while it exists in that manner, on what basis indeed would one establish the distinction between what is contradictory and what is not?
Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) reveals that a single entity consists of both the universal and the particular,

because of the distinction between the forms of appearance as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), and because of the apprehension of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This, however, is untenable.
For it is not logical that such cognitions of contradictory objects should possess validity, just like a cognition of doubt;
otherwise, even the object of doubt would be of a dual nature, because it has a dual appearance and because its two appearances share a common locus.
Now, it might be thought:
"The cognition of a collection of forms does not occur in that which is subject to doubt, as is the case with that which possesses both general and particular characteristics."
Because there is the cognition "this or that," let there be no conjunction.
There might be conceptual construction;
but that too is not [the case], because conceptual construction is untenable with respect to a real entity (*vastu*). In that case, even a single thing would not possess a dual nature.
Because it is contradictory for a single entity to possess a dual nature;
in that regard, just as doubtful cognition is invalid due to its being a contradiction, so too is the apprehension of both the universal and the particular, because they occupy the same substratum.
It might be argued as follows:
doubt-cognition is not invalid because of contradiction,
but rather because it is sublated by determinate cognition.
In that case, however, where there is no definitive determination, there would be the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, just as in the case of sublation (*bādhā*), the invalidity of one [cognition] arises from its being set aside, so too in the case of contradiction (*virodha*), when two cognitions or even a single cognition assumes contradictory forms, there is a mutual exclusion between the apprehensions of those respective forms.
In that case, when one [of two alternatives] is excluded, certainty arises from the other;

however, when both are mutually excluded and possess equal strength, doubt remains. Thus, the apprehension of a universal or a particular from a state of doubtful cognition is not distinguished [from doubt itself].
Therefore, the description of one's own position is that the cognition "this object here is non-conclusive" (anaikāntika) is well-ascertained.
Moreover,
if oneness and difference were to coexist without contradiction, there would be no dual nature, just as a portion cannot be devoid of one of its two aspects.
Necessarily, by this person who establishes both difference and non-difference among categories—
just as it is maintained that while the universal is non-different, the particulars are different— the definitions of difference and non-difference must be stated.
In this context, the opposition of forms (*rūpavirodha*), which is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), is the definition of difference;
its opposite is the definition of non-difference.
For it is through the opposition of forms—that is, through the synonym of mutual non-existence—that specific particulars (*viśeṣa*) are differentiated.
Even while those [particulars] are being divided, the universal remains undivided; for the opposite is not the case.
In that regard, if there were a contradiction between the universal and the particular in their own nature, it would be a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).
There is no unity [between them] as there is none between distinct things.
Now, if you accept a contradiction in their essential natures because the cognitions of the universal and the particular arise with a common substratum,
then it cannot be that one thing has a dual nature.
Because there is no contradiction in the intrinsic natures of the universal and the particular, duality is untenable in the absence of a distinction between them;

just as the universal aspect is not dual-natured, nor is the particular aspect, due to the absence of contradiction in their nature— for in that case, when one [aspect] is undivided, duality cannot exist.

Likewise, if there is no contradiction in their essential natures regarding the cognition of co-referentiality between the universal and the particular, then there is no mutual exclusion of their identities.
Duality is not tenable;
furthermore, if there is a contradiction in form,
there is no unity.
If it is thought:
"Multiplicity does not arise from a contradiction in intrinsic nature,
nor does unity arise from its absence."

Since there is no contradiction in their essential natures (*svarūpa*), duality would not exist between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) merely because one part [of them] exists like the other; rather, duality arises from the difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*) as perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*). And since the universal and the particular are apprehended as being mutually identical, even though there is no contradiction in their essential natures characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), duality exists due to the difference in form as perceived by the intellect.

In the case of a part, however, there is oneness due to the non-difference of its form; therefore, because a single entity is grasped by two distinct cognitions, it possesses a dual nature. To this, it is replied:
If this [cognition of oneness] occurs only with respect to a portion of the object due to the cognition of oneness, then that [oneness] does not exist in the thing-in-itself.
If it does not exist, how can there be oneness? If it does exist, how can there be a dual nature?
If, then, because cognition grasps a single form, there is no difference in the part,
the object itself must be examined:
even in that case, does cognition grasp a single form or not?
In that regard, if the cognition of an object does not apprehend it as having a single form—
since an object consists of both the universal and the particular— it must be apprehended by a cognition of two forms.

How can there be unity of an entity? Because the non-difference characterized by non-difference— the identity of form with cognition— is absent, while the difference characterized by difference— the diversity of forms— is present.
Now, if cognition apprehends an object as having only a single form,
and not as possessing a dual nature consisting of parts; or if it is thought:
The definition of difference consists in a distinction in the nature of cognition and the absence of mutual identity.
In that regard, particulars such as cows and the like are apprehended by cognitions of distinct forms and are mutually non-identical;
however, this is not the case for the universal and the particular,
because they are understood as being mutually identical despite the difference in the forms of their respective cognitions.
Even so, because the universal and the particular lack the characteristic of difference, they do not possess a dual nature, as has been stated regarding [the case of] parts.
If one should think:
The non-difference of the form of the cognition and the mutual apprehension of their own natures are the two characteristics of non-difference.
In that regard, there is oneness of the part because its form is non-different [from the whole],
and because both are perceived as having each other's nature; however,
for the particulars, there is no non-distinction of form within the cognition.
They are not distinct because they do not possess each other's nature;
for even if there were the characteristic of non-difference consisting in the possession of each other's nature,
and if the characteristic of difference— consisting in the absence of both— were non-existent, [they would still be non-distinct].
There is no dual nature;
nor is it logical for a single non-difference to have two characteristics,
for it is the non-difference of characteristics that establishes non-difference.
And its difference [would entail] difference;
if identity exists even when there is a difference in characteristics,
and if otherness exists even when there is no difference in characteristics, [then identity and otherness would be indistinguishable].
The definition itself would become meaningless;

moreover, if there were no distinction between the universal and the particular, the futility of a subsequent cognition would result, just as it occurs when [the object] is already grasped in a single aspect.
If it is argued that there is meaningfulness due to diversity, why is there not meaninglessness due to oneness?
The very occurrence of a subsequent cognition excludes the identity of the universal and the particular as a single entity;
for that [subsequent cognition] is meaningful only when there is a difference in nature, as in the case of distinct objects,
because it consists in the apprehension of what was previously unapprehended.
But if there were identity, just as no distinct cognition is sought for the division between the universal and the particular once they have been apprehended by their own respective cognitions,
so too a distinct cognition would not be required after the cognition of the universal for the apprehension of the particular;
nor would a distinct cognition be required after the cognition of the particular for the apprehension of the universal.
Now, if there were no absolute non-distinction between the universal and the particular,
but rather a distinction as well,
then [the universal] would possess meaning through that distinction.
That is incorrect. Even so, how is it established that [the word] possesses meaningfulness because of its distinction, just as [a distinct object] does?
But is there not, on the other hand, futility— like that of a single part— due to non-difference?
For when difference and non-difference are equal, why is it that there is no apprehension by a single cognition on account of difference?
But is it not the case that because there is no distinction [between the two], there is no apprehension [of them separately], and thus other cognitions are redundant?
Furthermore, the absence of an effect when there is an absence of a cause is established by its very nature as a general rule (*autsargika*);
the presence of an effect when there is a presence of a cause is the exception (*apavāda*) to that.
In that case, because there is a causal relationship within non-difference, it is logical that both are apprehended by a single cognition alone.
It cannot be said that, despite their unity, there is no cause for the apprehension of either one.
Even if it were somehow claimed that such a cause does not exist;
Nevertheless, there is still [the possibility of this], because of oneness;
