for in that case, the state of being the effect would follow from the state of being the cause,
since that [oneness] is the cause.
But non-existence is not the cause of non-existence;
rather, non-existence is established by its own nature as the effect. Its causal basis is that which brings about the cessation of the existence of the effect.
And that reason exists in both cases for the time being;
however, non-existence is irrelevant,
because it is not a cause.
Moreover, the universal is not the essence of the thing, nor is the particular; rather, it is the manifold itself.
Since that [manifold] lacks continuity, this doctrine of difference arises from a mere change in terminology.
For one for whom a single entity possesses both natures, neither the universal alone nor the particular alone constitutes the essence of that entity;
for if it were either of those alone, it would follow that there is a distinction between entities.
Therefore, the variegated nature of an entity consists of both forms combined.
Furthermore, there is no persistence of the variegated [entity] elsewhere;
and that which does persist is not of the nature of a real entity.
Thus, by resorting to another term, it is established through that other term or through a reason that differences alone are real, or that a single thing is dual-natured.
Because that which follows [the object] lacks the nature of a real entity, it is the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
It might be argued: "Let it not be a real entity; however, its being a part thereof is not denied."
Otherwise, even conceptual construction would not exist without a seed.
Furthermore, what is this so-called "aspect"?
It is certainly not the thing-in-itself.
It has been stated that if a thing were of the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) alone, the consequence would be its differentiation.
Nor is there a thing that is itself a thing distinct from the thing [itself], because that would entail the existence of three things: the universal, the particular, and their possessor.
Now, it is neither the entity itself nor something other than the entity;
by process of elimination, it is the object of conceptual construction, indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality.
But surely a part is neither a distinct entity from the whole, nor is it the whole itself?
Because it lacks parts in both ways;
nor is it a non-entity, for that very reason.
Indeed, a sky-flower does not become a part of anything.
In that case, if the parts are pervasive, then the entity itself must be pervasive, because it is not distinct from them.
This is not sound.
Since another part is not pervasive, why is the entity itself not non-pervasive?
Rather, it lacks pervasion (ananugama), because it consists of a collection and thus ceases to exist even in the absence of a single member.
To explain:
Alternatively, the entity (*vastu*) consists of the universal and the particular in mutual dependence,
or it is their aggregate;
in either case, since there is no particular apart from [the universal], there is no persistence of the entity.
If each [aspect] were a real entity independently, then no single entity could possess the nature of both; thus it is well said:
"Because that [entity] lacks continuity, this doctrine of difference is merely another name for the same thing.
Or else, because all entities are non-different from that [ultimate reality], they are not truly [different] from it.
The recourse to the doctrine of non-duality would be by means of another mode of expression.
Alternatively, if one follows the reality by means of the persistence of its constituent parts, there is the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda).
For instance,
a cow is first of all a cow in itself.
Because it conforms to the nature of existing substance and so forth, and because it conforms to the entity of a horse, it is a horse.
Thus, in this way, a cow is both a cow and a horse;
for even a horse is a cow, by virtue of its conformity with the entity of a cow through its adherence to the nature of existing substance and so forth.
Thus, in this way, even a horse is both a horse and a cow;

likewise, because all entities are neither identical to nor different from that [reality] through their existence and non-existence, it has been stated by another mode of expression that the world is non-dual (advaita).
True, duality also exists.
Because there is non-difference [of the universal] from its presence and absence;
this is not sound.
For if a cow were also a horse, then a cow would be a horse and a horse would be a cow.
How, then, can there be any difference [between them]?
Even the expression "a cow and a horse" (or "both a cow and a horse") is likewise devoid of any basis for denoting a distinction.
For this [distinction] is possible only when the difference between a cow and a horse is established.

However, if "cowness" and "horseness" were to apply to each [individual] cow and horse respectively, there would be no difference [between them], and thus that [distinction] would be entirely without foundation.
[Objection: But surely, the establishment of their distinctness follows from the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the specific parts.
And thus, the world consists of both duality and non-duality.
Now, if difference is established through the exclusion of specific qualities,
is there no conformity with another entity because the thing possesses both forms?
The nature of a horse does not become the nature of a cow;
yet, if there is a continuity [of identity], would a horse also become a cow?

In that regard, it was stated in the previous section that the theory of difference (*bhedavāda*) [is untenable] because the entity lacks persistence and because that which persists is not a real entity.
Now, even though there is the exclusion of specific qualities (*viśeṣavyāvṛtti*), that entity persists; thus, "it becomes a cow" (and according to the edition, "it also becomes a horse").
How is their difference established? If it is thought:
"The entity 'cow' is both inclusive and non-inclusive;
thus, a horse is a cow."
A cow is indeed a cow; for in that case, the entity "cow" certainly exists. Therefore, its distinctness [from other entities] is established.
Now, how should the subject of the cow be explained? Is it that which is necessarily a cow,
or is it that which is not necessarily so?
In that regard, according to the first conception, there is no persistence of the entity; thus, entities are non-continuous.
According to the second, because one entity persists through another entity, there is non-duality (*advaita*).

In every case, by whatever specific characteristic one establishes this entity "cow" as distinct from the entity "horse," since that which possesses that specific characteristic does not persist [in others], there is the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*).

Now, because of the fault of non-continuity (*ananvaya*), the doctrine of non-difference (*abhedavāda*) does not rely on any particularity; thus, the conceptualization of both duality and non-duality is untenable.
By this, the perspective (*naya*) of those who take substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*) as their objects is refuted;
for even among them, there is either only the perspective of substance or only the perspective of modification.
And those [things]—substance (*dravya*) is eternal, such as clay, gold, and so forth.
Of that... [Ms A; tasya tu]
And its modifications— such as the jar, the necklace, and so forth— which are called "particulars" (viśeṣa), are non-separate [from it] whether they pass away or come into being;
yet they are not the substance itself.
Because it possesses stability,
and they do not deviate from it absolutely, since no difference is perceived.
Because the substance itself is perceived in the form of a necklace and so forth, the object thus consists of both substance and mode.
Now, (Ms B; atha – edition)
If it were merely the substance,
then since nothing is produced or destroyed when a *vardhamānaka* (a type of vessel) is broken to fashion a *rucaka* (a necklace), those who desire [either] would experience neither joy nor sorrow.
On the other hand, if it were merely a mode (*paryāya*), [the same fault would apply].
For one who desires gold, neutrality would not exist.
For if gold were merely a mode (paryāya), then since the gold would perish upon the destruction of that mode, how could there be neutrality when the mode is destroyed—
or even when it arises?

Therefore, because a real entity consists of both substance and modes, and because arising, persistence, and destruction are possible within a single locus, they maintain that while the persistence of the substantial form constitutes neutrality (*mādhyasthya*),
joy and sorrow are respectively accounted for by the arising and destruction of the two modes.
Their theory as well is refuted by this very same method;
for,
even if their [atoms] were to possess connection with another entity, they would consist of mere substance, since there would be no parts.

Now, if it does not follow through to the entity (*vastu*)— since an entity consists of both substance (*dravya*) and modes (*paryāya*)— and because one mode does not persist in another mode, then entities would be non-concomitant and possess an exclusive nature (*vyāvṛtta-svabhāva*).
For that which is imagined as persisting would, by its very nature, lack substantiality and be merely a mode (*paryāyamātra*).
For that which is stable is called a substance (*dravya*),
yet there exists no single entity whatsoever that is stable in this manner;
rather, the conceptualization of a portion extracted from a thing as being stable is merely a construction.
Because the object is manifold,
whereas that [consciousness] is not so; and furthermore:

Because arising, persistence, and destruction are co-inherent in a single entity, it would follow that joy, indifference, and sorrow must either all exist or none exist at once; this is a logical impossibility.
For one for whom the modes (paryāya) are indeed distinct from the substance (dravya),
there is neutrality for one seeking the substance alone, because there is no destruction of the persistence of the substance and no production of anything new;
whereas for one seeking the necklace (rucaka), there is joy due to the production of that new thing.
For one who desires a *vardhamānaka* [vase], grief arises from its destruction;
such a distinction is established for him,
but not for one for whom the substance (*dravya*) is not something other than its successive states (*paryāya*).
But for one who holds that the substance is not other than its modes—
such that the modes are not distinct from the substance—
for him, when origination, persistence, and destruction are co-inherent in a single locus, one who seeks the substance would remain indifferent [toward the modes].
And it should not be so;
joy and sorrow might both occur, or they might not occur;
for that substance does not remain fixed at all.
The new arises and the old perishes;
therein, due to the destruction of the former and the arising of the new, there would be joy and sorrow, and not equanimity.
Furthermore, it would result in the untenable consequence that neutrality would exist [only] upon the persistence [of the object];
likewise, for one desiring a *vardhamānaka* vessel, there would be grief due to its destruction.
And it would not exist because of its persistence;
and yet there would be joy due to the arising of that which was previously non-existent,
and yet it would not come to be.
Because of the persistence of the very same [entity] from before,
and because of its destruction, there would be sorrow;
however, if there is also difference, this fault does not apply.
Why should it not be the case that there is also non-difference?
Or, if there is no absolute non-difference,
then there is no confusion [of categories].
Nor is the established position that there is no absolute non-difference tenable;
for one who accepts non-absolutism (anekānta) everywhere, there is nothing whatsoever anywhere that is absolutely [so], by virtue of which this distinction could be stated:—
"There is no absolute non-difference, and thus there is no confusion;
likewise,
there is no absolute [identity] of all entities from every perspective."
This entire world everywhere has thus reached a state where there is neither engagement nor withdrawal.
For when there is uncertainty regarding all modes of existence, such being the case,
this world would not engage in action anywhere after having ascertained a particular mode that accomplishes a desired end,
since that [mode] does not remain exactly as it was.
Nor would he turn back from it,
because he is not otherwise;
likewise, he would not turn back from the cause of suffering.
It is not exactly as it appears,
nor does it fail to cease,
because it is not otherwise than that.
Thus, alas, he would fall into a miserable state.
Or rather, as it was said:
"Whether joy, indifference, or sorrow should or should not occur is difficult to determine."
Regarding this, they might say:
"Since all types [of states] exist in all things without exception, what difficulty is there? For instance, joy, indifference, and sorrow do not exist exclusively."
"It is not the case that they do not exist at all.
To this it is replied: "It is not absolute for all things."
If, indeed, the existence or non-existence of joy and the other factors were not indeterminate— [that is, if it were certain]—
then one who desires joy would not engage in the means for achieving joy, because joy would already be present.
Nor would it be the case that [the person] does not act,
because of the non-existence of that [desire].
Likewise, one who seeks the cessation of suffering would not avoid contact with the means of suffering.
Because it does not exist;
nor would one fail to avoid it, because it does exist.
"Alas! The entire universe has thus fallen into a state where neither engagement nor withdrawal occurs.
In this way, there are not two entities, nor is there a single entity possessing a dual nature.
In this regard, two things remain:
difference is real, and the conceptualization of non-difference based upon it.
Alternatively, non-difference is real,
and the conceptualization of difference is based upon that;
in this regard—
Since difference is relative, it is preceded by the apprehension of difference;
one does not perceive a single cognition as one, nor does one perceive difference, for that would entail the loss of reality.
The conceptualization of non-difference does not occur by taking difference as its basis.
Why? Because difference is relative; it cannot be apprehended without depending on something else.
And difference that is not apprehended cannot serve as the basis for the conceptualization of non-difference.
Furthermore, if this [difference] were dependent upon another, its apprehension would be untenable;
for the two entities, "other" and "self," cannot be established unless their difference has been apprehended,
and it has already been explained at length that there is no apprehension of difference without the establishment of the other and the self.
But the apprehension of non-difference is not dependent on the apprehension of non-difference,
nor is it dependent on the apprehension of difference.
Because it would entail the loss of non-difference;
for when difference is apprehended, there is no room for non-difference.
In that case, having apprehended non-difference and taking it as a basis, if one is unable to ascertain it as it truly is, the conceptualization of exclusion becomes possible.
Just as in the case of jars and other objects, which are apprehended by a single cognition, there is a conceptualization of the division of parts;
yet, in that instance, there is no conceptualization of non-difference based upon difference.
For difference resides only in atoms.
And those [entities] are beyond the reach of the senses.
But surely even oneness is to be determined by a synthetic cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*),
and that [cognition] does not occur without a distinction [between the objects].
For if difference were not touched upon (or, if there were no contact with difference), what would be synthesized by what?
This has already been answered.
In that case, an object existing at the same place and time could not be one.
And if there were no such unity, upon what basis could there be a suspicion of difference, such that by reconciling it, oneness is asserted?
Moreover, this—that diversity is based on non-differentiation—is to be personally realized by everyone.
For it is thus:
the mere object is perceived by a cognition arising at the initial moment.
To claim that even difference shines forth without being conceptualized is an extreme act of temerity.

The first non-conceptual perception has as its object the mere thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). However, it is known through personal experience (*pratyātmavedanīya*) that the subsequent conceptual cognitions do not penetrate the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*).
This might be argued:
Perception grasps only that which possesses a specific form;
however, because it is untouched by verbal expression, that distinction is not perceived in the same way as it is in conceptual cognition.
That is incorrect, because it is contradictory.
It is a contradiction to claim that no distinction is perceived in perceptual cognition and yet a distinction manifests therein.
Therefore,
it is called an extreme audacity for one who contradicts direct experience itself, asserting that perception consists of a clear manifestation from which all non-selfhood is excluded;
to him, the following reply is given:
"It is said that perception is the means of establishing [an object]," and so forth; this has already been stated.
Furthermore:
And consciousness is established as having as its object the mere thing-in-itself;
however, even in the case of sensory cognitions, there is a lack of stability regarding specific particulars.
Since the existence of two distinct entities is untenable and it is impossible for a single entity to possess a dual nature, one of the two must necessarily be assumed to be false.
It is logical that the appearance of the specific [attribute] is false, as this is observed in cases of error such as the perception of silver;
however, this is not the case for the appearance of the mere object itself.
For the deviation of the mere object from cognition is never observed anywhere,
since that very object ultimately appears [in the cognition]. For one who has perceived its existence, the postulation of it [as being the object] is the simpler [explanation].
Because fitness is already established [in this case], whereas in the other case it would have to be postulated.
This might be argued:
Cognitions arising from the mind alone are established as being capable of [conceiving] falsity,
but those born of the senses are not;
for distinctions are apprehended by sensory cognitions.
And this is the correct view,
because errors conform to defects of the sense faculties. Furthermore, as for the opinion of one who holds [the following]—
Entities have excluded intrinsic natures;
therefore, they must be explained as having the nature of mutual non-existence,
or as being qualified by it.
Otherwise, the word "exclusion" (vyāvṛtta) would not possess meaning,
because it has mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) as its cause.
In that regard:
It is not possible for all things to consist of mutual non-existence;
therefore, let them be perceived as distinct only with respect to their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and not by way of their own nature.
When one thing exists independently, the other, which consists of its absence, is established; however,
all things cannot be conceived as consisting of mutual non-existence, because that would involve a state of mutual dependence.
Now, if it is argued that the qualification is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*),
then let it be granted that even those things which do not have that as their nature are understood as such through association with the qualification;
however, there would still be no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*).

Now, is it not the case that there is no such thing as mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) which could be either the essence or a qualifier of entities? This is merely a conceptual construction (*arthasiddhi*). If there is no such thing as mutual non-existence, [how can it be established?]
Thus, non-difference is established.
Moreover, because the universe is characterized by difference, it can be inferred that this difference has non-difference as its material cause;
for it is observed that the differences [of reflections] in jewels, swords, mirrors, and so forth, have the undivided face as their material cause.
And there is no production of another entity therein,
because of the contradiction in their transformation.
This might be argued:
Non-difference, too, can be inferred as being based on difference, because the non-difference of a forest is based on the difference of individual trees;
[we reply: no, for that would entail the consequence of the absence of difference.

For in this way, not even a single atom is indivisible; for even that non-difference would itself depend upon difference, just as a forest and the like do. Likewise, the non-difference of its parts would also depend on further differences, leading to an infinite regress. Since no single entity exists [independently], there could be no non-difference consisting of the aggregation of such entities.

Now, if that [universal] were to reside in some [particular] alone, then its non-difference [from others] would not be based on difference; thus there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is what is being stated:
Just as in the case of the face and its reflection in water and so forth, difference has non-difference as its basis;
however, non-difference does not have difference as its basis in that way, because such [difference] is absent.
Moreover,
because each [part] is permeated by the whole, difference is considered false in its non-difference,
just as there is no difference in the moon despite the difference between its waves.
Because each individual member of the universe is permeated by non-difference, their difference is false,
just as in the case of the moon reflected in the waves of water;
for there, in each instance, there is the underlying continuity of "the moon."
Likewise, although the universe is diverse, each [individual] is "this" or "that."
The word *arthaḥ* is in apposition with the word *vastu*; however, although the particularity of the tree (*tarubheda*) is not false, [it is not the object of the cognition].
Furthermore, the conceptual inclusion based on non-difference as "forest" does not apply to each individual [tree],
for there is no cognition of "forest" with respect to each tree individually;
therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason] by that example.
And it is for this reason that it is said to be "each one.
Furthermore:
let there be the majesty of the One alone, such that it manifests as if manifold.
But because of parsimony, those things which are distinct do not appear as if they were non-distinct.
First of all, this proponent of difference (bhedavādī) must be asked:

how is it that there is an appearance of non-difference and a corresponding conventional usage with respect to things whose specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are mutually excluded? If [you say] it is due to similarity (sādṛśya),...
That [universal] is untenable in the case of things that are absolutely distinct.
Now, if it is argued that this is because the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is not perceived—
for who is capable of perceiving the exclusion of color in the case of gunja berries, coral, and the like?
This is incorrect;
for if that which has a distinct nature were not apprehended when it is not being perceived, then its apprehension would simply not occur at all.
Now, [the opponent claims] that because there is a difference in nature between ascertainment (*niścaya*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no ascertainment [of the object by perception].
That is incorrect, because we observe the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of both forms [simultaneously]. To explain:
Furthermore, in the case of Kālākṣī, we observe both the conventional usage based on the commonality of "cowness" and the exclusion from other cows;
and this [usage] is not possible unless there is a determination of the exclusion from other cows.
Now, this is because they perform the same purposeful action, and thus their exclusion from non-performers of that action is identical.
That too is incorrect, because since causal efficacies (*arthakriyā*) themselves differ, it is impossible for their exclusion from non-performers of those actions to be identical.
One thing does not have the same causal efficacy as another that is to be accomplished by it, such that their exclusion from non-performers would be equal.
Furthermore, the exclusion of the intrinsic nature of entities is not uniform because each entity differs from the others.
If, on the other hand, they lack an intrinsic nature,
how could their exclusion be uniform?
Now, [if it is argued that] it has beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*) as its material cause and does not depend on specific features existing in the object—
that too is incorrect, because of the restriction (*niyama*).
For indeed, only a certain appearance occurs only in relation to certain individuals.
Some manifestation of non-difference—(as in the edition)—is not tenable if it were based solely on latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, one must postulate that by their very nature, some things possess the capacity for a certain apprehension of non-difference while others do not; thus, the extraordinary potencies of entities, which are contrary to their [apparent] inherent natures, must be inferred.
That being so, because such a conceptualization would involve greater complexity,
let the majesty belong to the single [consciousness] alone— that which, though one, appears as if manifold— since this conceptualization involves less complexity.
But those superior capacities do not belong to distinct [entities],
such that these appear as if they were non-distinct (*abhinnā ivāvabhāsante*); and yet, there are linguistic conventions of distinction (*bhedavyavahārāśca*).
Just as for those who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference, the conventional usage of non-difference is established in accordance with how things appear;
for it is thus:
for those who maintain absolute difference, there is a conventional usage of non-difference exactly as it appears.
It is not according to the actual state of things;

for even for those who maintain the theory of inherence (*saṃsarga*), since the object that is the universal is a distinct entity from [its particulars], the linguistic usage of non-difference regarding differences occurs only according to how it appears.
This is also the case for those who maintain that [the universal] is not a distinct entity.
Because those [appearances] are also variegated, and because that object lacks continuity, the dual conventional usage occurs exactly as it appears;
it has been shown that this does not follow from the actual object.
Thus, outsiders explain the establishment of continuous conventional usage according to how things appear.
In the very same way, those who possess discernment through the Vedānta speak of the application of the conventional usage of difference.
[Thus ends the section on Reasoning (Tarkakāṇḍa) in the Brahmasiddhi composed by the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra.
//The Section on Injunction (Niyogakāṇḍa)//

[KS_74] Thus, because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, and because it contradicts the injunctions regarding ritual action, those who maintain that the Vedāntas have only a figurative meaning when their literal sense is accepted are now being addressed: the authority of the Veda pertains only to matters that are to be accomplished (*kārya*).
It is not in the form of an existing entity;
for it has been stated thus: "Dharma is a purpose characterized by Vedic injunction."
In other words, the meaning of the Veda has *codanā* as its sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And *codanā* is an injunction that impels one to action; therefore, the Veda is authoritative with respect to matters that are to be accomplished (*kārya*).

However, even the Vedāntas, which possess authority regarding the duty of realization, bring about an understanding of the reality of the Self—which is subordinate to that [duty]—by means of that [duty];
therefore, they too do not transcend being centered on what is to be done (*kāryaniṣṭha*).
Thus, having raised the objection: "In that case, how is it that the Mantras and Arthavādas, together with the Upaniṣads... [the author continues].
For it has been stated: "An injunction [concerns] what has come to be, what is coming to be," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

An effort is made to awaken those who think that the injunction (*codanā*) itself, which makes known its own purpose— the thing to be accomplished— also makes known such matters as already existing entities (*bhūta*); for there are three ways of understanding Brahman.
First, there is that which arises from the word;
another, which follows from the word, consists of the continuous stream [of practice] denoted by such terms as meditation (*dhyāna*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and worship (*upāsanā*);
and another, which, having attained completion from that [preceding stage], is free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and consists of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Regarding that, it is said with reference to the first [alternative]: "The self-cognition of sound and so forth is not something to be enjoined;
for it occurs spontaneously to one who has studied the Veda, just like the understanding of ritual action. (MBs 2.1)
For since Brahman has a nature that cannot be apprehended by any other means of valid cognition, the knowledge whose object is its nature as apprehended through verbal testimony must be enjoined.
In this regard, that knowledge which arises from the word alone is not something to be enjoined, because it occurs even without an injunction, just like the comprehension of a ritual action.

Just as the comprehension of the meaning of the Vedic sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" occurs solely through the authority of that very sentence and does not depend upon another injunction, [so it is here].
Thus, the realization of the Self arises independently of any injunction, due to the authority of the statements that express the true nature of the Self;
for when a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists, the cognition of the object of knowledge (prameya) arises solely through its own capacity.
Indeed, when the complete means of knowledge along with its auxiliary factors is present, even the person's desire is not required for the arising of knowledge.
Since there is an understanding even of what is undesirable,
let alone [the case of] injunction;
he demonstrates that very independence from injunction regarding the understanding of action:

In this understanding that "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," no other injunction is required, because that would lead to an infinite regress; nor is this [understanding] established by the ritual act itself.
In the engagement [of an agent] through the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence enjoining ritual action, no further injunction is required,
nor one inherent within that [action itself]; for if it were another, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

Because even for the knowledge of their meaning, another injunction must be required, and because that [injunction], having action as its object, lacks the capacity to enjoin the understanding of that [meaning].
Now, it may be argued: "Just as another injunction is required for the apprehension of these..."
Regarding the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied," there is no infinite regress;
for the same would apply to the understanding of its meaning as well.
And there is an injunction:
"The entire Veda is to be studied.
This is an unequal comparison.

For even one who has not been prompted [by an injunction] proceeds to study the sentences of the Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) because they have been studied by other persons, and from that [study] he proceeds to study those sentences as well as others,

just as one incorporates the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) belonging to another recension (*śākhā*) through mere hearing. Indeed, it is not only the sentence one has studied oneself that prompts action.
As it is with one person, so it is with other persons as well;
because [the Veda] is beginningless, just like the study of that [Veda].
However, an injunction for understanding does not impel one toward understanding if its meaning has not already been comprehended.
If the comprehension of that meaning depends upon an injunction, then that [meaning] itself does not prompt one to act, because its purpose has not yet been understood.
There would be a mutual dependence:
activity proceeds from the understanding of that meaning, and the understanding of that meaning occurs for one who is already engaged in activity.
Therefore, another injunction would have to be sought, leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, the statement "the entire Veda is to be mastered" is not an injunction for a transcendental result (*apūrvārthavidhi*),
for its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action (*karmāvabodhana*).
Thus, the meaning established by logic is demonstrated.

Furthermore, if this were a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), then the knowledge of the meaning—which is already implied by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*)—would not need to be stated [separately]. (Note: *jñānam ucyeta* is the reading in the edition.)
Nevertheless, in the case of the cognition arising from Vedic sentences that express the nature of Brahman, a separate injunction is not required,
as is the case with sentences enjoining ritual action (*karma*).
Just as when [the duty] is established by a general injunction such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," no other [injunction] is required, for that would lead to an infinite regress.
Even though there is an injunction, it requires something else;
nor does this [injunction] apply solely to that [act],
because its object is the ritual action (*karman*).
Thus, even in sentences intended for the realization of reality, an injunction need not be expected,
because the awakening to reality arises from the inherent power of the sentence itself.
Furthermore—
Activity toward the fruit arises from the understanding of what is to be done, and that [understanding] follows from the injunction;
because of this mutual dependence, this is not a verbal cognition, nor is it a further [cognition] for us.

The purpose of an injunction is that activity which arises after one has understood what is to be enjoined from the word; it is not the understanding of the thing to be enjoined itself that originates from the word,
for that would involve mutual dependence.
Since activity occurs once the meaning of a word has been understood, and understanding occurs for one who is active,
there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), namely that the understanding of a word's meaning arises from the very understanding of that word's meaning.

However, mutual dependence has been stated because [in that case] both are equally untenable. But as for the realization of reality that arises from a sentence whose ultimate purpose is the realization of reality, that is not something subsequent to the cognition of the word's meaning.
But it is that very same [person];
moreover,
once awakening has arisen, one is not to be urged [to act], much less so when there is no awakening.
Therefore, when there is no certainty regarding a word, one seeks another [word] distinct from that [first one].
It arose [in the mind],
beginning with: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second."
From the sentence ending with "That thou art," there arises the realization of the reality of the Self because the words possess meanings that are mutually related;
what else, then, could an injunction accomplish?
One who has not yet set out on the path is certainly not one who can be incited to do so;
furthermore, if the arising of the realization of reality does not occur merely through the synthesis of the meanings of the words, then such a person is all the more incapable of being incited.
Because it is impossible for there to be an awakening to reality through verbal [knowledge].
It might be argued:
"Even when the manifestation of reality has arisen from verbal [knowledge],"
One should be led to certainty,
thinking "it is thus"; that is not so.
If the ascertainment arises from that word itself, it has already been produced.
But if the ascertainment comes from something else,
then there is a desire for another thing, which entails dependence upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the word would not be the basis for the ascertainment of reality.

Thus, first of all, an injunction is not required for the sake of ascertaining reality. Now, it might be argued that the injunction is sought in order to eliminate the possibility that the meaning is unintended.
When it is said that "the meaning must be understood," it would be something to be known, not something unintended for expression.

Furthermore, it is held that even if there is a comprehension of meaning from a sentence, its *tātparya* (intended purport) is difficult to establish, because a statement whose primary object is an already existent fact would be purposeless.
Or there may be doubtfulness, since we observe that even when there is no intention [to convey meaning], this occurs in the case of *japa* mantras;
however, when an injunction (*vidhi*) exists, because the knowledge of the meaning is enjoined, the meaning cannot be unintended.
Therefore, for the sake of ensuring that the intended meaning is conveyed, an injunction must be sought.
That is correct; for words in both common usage and the Veda have their purpose directed toward meaning, as expressed in the principle:
"But the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [in the two cases]."
For it possesses the nature of a general rule.
The subordinate status of words with respect to their meaning is the general rule;
however, in common usage, there is an exception where, due to other causes, the word's own form becomes primary and its meaning is not intended to be expressed.
The same applies in the Veda as well.
Because the capacity of words is something to be understood by the world;
as it has been said:
"But the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from what is already known]."
Moreover,
the fact that the injunction for Vedic study has a perceptible purpose is not different here; otherwise,
the entire meaning of that injunction would be rendered unintended.

Just as in the case of ritual injunctions, where it is said, "For its purpose is seen to be the understanding of the ritual," one does not postulate another fruit from the study of those whose meaning is not intended to be disregarded, so too it is with the Vedāntas, since the understanding of the reality of the Self is directly perceived [from them].
And it will be stated that there is no futility in the realization of the true state of affairs;
this is likewise the case regarding the injunction for realization.
Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way.
Otherwise, along with the injunctive [word], the entire [text] would lack the status of having an intended meaning;
for while the status of other words having an intended meaning is dependent upon the injunctive word, there is no such dependence for the injunctive word itself.
And thus, if that [injunction] were to have its meaning unintended, the others would likewise be so.
Now, if the injunctive [text] is inherently intent upon the meaning because its purpose is seen [to be practical], then the others would also be so; consequently, that injunction would be useless.
An injunction is desired for the sake of establishing that knowledge is a human goal;
however, it is also unseemly to claim that in all cases the status of being a human goal depends upon an injunction.
The understanding that the realization of the self is a means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) depends upon an injunction;
even though the realization of the nature of the self arises from the words [of the Upanishads], the comprehension that it is a means to the human goal is due to an injunction—this too is not sound.
For, because it pervades the object of knowledge, there is no further fruit other than the cognition itself.
If it is claimed that liberation is desired, it is not so, because it would entail a deviation from reality.
For the visible fruit of knowledge is indeed this:
the pervasion of the object of knowledge by the knower, and its manifestation (its luminosity) toward the knower.
But that which is unperceived and occurs at a later time— that for the sake of which an injunction would exist— is not [the object of perception].
This might be argued:
It is also maintained that liberation is another fruit of self-knowledge;
that is not so, because it is not something to be accomplished.
This liberation is not produced by causes.
Because of the deviation from reality; for if it were an effect, it would perish, and upon its destruction, there would be renewed cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
Furthermore, the absolute cessation of cyclic existence is called liberation (mokṣa).
Is it not the case that even destruction, being an effect, does not itself perish?

True; however, this is said with reference to liberation (*mokṣa*) as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), characterized by unsurpassed bliss and unsurpassed sovereignty, because there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the destruction of an effect and its positive counterpart.
It is simply untenable for the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)— which consists in the absence of the future conjunction of body, sense organs, and intellect— to be an effect.
Although the cessation of the cause of bondage is indeed an effect,
even as an effect, it does not entail the consequence of being impermanent.
Nevertheless, since that [ignorance] is not distinct from the knowledge of reality, it cannot be established by means of that [knowledge];
for ignorance is the cause of bondage,
and its cessation occurs precisely upon the arising of the knowledge of reality.
Alternatively, liberation is stated to be the abiding in one's own nature in the passage: "Having attained the highest light, he stands in his own form.
And if it were something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it could not be the abiding in one's own nature.
Therefore, one would fall away from liberation.
As for that which [the opponent says]: "He does not... (or "And he does not," according to the edition)—
On the authority of the Vedic scripture stating, "He returns again," it follows that even liberation, as an effect, is eternal; thus,
one may rely on that [scriptural authority] even if it contradicts what is observed.
Since scripture teaches that there is no other goal [than liberation],

when one who has known the reality of the Self perceives the non-dual, pure luminosity of the Self, and ignorance has been completely uprooted, bondage can no longer occur due to the absence of its cause; therefore, scripture merely restates through a present-tense description that which is already attained, treating it as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

In that case, how could there be the attainment of infinite fruit on the basis of its authority? For instance, from the mere statement of a present fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*), non-return is not understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
nor is there any connection with a desired object (*kāma*).
Since the state of being something to be accomplished (sādhyatā) would otherwise be understood [from the injunction itself],
it must therefore be an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Furthermore, as for the postulation of a fruit that arises from an explanatory passage (arthavāda),...

That [desire for fruit] is also untenable in the case of knowledge, since its visible fruit is the manifestation of the reality of the object of knowledge and thus leaves no room for further expectation;
furthermore, its status as a human goal will be explained later.
Others, however, say:

Without an injunction (vidhi), a statement would be devoid of purposeful action and would merely repeat an existing fact; and repetition occurs only when the subject matter is within the scope of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Its validity transcends dependence on other means of knowledge;
it is established in the sense of an injunction, which lies beyond the scope of other authorities.
Like a sentence prescribing ritual action, it attains the status of a valid means of knowledge independently;
even in the absence of another's activity, that injunction exists solely for the sake of its own validity.
Without an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no cognition of the instruction regarding what is to be done.

A thing as it exists is understood to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which is already so; and since a restatement has as its object another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a statement whose meaning is an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) is said not to have [independent] meaning because it depends on that other means. Thus, due to this dependence, it lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*).

However, because the meaning of an injunction (vidhyartha) is not the object of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), a statement whose content is that [injunction] is an independent authority, like a scriptural injunction for ritual action (karmavidhi).
And the meaning of an injunction is not the object of any other means of valid cognition;
for there is no comprehension of it from anything other than the verbal cognition of the word "do" (kuru).

This being the case, although in a statement directed toward the realization of reality there is no activity subsequent to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning and thus no fruit of an injunction,
one must nevertheless seek its status as resting upon an injunction for the sake of its authoritative validity.
To this it is replied:
Does the state of being a restatement consist in the fact that its object has been established by another means of valid cognition, or rather in the fact that its object is an existing thing?
For even a statement whose object is an established fact [is not necessarily a restatement]. (MBs 2.13)
It does not make that [object] known by means of an object already obtained through another means of knowledge;
nor is it dependent upon that [other means], if this is what is intended by "reiteration" (anuvāda).
What, then, is restatement (anuvāda)?
It is the state of having a meaning not distinct from another realization;
it is the demonstration that [the object] has been realized by another means of valid cognition (māna).
Or is it merely the fact that its object is real?
In the former case, let it be dependent because its object is not distinct from what is apprehended by another means of cognition;
however, that which makes known even a real object as one not already apprehended by another means of cognition is not a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*).
It is not dependent [on something else],
because there is no further practice due to the contact with what was previously realized.
Now, another interpretation:
If it is argued that the cause of dependence is simply the fact that [the word] has a pure,
established meaning, then the reason for that dependence is its connection with another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).
In the case of the Veda, which has its origin in a non-human source, there is no [need for corroboration] even regarding matters of fact (*bhūtārtha*).
If it were merely a restatement of a matter of fact, it would be a mere *anuvāda* (reiteration); there is no reason for dependence [on other means of knowledge] therein.
It is not the state of being a matter of fact itself that is the cause of dependence.
Because even for the two [means of knowledge], perception and inference, which have real objects, there is independence; therefore,
whether the object is real or unreal, contact with another cognition is the cause for dependence on another means of knowledge,
as is seen in the case of memory.
For that [word], since its meaning is not distinct from the realization [of the speaker], depends upon that realization as its means of proof.
And thus, a statement originating from human intellect—whether it correspond to reality or not—is dependent.
For from it, there arises a cognition regarding an object that is indeed mixed with that [realization].
But it does not [function] independently regarding an object without depending on prior comprehension,
as it has been said:
"Moreover, from a human statement..."
Thus, there arises the cognition, "This person knows thus," but not the cognition, "The object is thus";
because the Vedic word does not originate from human intellect, even when its subject matter is an existing fact, there is no ground for its being dependent on something else.
This is because the confusion regarding prior apprehension is caused by human connection [to the text].
It might be argued:

even in the case of a non-human (apauruṣeya) work concerning an existing fact, there is the possibility of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward that same object, and thus it would depend upon that.
For instance, since another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) might possibly exist regarding that same object, its non-contradiction with it could also be suspected;
therefore, in order to preclude that [possibility], its corroboration by that [other means] must be required.

But when the object to be accomplished is impossible, there can be no suspicion of contradiction from any source, and thus nothing need be required. To this it is replied: "Nor is that dependence justified by mere possibility alone. (MBs 2.16)
For if those two were dependent [on something else], no distinction between them would be perceived.
Since both occur with respect to the same object, on what basis could it be said that "the word is dependent on that"?
Furthermore, why would that [scriptural testimony] not depend on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

If it is observed in the world that verbal testimony has as its object what is already apprehended by another means of valid cognition, then it follows that it possesses no authority whatsoever regarding that which lies outside the scope of other means of valid cognition.

For while it might be possible [for human speech] in the case of an object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because another means of valid cognition is available there, it is difficult to find elsewhere due to the absence of such a means.
Now, if the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition were caused by the fact of being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) in the case of worldly words, [then...]
It is not the case that [the word's] efficacy is produced by the power of the word itself;
rather, the word’s efficacy pertains only to an object that is not already intersected by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, it is not because of the possibility of another means of valid cognition that the word alone is dependent.
Furthermore, because that [cognition] arises from words, it would be dependent upon words.
What follows from its being dependent? It would be invalid (apramāṇa).
In that case, it is not logical for there to be a dependence upon verbal testimony;
for if its own validity were established, then one would have to depend upon its correspondence or non-correspondence with reality.
However, since verbal testimony lacks intrinsic validity, that [knowledge] is not a means of valid cognition by depending upon words.
It is indeed a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), because it is independent.
Why would verbal testimony lack validity?

Because it depends on another means of valid cognition, and because its own validity depends on that [other means], while the independence of the word [itself] would follow from its lack of validity; thus, there is a circularity of mutual dependence.
For if verbal testimony (*śabda*) were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object, then that [other means of cognition] would also be dependent upon it, just as verbal testimony is,
because there is no distinction between them.
Alternatively, even if verbal testimony is possible, it would not be dependent upon that [other means].
Even if that [connection] were possible, the word would not be dependent,
because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. Moreover:
Thus, perception and inference function with respect to each other's respective domains.
It would follow that there is no distinction [between them], as they would be mutually dependent;
even a sense-organ would be dependent when it has another sense-organ as its object.

If dependence were based merely on the possibility [of another means], then since perception and inference can both occur regarding the same object, they would be mutually dependent, resulting in the undesirable consequence that neither is authoritative.

Likewise, in the case of existence (*sattā*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and substance (*dravya*), which are perceptible by multiple sense organs, it would follow that each sense organ is dependent upon the other sense organs.
Now, if you argue that dependence belongs only to verbal testimony (*śabda*) when another means of knowledge is possible, [we reply:]...
A specific reason must be stated.
If it is argued that this is because we observe that the object is already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it has been said in response to this:

if this were a property belonging to verbal testimony alone, then, precisely because of its impossibility [in other cases], it would result in the lack of authority for perception and the like regarding their own objects, just as in the case of the statements of the Buddha and others.
However, when there is the possibility [of perception], its validity is appropriate—just like the word of a trustworthy person—with respect to an object of the senses;
as it has been said:
"And if that [word] comes from a trustworthy person, or if it concerns an object of the senses..."
"That is indeed not false.

Now, if this [Vedic] dharma were of human origin, then even for a non-human (apauruṣeya) word whose object is accessible through other means of valid cognition, there would be dependence [on those other means]. However, since it is not so, [the Veda is independent].
Furthermore, while some inference has as its object that which has already been apprehended by perception, the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] does not have such a dependence on perception;
nor is it the case that all perception is preceded by scripture, as is the case with perception whose object is the discrimination of musical notes such as *ṣaḍja*.

Likewise, even if human words are seen to have objects already apprehended by other means of knowledge, the same does not apply to the non-human [Veda], for its subject matter is also a real entity (*bhūtārtha*).
Otherwise, it has been stated that there would be a lack of validity because other means of knowledge would be even more impossible.
Furthermore,
because [the attainment of results] is impossible, the injunction regarding medicines and the like possesses independence.
It would follow that the worldly [conception] is preceded by the cognition of a person.

In that case, there is an application [of the word] and thus a mutual dependence; however, in the Vedic context, even that [application] is not preceded by human intelligence, and therefore its independence is asserted.

If the Vedic statements, which are focused on that [injunction] regarding the object of performance— the meaning of the mandate— are independent because no other means of knowledge is possible for it,
then [it would follow that] one who desires freedom from fever should drink this medicine,
and one who desires heaven should eat sand.
Thus, even worldly statements would attain validity as being independent and culminating in their purpose.
Now, if the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) therein were preceded by human intention,
then there would be dependence upon that [intention].

In the Veda, however, even the relationship between the means and the end is not preceded by human intention; thus, it possesses independence. Furthermore, the connection among the object, the person to be enjoined, and the injunction is, in worldly speech, fashioned by human intellect.
In the Veda, however, the injunction alone is not preceded by human intellect;
that too [is thus established], which constitutes its independence.
It is said:
Thus, it is precisely due to human intellect that there is dependence;
for even when other means of knowledge are impossible, there is dependence in that case.
If even a sentence whose content does not terminate in an effect of another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) were to possess dependence on something else due to its connection with a person,
then it follows by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the very fact of being preceded by human cognition is the cause of that dependence on other means of knowledge;
for in common worldly usage, such dependence exists whenever that [human cognition] is present.
In the absence of that [human authorship], because the Veda is independent,
there is no possibility of another means of knowledge regarding its subject matter;
yet even in the absence of such [independence], we observe dependence upon worldly convention in the case of secular injunctions.
Now, it might be thought:
"In the Veda, there is a focus on injunction (*niyoga*) and a predominance of application (*viniyoga*);
in the world there is no such dependence [on the Veda], whereas in the Veda there is dependence on the world. (MBs 2.22)
Vedic speech culminates in an injunction (*niyoga*),
and since that is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is independent (*anapekṣatva*).
Worldly speech, however, is grounded in the relationship between a goal and its means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*).
Because it has as its object another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is dependence;
this kind of distinction is not based on the inherent capacity of the word alone.
A word whose capacity is understood from common worldly usage is also expressive in the Veda.
This is not a distinction of power belonging to the mere word itself— regardless of whether it is connected or disconnected from a person—
such that in one case the meaning of the word is an injunction (*niyoga*), while in another it is an application (*viniyoga*).
Just as the word "cow" [denotes] that which possesses a dewlap and so forth,
and the word "horse" [denotes] that which possesses a mane and so forth; for since their capacities are understood from common worldly usage, they are likewise expressive in the Veda.

If the meaning of a word is its application (*viniyoga*) in the world, then its capacity is understood to reside in that very application, not in the injunction (*niyoga*). Consequently, even in the Veda, the authoritative meaning would consist solely in application.
Now, having known [the object] through another means of knowledge, a person employs speech regarding that object;
therefore, that [speech] is based on reality, while the other [means of knowledge] is established otherwise.
Now, it might be thought: this is not a division of the capacity belonging to the word alone;
for the innate capacity of a word consists precisely in its culminating in an effect.
For it is thus:
the meaning of the injunction (niyoga) is that which is to be accomplished (kārya),
and the connection of something else is understood as being for the sake of that which is to be accomplished.
But the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the effect is not for the sake of anything else;
therefore, because it is an effect, the niyoga has that [effect] as its primary element.
As for the person, he employs the statement there after having understood the object through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, an injunction (niyoga) is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition;
therefore, it ought not to be applied there. However, because application (viniyoga) exists in that manner, its application is appropriate there.
Therefore, human speech has application as its primary focus,
whereas Vedic speech, because the mandate (*niyoga*) is a task to be accomplished through capacity, has that [mandate] as its primary focus.
To this, it is replied:

Because it depends upon another means of knowledge, its object might be one that is capable of being established by another pramāṇa; alas, its scope is not such that it requires dependence on another pramāṇa.

If it is assumed that human speech has the status of an application (*viniyoga*) because a person employs words regarding an object already apprehended— due to its dependence on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— then its object is one for which another means of valid cognition is possible.
However, it is not the case that human speech is dependent simply because its object is one for which another means of valid cognition is possible.

Because an object of that kind is caused by dependence [on other factors], a person employs speech after having understood [the matter] from another means of knowledge (*māna*) in order to communicate it to another; it is not for no reason. Therefore, that [speech] is dependent upon that [other means of knowledge]. (MBs 2.26)
The intermingling of other means of valid cognition [in speech] arises from dependence, not from possibility;
for a person's utterance is intended to make known their own apprehension,
and therefore, in that [utterance], there is an intermingling of other means of valid cognition.
The meaning is: "this object may have been perceived.
Therefore, in that case, only possibility and impossibility regarding its perception would need to be considered, provided there is certainty regarding the perception.
Its apprehension is possible,
and he does not speak of that which cannot be apprehended; thus, there is validity in this regard.
Just as in the case of a trustworthy person regarding a matter within the scope of valid cognition;
however, where perception is simply impossible, such as in the case of the words of the Buddha and others concerning matters already seen,
and where the possibility of the utterance of speech exists even though [the object] is not perceived.

In that case, [the Veda is authoritative] because it lacks any other means of invalidation; however, even in the case of human speech, there is no dependence on that [lack of invalidation] simply because another means of knowledge is possible.
Therefore, [the distinction between the two is] authorlessness versus authorship. (MBs 2.27)

When the causes for independence and dependence have been described by the wise, even that which refers to an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) is dependent; therefore, it does not arise from human intellect.

For this very reason, since the experts in logic have demonstrated that being authored by a person (*pauruṣeya*) and not being authored by a person (*apauruṣeya*) are caused respectively by dependence and independence, they have made an effort to refute authorship by stating: "The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate" (*autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ*).

Since the relationship between word and meaning is innate, the word does not originate from human intellect due to its independence; thus, the comprehension of meaning from a word is not conflated with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is therefore independent.
But surely, even if other means of valid cognition are impossible, an effort has already been made [in the definition] with the words "when there is contact with the existent"?
True.

This is for the sake of establishing the restriction that "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition, and nothing else," but not for the sake of [establishing] that "it is indeed a means of valid cognition."

Now, even if other means of valid cognition were possible, if the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not undermined, what is the purpose of rejecting those other means of valid cognition? [The answer is:
It is for the sake of the knowledge of the true nature of *dharma*.

For if other means of valid cognition were possible, then even the Dharma taught by those such as the Buddha—who are held to be omniscient—could be apprehended through them; in that case, the true nature of Dharma would not be definitively determined.
This effort is undertaken for the sake of such determination.
It is for this purpose that the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is sought, and not for the sake of some unseen result.
Alternatively, there would be a sublation of the injunction due to its contradiction by that [perception],
or there would be doubt if they were of equal strength; therefore, its impossibility is established.
But it is not because of the possibility of that [non-existence] that there is dependence. [Objection:
Surely its non-existence would be what is depended upon. [Reply: Granted.
But a word does not convey its object by depending on another means of valid cognition;
for that which conveys an object does not itself depend [on such a means].
That which is required does not establish that [object].
For the mere absence of a contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a cause for comprehension.
Moreover, if invalidity were to arise from the mere possibility of contradiction, then even perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid cognition would be subject to it.

Moreover, invalidity due to the possibility of contradiction would be unavoidable even if [the Veda] were restricted to what is to be done (*kāryaniṣṭha*), because it is accepted that the cognition of an existing entity (*bhūtārtha*) occurs by way of its being something to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*).
For in that case, there is the possibility of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Because an existent fact (*bhūtārtha*) is the object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is described as being directed toward an action (*kāryaniṣṭha*).

For if it were the object of another means of valid cognition, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); thus, it would convey its meaning by depending on another means of valid cognition—namely, "this has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition."
Thus, it is not independent;
however, it is independent when its purpose is the accomplishment of an action,
because that [action] is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition.

Since there is no dependence [on other means of knowledge] in the manner already stated, it is well said: "Even though its object is an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*), it is not dependent; therefore, it does not arise from human intellect.
Now, our word-meanings do not participate in a relation without an action.
What has come of fate? Even that [fate] is easily obtained everywhere through one's own existence and other such means.
If it is thought:
"The meanings of nouns cannot be connected without the meaning of a verb;
for action is the cause of the conjunction of word-meanings, since in its absence there would be a state of expectancy."

Therefore, it is established that the entity such as Brahmā and so forth is not within the scope of words, because a word does not convey meaning when its conventional relation [to its referent] is unknown;
nor is it the meaning of a sentence, because the meaning of a sentence consists of a relational synthesis (*saṃsarga*),
and there can be no synthesis of word-meanings that are devoid of action (*kriyā*).
Even so, let action be accepted; and by means of that, let the establishment of the connection between word-meanings be hoped for. There is no purpose whatsoever for an injunction.
Moreover, that action [of existence] is easily available everywhere, even when not explicitly heard, as in the case of "asti" and so forth; for it is said:
"The verb *as* (to be), followed by the present tense (*bhavantī*) and in the third person, is understood even when it is not employed.
In this regard, a sentence intended for the realization of the nature of Brahman has its ultimate focus on the meaning of "is" (*asti*).
The connection between word-meanings therein is based upon that [Being].
And since Being is by its very nature primarily existent, the establishment of the qualified entity occurs through it.
Regarding this, they say:
There is no existence whatsoever other than being cognizable by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For instance:
that which is cognized by a means of valid cognition—therein...
The worldly convention is that "it exists" in the case of what is present, and "it does not exist" in its opposite; indeed,
no other cause for the distinction between existence and non-existence is observed.
If it is argued that [the existence or non-existence of a thing] consists in the presence or absence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), we say no;
for even those two depend upon the presence or absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain:
If the linguistic convention of "existent" regarding an effect were itself dependent upon another effect, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, even at the end [of the series], the convention of "existent" must arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone, and the convention of "non-existent" from its opposite.
If this is so, then let the conventions of "existent" and "non-existent" be based respectively on the presence and absence of a means of valid cognition right from the very beginning.

And likewise, a sentence whose primary referent is the sense of "existence" (asti) makes its object known only by depending on another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because being an object of a means of valid cognition is itself the meaning of "existence. To this it is replied: "Being cognizable by a means of valid cognition is not considered to be the [intrinsic] nature of the object."
For it is from pride alone that the notion arose: "I exist" and "I shall exist."

For this [cognition] occurs regarding fire and so forth when they are inferred by means of smoke and the like; otherwise, it would differ at a later time, yet it certainly does not arise in three ways.
The meaning of "it exists" is not the state of being cognizable by a means of valid cognition; nor is it the object of the cognition "it does not exist."
For it is from valid cognition alone that threefold understanding arises:
"There is fire here because of smoke"; "It has rained because of the specific swelling of the river"; [and so forth].
"Because of this specific rising of clouds, there will be rain"— in this case,
if the cognition takes as its object the domain of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it would indeed be a cognized object (*pramita*), but not from the means of valid knowledge itself.
For prior to the arising of the means of valid knowledge, there is no connection with a means of valid knowledge.
Furthermore, this cognition is based on its connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If, out of impudence, one were to claim that it occurs only at a later time, then its threefold nature would be untenable.

Because the connection with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is non-different [from the object], even when objects exist at different times, the cognition, by virtue of its own connection, apprehends the thing; nevertheless, it does not itself become divided, nor is there in this way any dependence on another.
Now, it might be thought: "An object is apprehended by a means of valid cognition precisely as being related to a self;
therefore, even for that which has the relation to a means of valid cognition as its object, there is no subsequent temporal occurrence of the cognition 'it exists'."
Because an object is perceived precisely as being related to one's own self,
even so, the word "exists" (asti) would apply everywhere;
there would not be a threefold distinction.
Because, in the case of every valid cognition, there exists a connection with a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, this does not entail a dependence on another means of knowledge in the case of a statement whose object is an existent thing (*astyartha*), since the very connection with that [first] means of knowledge constitutes its being an existent thing.
Alternatively, it may be maintained that its being cognizable by another means of knowledge occurs in three ways through an inferential mark (*liṅga*).
If it is argued that the inferential mark (liṅga) might also be dependent [on another], because its own establishment arises from that very same [dependency]; 2.33.
If that independence [of the Veda] is not prevented by punishments within the Veda itself,
then it might be thought: "It is precisely through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that [the object] is understood by means of the inferential mark (*liṅga*)."
Therefore, there is no subsequent time [for it].
And that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists in the three times; thus, it is of three kinds.
But what, then, is that?
It is direct perception (pratyakṣa). For instance,
when a vision has occurred, for someone, that which has occurred is direct perception.
That which is in the future [is called] "future," and that which is in the present fire is "present";
and this is merely conventional usage.
Because that [perception] is absent in the case of what is always inferred;
moreover, the inferential mark (liṅga) would likewise be non-authoritative due to its dependence on another means of knowledge.
If it is argued that there is independence because the existence of the other means of knowledge is established from the inferential mark itself, [we reply:]...
For instance: it is only when another means of valid cognition exists that the inferential mark (liṅga) is now a means of valid cognition;
and in that case, nothing else is required.
The establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs by way of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This rule is not prohibited even in the Veda;
for even a Vedic statement that is focused on an object is a means of valid cognition only insofar as there exists a means of valid cognition for that specific object.
In that regard, it is independent;
and the establishment of a specific object occurs through that means of valid cognition—this is the same [in both cases].
Its occurrence pertains to a non-worldly object (or, according to the edition, to an inferential object).
But it is not like the meaning of the Buddha’s words.
In this regard, [the position] is inconsistent because it accepts direct perception as the means [of knowledge].
It might be thought: "In this way, the validity of the inferential mark (liṅga) is appropriate."
Because another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is possible regarding that object;
for in the case of rain and such, another means of valid cognition is indeed possible. Therefore, the comprehension of the object occurs by way of that [other means].
But this is not accepted in the case of Brahman, which transcends all particularities and is based solely upon the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
In that regard, just as in the case of the statements of the Buddha and others, [it is said]: "This person knows thus."

Thus, because knowledge regarding supersensible objects is impossible for those established in [inferential] knowledge, there can be no validity regarding the object for those who teach supersensible matters;
the same would apply here as well.

However, just like the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) whose domain is a possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), validity is appropriate for a logical mark (*liṅga*) even though it is established upon a means of valid cognition.
That is incorrect, because direct realization is admitted even regarding Brahman upon the cessation of ignorance;
however, for those possessed of ignorance, that [realization] is said to have the sacred tradition (āmnāya) as its sole basis.
Moreover:
If being an object of cognition itself were existence, how could there be a threefold nature of the means of cognition?
Therefore, because of that connection, a threefold nature of the object is not tenable.

Furthermore, if it is by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) that the means of valid cognition itself is measured, and if being-measured is itself existence, [then the object would likewise be non-existent].
In that regard, because it is being cognized, every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed existent;
and what is existent is said to be present.
Since the means of valid cognition is present therein, [it applies] to every object.
It should simply be "it exists.
There is no threefold nature of objects based on the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition.
Because that which is being measured exists, and because that which exists is present.
Furthermore, this person should be asked:
is existence the connection with a means of valid cognition, namely the conjunction with a presently occurring means of valid cognition?

Is its opposite non-existence (*asattā*), or is it merely the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*) that does not depend on any specific time? In this regard: "Existence is the connection with a present means of valid cognition; non-existence is its opposite. (MBs 2.36)
If, in that case, non-existence were attained regarding the object of memory,
then there would be no connection with a present means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which is being remembered.
But surely, because destruction is possible in the case of what is being remembered, [non-existence] does not exist at all?
The conventional usage is "it exists";
this is true.
Even "it does not exist" does not exist.
If existence is the connection with a presently functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then non-existence is its opposite;
thus there would only be "it does not exist," and not "it exists."
Therefore, existence and non-existence are distinct from that;
if [existence] were merely the application of a means of valid cognition, then non-existence would be its opposite.
The retention of honey is achieved through a jar that has been measured and then lost;
once it has been measured, there can be no further desire to know its existence or non-existence.
