If existence were merely the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*) without depending on a specific time, then even an object that has perished after being cognized would be "existent" just like one that has not perished; for there would be no difference in its existence, leading to the absurd consequence that it could perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*).
If it is argued that this is not the case because there is a distinction between what has perished and what has not perished:
In that case, it is that very distinction which is the cause for establishing the conventional usage of "existent" and "non-existent," just as it is the cause for establishing causal efficacy;
it is not the application of a means of valid cognition. Indeed, this [distinction] is seen in the world to follow precisely that [usage].
Indeed, people do not metaphorically designate as "existent" that which has been measured and then perished;
furthermore, worldly people would not seek to know the existence or non-existence of an object already cognized.

Because the mere fitness for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established, and because existence (*sattva*) has that as its defining characteristic. Alternatively, existence is the fitness for a means of valid cognition.
That which has perished is lost; that which has fallen from it is displaced; and to say that it is "somewhere" while being remembered is likewise not beautiful.
Now, it might be thought:
existence is not the connection with a presently existing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it merely that connection [to a means of valid cognition] independent of time.
Rather, it is the capacity with respect to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since that [capacity] has perished and ceased, there is no consequence of its existence.
However, in the case of what is being remembered, because it has ceased from one [aspect] but not from another, there is no non-existence of everything.
This too is not tenable,
because it involves the abandonment of what has been accepted.
For instance:
Thus, existence (*sattā*) is described as being nothing other than the very nature of the object (*arthasvabhāva*).
Existence is the nature of the object that is fit for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogya*);
the distinction between the conventional designations of "existent" and "non-existent" is based solely upon the nature of the object itself.
It does not have the presence or absence of valid cognition as its limiting condition; rather,
this is merely a method of explaining it, and there is no contact with valid cognition.
Just as when it is stated that "an object capable of producing a cognition with a non-blue form is blue," the word "blue" is not an adjunct (*upādhi*) to the cognition of blue;

and since that [object] is denoted by the word "exists," a sentence whose primary referent is the meaning "exists" is grounded in the intrinsic nature of the object. How, then, could there be dependence [on other factors]?
Because it does not touch upon [any external] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It might be argued as follows: let it be that the distinct intrinsic natures of objects, which are fit for being means of valid cognition and are denoted by the word "existent," are themselves existent; there is no single [universal] existence.
Let it not be so; this is not what is to be proven:
namely, that the word "exists" (asti), which denotes the intrinsic nature of an object in every respect, does not have its cause in the application of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For if there were contact with a means of valid cognition, there would be dependence [on something else].
But multiplicity does not entail any fault;
moreover, if it were multiple, how could there be the application of a single, undifferentiated term? For instance:
A single word might function by relying on a qualifier or a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) that is non-different among things that are different;
or it might be a common term (*sādhāraṇa-śabda*) based on different causes, like the word "akṣa" and so forth.
In that regard, first of all, commonality is not tenable among things whose natures consist of infinite objects.
Because of the capacity for grasping the relationship [between word and object].
For words such as "eye" (*akṣa*) and so forth must either have limited classes (*jāti*) as their objects, or be characterized by limited indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*).
This might be argued:
"The word 'sat' (existent) is common to those objects characterized by the three universals, namely *dravyatva* (substantiality) and so forth; therefore [the universal 'existence'] does not exist.
This is not so;
for whoever denies existence (*sattā*) necessarily denies substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the others as well.
Indeed, for one who has seen fire, there is no tactile perception of it in water;
furthermore, universals, particulars, and inherence also truly exist.
The word "existent" applied to them is not merely figurative, because the cognition [of them] is not different [from that of other existents].
Furthermore, there can be no metaphorical usage (upacāra) without a commonality (sāmānya);
and if such a commonality exists, that very thing is the referent of the word "existent" (sat),
and that itself is existence (sattā).
Because the cognition is identical.
Now, it might be thought: in all philosophical systems, all categories of entities are subsumed under certain limited properties.
The word "existent" (sat) is a common term for all infinite objects that are characterized by that [existence].
That is incorrect;
for a collection does not exist without its members.
In that case, if [it were] by virtue of being the referent of the word "existent" (*sacchabda*), [then...]
If the inclusion were "the meaning of the word *sat* consists of these many varieties," there would be no exclusion of other objects;
in that case, there would be no inclusion of all objects.
Just as in the case of the statement "the referent of the word 'cow' is ninefold," it is not the case that others simply do not exist;
in that regard, no understanding of the true nature of the object could arise from mere disputations.
Now, it might be argued that the meaningfulness of disputations is not what needs to be established.
We do not say that the meaningfulness of doctrines is what is to be proven;
rather, proponents [of various views] accept some single nature of an object,
of which this [number] "five" [is a predicate].
The phrase "six," and so forth, is a summary of the classifications;
for without a single inclusive [category], there can be no placement of intermediate numbers.

Now, if the summary is based either on being fit for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogya*) or on the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), such that it is asked whether an object possesses this much fitness for a means of valid cognition or this capacity for causal efficiency—then [the summary is established].
Let the meaning of the word "existent" (sat) be indicated by those two alone;
the presentation of limited attributes is useless.
In that case, there would be nothing but a general term.
There would be no commonality of denotation;
and if the causes were distinct— as in the case of words such as *akṣa* and so on— then due to the difference in their causes, there would be doubt rather than the cognition of a specific meaning.
For cognizers do not entertain doubt regarding the distinct causes [of cognition] such as "the jar does not exist," just as they are free from expectancy in the case of "the cloth is white."
Likewise, the notion "the jar is non-existent" is also [not a doubt].
As for the doubt as to whether something is a substance, a quality, an action, form, or consciousness,
that does not belong to ordinary people.
Ordinary people, however, apprehend the sign as being undifferentiated.
Consequently, there is doubt regarding the meaning, not regarding the word.
Why? Because the cognizer’s sense of expectancy is satisfied even without the cognition of a specific distinction.
For where there is doubt due to the capacity of the object,
as in the case of "Let the tree be cut," regarding [the various tools] such as the axe, the hatchet, and so forth;
In that case, there is a state of non-expectancy even when the specific nature of either one is not understood,
because any [entity] whatsoever may be taken as the material cause;
otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.
But where [the meaning] is derived from the word itself, there is merely expectancy in the absence of a cause for understanding a specific [meaning].
Thus, a common term does not have multiple grounds [for its application].
Even a single qualifier would have to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and it has already been stated that this is untenable even prior to the arising of a cognition permeated by the word "existent" (*sat*), because [the text says]:
"Since cognition arises from the means of knowledge itself."
Thus it is by way of elaboration.
Moreover, even from the effect, it is determined that the means of valid cognition has indeed occurred;
in that case, how could there be its qualification?
Indeed, an object does not become qualified when its qualifying attribute is absent;

nor does a doubt permeated by the designation of something qualified arise when the absence of the qualifier has been ascertained, just as there is no doubt such as "Is he a man with a staff or not? once the absence of the staff has been ascertained.
Furthermore, in the case of treasures long buried in empty cities and the like, even when there is a certainty regarding the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
a doubt arises as to whether they "exist" or "do not exist.
Therefore, an existent object is something other than that which results from the application of a means of valid cognition.
Where this doubt arises,

even the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the word "existent" (*sat*) is not applied to things that have been cognized and subsequently destroyed, and because there is doubt regarding that which is being remembered, as it is permeated by the notion of existence.
Since that which possesses a connection with a valid means of cognition is characterized by such a means of cognition, it must indeed exist;
it cannot be non-existent, nor can there be any doubt regarding its existence.

Even for one who qualifies or characterizes the referent of the word "existent" by means of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), that person too could not apply the word "existent" prior to observing the effect.
Now, if one were to say that causal efficacy is simply the production of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the same objection would apply].
The cognition of existence would not arise from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.
Alternatively, if it is held that this [cognition] is conceptual and occurs subsequent to the means of valid cognition,
it would not arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*).

If, on the other hand, it is only that which already has its connection with the effect ascertained that is inferred by means of the mark (liṅga), then in that case there would be an absence of any object of knowledge (prameya).
For instance:
For the meaning of "existence" (asti) is indeed "having an effect" (kāryavattā), and that has already been apprehended.
To say that "having an effect" is understood by means of "having an effect" itself is illogical.
Furthermore, since cause and effect cannot exist simultaneously, a specific qualification (viśiṣṭatā) is untenable.
If, on the other hand, it is a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa),
then it would follow that even a past entity must possess existence.
And it has been stated that when something is being remembered, doubt would not arise;
therefore, just as the referent of words such as "blue" is the intrinsic nature of the object itself, and is not characterized by its effect, [so too is the case here].
It is not characterized by a means of valid cognition, because that would lead to an infinite regress;
rather, its own nature is established as it is determined by the means of valid cognition.
Thus, it is logical that the nature of the real object is also [unestablished].

For if the distinction between the conventional designations of existence and non-existence were based on the presence or absence of a causal means of valid cognition (*kāryapramāṇa*), then that very distinction would never occur; for it would follow that the distinction between the conventional designations of the presence and absence of a causal means of valid cognition itself would also be based on that [further causal means], leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman consider that the single nature of reality is existence (*sattā*).
Now, it may be thought:
Capability is not the intrinsic nature of the object;
rather, it is the existence of the causes of valid cognition. And for non-existent things, the causes of valid cognition do not exist.
That is incorrect:
buried in the earth, devoid of characteristics, impossible to perceive,
and lacking a perceiver, that which transcends everything cannot even be fit for such a designation.

Regarding an object buried in the earth, which lacks connection with the senses, is not perceived as invariably concomitant [with its cause], cannot otherwise be accounted for if it were not known, and whose observer has vanished— there exist no grounds for its cognition such as perception, inference, presumption, or verbal testimony. For comparison (*upamāna*) has similarity as its object.
The cause for that is utterly remote;
it transcends the applicability of all means of valid cognition,
yet it is not non-existent.
But how can there even be existence for this [subject]?
Even so, there is doubt.

In that case, if existence were characterized by the fitness of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and a logical reason (*hetu*), then because of the certainty regarding the absence of such a means of valid cognition and logical reason, there would be no doubt.

Now, if it is argued that some specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is what is fit for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the response is: "Existence" (*sattva*) is unsuitable because it would result in abandoning the subject under discussion; this has already been stated.
Alternatively, by this [argument], the view that the meaning of the word "existent" (*sacchabda*) is something qualified by a means of valid cognition is refuted.
When the absence of a qualifier has not been ascertained, it is not logical for there to be a doubt permeated by a word denoting a qualified object.

Furthermore, since even non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), the capacity to be an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatā*) is not the defining characteristic of existence (*sattā*). To explain:
And as for the non-existent object of cognition, why does he establish it in that very way—as immeasurable—and not otherwise? MBs_2.41 //

Indeed, by one who desires the distinction between the categories of the existent and the non-existent, the non-existent must necessarily be established in some way; otherwise, there would be a confusion of linguistic and practical conventions (*vyavahāra*).
In that case, if it were not an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it could not be so established].
If the absence of all causal capacity is the object of the cognition of non-existence,
then it must be an object of knowledge (*prameya*) in that manner in every respect;
for if it were not determined as such by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why would it be of that nature?
Could it not be otherwise?

If there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding whether that [object] exists in such a way or does not exist in such a way, for what reason is there a partiality toward one side?
Furthermore—
How can a foot be placed down without first having ascertained the absence of thorns?
For its existence [is not known] through another perception, nor from what is in front, since that would lead to an infinite regress.

If the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) were not to proceed due to the absence of cognition, then how could there be the laying down of a foot— according to the rule "one should place one's foot purified by sight"— if the absence of insects, thorns, and so forth has not been cognized? For it is thus:
That [cognition] would arise either from the discernment of the earth and other things that are distinct from the insect, the thorn, and so forth;
or from the non-discernment of the insect and so forth;
or from the discernment of their absence.
In that regard, it cannot be due to the determination of another object, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of cognition] even when there is a thorn or similar thing;
for in that case as well, the determination of another entity exists.
Furthermore, it would follow [that the delimitation exists] even prior to the delimitation of a portion of the earth,
because the delimitation of some other object or another already exists.
Or, if you say it is due to the non-delimitation of worms, thorns, and so forth;
There would be no desire to know whether that [non-existence] exists or not;
for even through an effort preceded by such a desire to know, one obtains only the mere non-determination of that whose non-existence is not an object of cognition (*prameya*).
And that [non-existence] exists even prior to that [cognition];
however, an inquiry is appropriate for the sake of ascertaining non-existence only when the object of cognition is itself non-existent.
Nor is mere non-determination itself the object of inquiry.
Because it is established by itself;
for it is by means of a delimitation that it is negated.
Furthermore, because it is not an object of cognition, that non-existence as well is indeed immeasurable.
Now, if it is thought that activity occurs because the object of a means of valid cognition is not determined even when the conditions for perception are present—
that is incorrect.
The status of being an object of valid cognition is seen to have no utility here.
For [the cognition] is indeed employed in the apprehension of a non-existent object by way of not being the cause of anything else.
If activity [occurs] because of non-discrimination, then the status of being an object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is of no use;
for non-discrimination is equal in the other case as well, and activity proceeds from that.

That whose intrinsic nature is the object of cognition, and upon the determination of which activity occurs, has the status of being the objective domain of a means of valid cognition because it possesses utility through having no other cause.
This non-apprehension is not caused by a deficiency in the logical reason while the object itself exists, because its causes are complete;
therefore, it is due to the absence of the object.
Now, wherever there might be activity, there it belongs solely to pure consciousness.
If one does not desire absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) as the subtle object of consciousness,
then that [liberation] is not accepted as the sole object, since it exists even when mixed with form.
Furthermore, for that which is already distinguished, there can be no further qualifier other than the absence of anything else.
If it is thought:
"In a certain location on the ground or elsewhere, there is activity characterized by the placing of feet and so forth,"
"Because that [cognition] belongs to that [object] alone due to knowledge"—in this regard also, it must be considered:
what is intended by this "isolation" (kaivalya) of knowledge? Is it a restriction to a single object, a non-connection with other objects?
Or is it [the non-apprehension] of the object?

If it were of the consciousness, then even when a gross portion of the earth or the like has been cognized, there would be no investigation into the presence or absence of subtle things such as insects or thorns.
It would indeed proceed from the cognition that apprehends the bare ground alone;
or, if [it proceeds] from the object, [then...]
In this regard, it must be considered: is the isolation of the object due to its own essential nature, or is it due to its connection with a qualifier?
In that regard, it does not first occur by way of its own nature,

because even when mixed [with other things], that nature persists. Rather, through connection with a qualification, there occurs an activity characterized by the placing of footsteps and so forth, which results from a determination qualified by the absence of insects, thorns, and the like, attained in the state of isolation.
Since no qualifier of a different kind is observed apart from the absence of another,
what object could the cognition and linguistic usage "it does not exist" rely upon as its referent?
If the absence of the means of knowledge (*mānābhāva*) has already been refuted, what then remains of the absence of the object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*)?
Furthermore, by this [absence], the object of the cognition and the word "it does not exist" must be stated;
yet that [object] cannot be the intrinsic nature of a real entity (*vastusvarūpa*).
Because the same consequence would apply even in the case of a mixture;
it was stated that this is not only because of the absence [of the object], but also because of the absence of any other qualifier.
Now, is this not the meaning of "it does not exist"?
"It is not cognized by this [means of knowledge]," yet it is not that non-existence is thereby understood;
for this is contradictory.
"Neither exists nor is it cognized.
If this were the case, then the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would have been stated as the object [of the cognition], namely,
"it does not exist."

Thus, regarding cognition and its verbal expression, what fault could there be on the part of the absence of the object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*), such that one should bypass it and declare the absence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*) to be the object?
For there is indeed no distinction between those two insofar as they are both indefinable.

Now, it might be thought: "In the absence of apprehension, there is the delusion of apprehending the non-existent; this is the error consisting in the linguistic convention of non-existence. (MBs 2.47)
And since there is no perception of non-existence, just as there is no perception of darkness,
the cognition and the linguistic usage "it does not exist" would simply not occur.
How can these two be denied when they are perceived by all people? It is said in reply:
this is an error consisting in the determination of the opposite in the absence of the cognition of existence;

likewise, it is an error consisting in the conventional usage of the opposite in the absence of the conventional usage of existence, just as [it occurs] in the absence of seeing what is actually present in the world.
The delusion is that one thinks, "I see darkness. For there is no such thing as "darkness" that exists as an object of sight.
This [objection] is not sound.
In this way, there would be the delusion of perceiving the non-existence of the three worlds during deep sleep and similar states.
For one who does not discern anything at all, error is not possible;
for one who does not perceive the object of superimposition and the thing superimposed cannot experience the delusion that it is silver.
Non-existence is not distinct from that which is conventionally designated as its absence; it is merely a mental construct.
The perception of darkness is either the shadow of the earth or simply the absence of light.
An error of perception does not arise when that which is unseen is not apprehended;

for if indeed an error consisting of a contrary perception were to occur in the absence of seeing, then there would be an error of perceiving the non-existence of the entire universe during states such as deep sleep, just like the error of perceiving light where there is none.
Furthermore, there can be no error for one who does not discern anything at all.

For instance, one does not become subject to the delusion of silver unless one apprehends through cognition both the object of superimposition— the thing standing before one— and the thing to be superimposed— silver. Otherwise, there would be no misapprehension.
It is either memory or a general cognition;
moreover, it is not the absence of cognition that is the object of knowledge, nor is it the absence of linguistic usage.
There is neither the cognition of non-existence nor the linguistic usage of non-existence, because non-existence, as a qualifier, is not an object of cognition;
for in that case, since neither of the two objects to be superimposed is apprehended, there is no false cognition.

Having accepted that existence consists in fitness for being a means of valid cognition, the absence of defects is stated: "Or let existence be fitness for a means of knowledge; and let that be cognized. (MBs 2.51)
When that [scripture] is measured, the existence of the entity becomes the domain of scripture;
nor is there any dependence on it, because there is no distinction from the internal object.
Even those who do not assert that existence (sattā) is something distinct [from the object] may maintain that existence is simply the fitness for being an object of valid cognition (pramāṇayogyatā);
and let that itself be the object of cognition (prameya).
That object of cognition, which is the reality of the thing itself, is the meaning of the scripture;
nor is there the fault of dependence on other means of valid cognition,
because there is no admixture with other means of valid cognition.
Because one understands only this much: "it is capable of being apprehended by a means of valid cognition.
For even those who assert that existence is the capacity for being apprehended by a means of valid cognition do not hold it to be something distinct from that [capacity].
They also do not admit the contact with an internal object here;
for if there were such contact, another means of valid cognition would have to be sought. How so would it not need to be sought?

When a statement has culminated in its fitness to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*) but does not itself bring about the cognition of a specific existent object, then that specific object for which a particular means of valid cognition is suitable must necessarily be relied upon.
For what purpose is it so relied upon?
It is for the sake of attaining the existence of a distinguished entity.
But what, then, is the existence of a distinguished entity?
It is its fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatva*).

In that case, it is indeed already understood that [the object] exists, because the word "exists" culminates in the meaning of existence; for being fit for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-yogyatā) is what constitutes the meaning of "existence.
He shows that even if one accepts the intermingling with other means of valid cognition, there is no fault of falling into the consequence of invalidity:
Our word is not a means of valid cognition whose object is distinct from the objects of other means of valid cognition.
"In this matter, however, this object has been cognized by me independently;
yet it is dependent regarding the mere object, because the cognition of the object depends on something else."
However, even if an object is not sublated, if there is a sublation regarding the aspect of the means of valid cognition,
it becomes non-authoritative in that regard, just as the word of an untrustworthy person, though its content may be true, is not considered a valid means of knowledge.
Indeed, it is not the case that a statement is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) even when its object is already established by another means of valid cognition;
for the word of a reliable person (āptavākya) is indeed a means of valid cognition.
If it is asked, "How can a means of valid cognition be dependent [on another]?", it is said in reply:
That [cognition] is indeed independent with respect to this sense:
"This object has been cognized by me";
for it relates only to the object itself.
Because there is no cognition that "this is the meaning" in this way, and because there is the cognition that "this person knows it to be so," [the Veda] depends upon human knowledge.

In that regard, first, with respect to the apprehension [of the words], it attains validity due to its independence; and subsequently, the object [is established] by means of that [apprehension's] establishment.
How then is it said that some human speech, even if its object is not contradicted, is non-authoritative due to its dependence? It is replied:

although there is no contradiction regarding the object itself, that upon which its authority regarding the object depends—that is, the means by which it establishes it—is contradicted in its aspect as a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Because that [person] is unestablished, there is no establishment of the object by means of him; thus, [the scripture] is not a means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous matters, such as the word of the Buddha, because it is impossible for an ordinary person to perceive them.
As it has been said:
"In that case, the possibility of it being an exception arises from human incapacity";
and as in the case of the speech of a deceiver.
Because it is known through valid cognition that [the Buddha] does not speak of objects as they are not seen;

furthermore, the word of a reliable person (āpta) is not sublated regarding the object nor regarding the portion of its validity. Otherwise, how could there be linguistic practice based on a means of knowledge that is independent [of other cognitions]? (MBs 2.56)

Furthermore, the word of a reliable person (*āptavacaḥ*) is not sublated with respect to its object, nor with respect to the portion that constitutes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it falls within the scope of a valid cognition.
And because it is independent regarding the portion that is a means of valid cognition, and because it establishes the object by means of that [portion], it cannot be non-authoritative.
Otherwise, linguistic convention based on words would not exist.
Then, through the state of being the speaker, "mayā" (by me) is free from differentiation;
it is the self-awareness in which the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge has dissolved.
Let the Vedāntas proclaim an extraordinary means of knowledge distinct from other means;
for the object established by that [means] will be as valid as the word of a human being.
And thus, even though the meanings of the Vedāntic statements overlap with other means of valid cognition, there is no contradiction regarding their authority,
just as in the case of the words of a trustworthy person. To explain:

Let those other means of knowledge (pramāṇas) as well, by means of that [non-conceptual wisdom], bring about the understanding of that supramundane nature which is self-luminous and devoid of the distinction between knower and known;
and through that, let the establishment of the object occur, just as in the case of the words of a reliable authority (āpta).
However, there would be this much difference:—
Because there is no speaker in the Veda, there could be no such contact as "by me.
Having concluded this argument based on a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), he summarizes the subject at hand:
Thus, the state of being an object of cognition is not existence;
yet another opponent objects:
"But surely even the other [alternative] is not tenable."
For indeed, without a prior mental apprehension, there can be no conceptual construction of a universal.
Just as a reflective awareness arises in one who has seen a cow in one place,
such an awareness does not arise toward another existent that was not previously seen.
The application of a single word, however, should be accepted as being like [the case of] "one possessing a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth.
The apprehension of a perceived form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the conceptualization of a universal (*sāmānya*).
For example:
For one who has seen a *bāhuleya* cow, the cognition "this is that very same [animal]" arises with respect to a *śābaleya* cow;
yet for one who has grasped nothing at all as being existent, that [cognition] does not occur elsewhere.
The application of a single word, however, can occur even without a universal (sāmānya), being caused by connection with another property,
as in the case of words such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) or "cook" (pācaka).
To this, it is replied:
What indeed is this prior reflection, which follows the form of the preceding [object], belonging to the cognition?
Even within a different state, that [nature] certainly exists to some degree;
however, a complete conformity in every respect is not observed between a whole body and its severed parts.
If it is not like that, then one cannot deny its own nature merely on account of its difference;
for a jar and a bowl do not lack the genus "clay" merely because of their difference.
For the nature of the material cause that exists in jeweled water-jars is indeed not found in the case of a common clay pot; such a quality certainly does not belong to the latter.
What, then, is this "prior reflection"?
Is it the appearance of a prior form within the cognition,
or is it the subsequent synthesis of the former and the latter, such that one thinks, "This is that"?
In that regard, if the former alternative is taken,
it indeed exists within the other [alternative] in some measure;
for instance:
Through its distinction from the indefinable (*nirupākhyam*), the uniformity of existing things (*satām*) manifests;
otherwise, even existing things would manifest as being absolutely distinct from one another, just like the indefinable.
Now, if there were a persistence of all forms, [the following would occur].
Thus, even with respect to the intended object that has a universal as its domain, [the cognition] does not exist;
for there is no co-inherence (*anvaya*) between a humpbacked and a hornless [cow] in their entirety,
because that would entail their identity and result in the non-existence of the universal.
Now, if it is argued that [the cognition] is not of such a kind as that which occurs in the case of sugar-candy and the like,
that is incorrect;
for it is not tenable to reject the nature of the persisting entity (anvayirūpa) simply because of a particularity in its manifestation.
For that possibility exists even in the case of "cowness" and the like;
indeed, the kind of conformity of form that occurs when Devadatta is seen for a second time does not occur when one who has seen a broken-horned cow sees a hornless one.
Moreover, even within the scope of a common category, the similarity is not uniform everywhere;
for the conformity to the form of "jar" found in various jars and water-jars (*śarāva*) is indeed distinct from that of a single jar.
Yet, by that much, those two do not lack the universal of "clay-ness."
Because it appears as something slightly similar [to the first].
Now, regarding the second alternative, it is said here:
the claim that "that" is the subsequent reflection (*avamarśa*) is not tenable even as a manifestation (*prakhyā*).
For one who has beheld a precious gem, even that [reflection] does not arise in a common bowl.

The claim that "the cognition consisting of the synthesis of the prior and the posterior, which brings about the understanding of non-difference in the form 'this is that,' and which is the cause for the conceptualization of a universal even among distinct things, is called 'prior recollection' (pūrvāvamarśa)"— this too is not tenable;
for the establishment of non-difference does not arise from synthesis alone.
Also because there is an appearance of an undifferentiated form;
otherwise, a single object would not exist as having an identical location and time, for in that case, even in the absence of a difference in location and time—
"That" is the mental connection (*anusandhāna*).
Furthermore, for one who has seen [the jar] in a small bowl, it does not occur immediately.
The investigation [into the nature] of that [Self] is like [the investigation into] a headless torso;
yet, in this way, there is no deficiency in the genus "clay" (mṛjjāti).
For one who reflects, however—

The cognition "this belongs to that same class" is the same even with respect to other existing things. If the connection with a universal is equal [in both cases], why then is there a reflective judgment (*avamarśa*) as "that" in some instances and not in others? It is said in reply:
Therefore, when the common form predominates, reality shines forth;
whereas when it is diminished, distinctness appears because that [common form] does not manifest.
Because, even though the connection with the universal [of "jar-ness"] exists in both the jar and the arrow, the cognition "it is that" does not arise with respect to the arrow,
whereas it does arise with respect to another jar which possesses a greater degree of that universal;
therefore, it arises due to the predominance of the forms of the universals.
"That" refers to the manifestation of reality;
however, in the case of smallness, it is not so.
Because those [other means] do not arise, and because the application of a single term does not occur as it does in the case of "the one to be punished" (*daṇḍya*) and so forth, he says:
"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be known through its effect, since there exists a cognition that cannot be joined [with anything else]. (MBs 2.67)
Therefore, it arises first; thus, there is no equality with [the cognition of] a staff-bearer and so forth.

There is no cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) without the apprehension of the qualifier (*agṛhītaviśeṣaṇa*); nor does such a cognition of the qualified arise prior to the cognition of existence (*sadbuddhi*).
The apprehension of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs either at that very time or subsequently;
for it is from the means of valid cognition itself that [the result] arises.
And the means of valid cognition is apprehended after the cognition has occurred, because it is inferred from the effect, which is the act of cognizing.

Therefore, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not apprehend it, that [existence] is devoid of connection with such a means; thus, it is not caused by a conjunction with a means of valid cognition.

If, then, there is no conjunction with a means of valid cognition regarding the object "it exists," how can there be an occurrence of time following the time [of that existence] with respect to the object "it exists"?
"Is there a well?
"There was a well.
"There will be a well"?
This is because the difference is conceptually constructed by that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),

just as the existence of Devadatta appears differentiated when the limiting adjunct of conjunction with Pāṭaliputra is present. Nor is it the case that "there can be no relation between word-meanings without an action."
Thus, he states that there is no disagreement among those who understand the systems of word and meaning: "And other wise ones [hold] that it is established by the mere relation. (MBs 2.68)

They say that a king’s word is devoid of action, as are fruit-bearing trees; yet, even in the absence of action, a relation is perceived in such expressions as "This man belongs to the king" and "These trees have borne fruit.
And here too, there is no "action of existence" (*astikriyā*).
Thus it is appropriate;
for here, the existence of a person whose connection to royalty is already known, or the existence of fruit-bearing trees, is not understood as that which is to be established.
Indeed, these two sentences do not culminate in [the expression of] mere existence.
However, regarding the man's connection with the king and the trees' connection with the fruit— this man who...
He said to the king: "These trees have borne fruit," not "that royal official."
"Therefore they exist"; and "those that have borne fruit exist.
As for what some say—"Let it be understood"—[it is as follows].
Thus, one might think that there is possession of action by means of the rule for the performance of an act;
however, since the cognition [of the act] is established through the word itself, that too has already been refuted.
Furthermore, there is no sentence devoid of action, and in respect to action, there is dependence [on other factors].
Nevertheless, he says that there is no fault:
"And because it concludes with the act of production, its specific [nature] is capable of being understood. (MBs 2.69)
"This cause arises from such a cause"—
even from a sentence terminating in the act of origination, namely "the world is born from such a cause," the existence of that kind of cause can be understood.
For example:
"From such a tree this fruit was produced"— this implies the existence of a tree of that kind.
And likewise, certain scriptural passages establish Brahman in this very manner:
"All these beings, indeed, arise from space alone";
"Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all the gods [proceed]," and so forth.
Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its thread],
and just as herbs arise upon the earth;
"Just as hair and body-hair arise from a living man, so does this entire universe arise here from the Imperishable."
This is the truth:
"Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge,"
"Thus, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also dissolve."
Likewise:
"For the divine Person is formless; he is indeed without exterior or interior, unborn, without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable."
"From this are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe."
Thus it was said.

Now, he objects that an injunction must indeed be resorted to for the sake of the connection between word-meanings: "But in the utterances of persons, the connection [of meanings] is dependent upon other means of valid cognition. (MBs_2.70)
In other cases, however, the meanings of words are connected with one another in dependence upon an injunction;
there, the arrangement of words serves to fulfill the speaker’s intended meaning.

In the case of an object cognizable through other means of knowledge, the speaker’s intention is established for the sake of accomplishing the meaning of an injunction in the Veda; for in its absence, [the injunction] would be incoherent.
The apprehension of a qualified object is an error; it is a delusion of grasping where there is no [actual] grasping.
For in the world, the co-utterance of words is intended for the accomplishment of a desired meaning, and a desired meaning is not accomplished by a single word alone.
Furthermore, the object intended for expression is apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, in that case, the syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*) depends upon that other means of valid cognition.
Consequently, when there is a contradiction with that [other means of cognition], there is simply no connection between the word-meanings.

Regarding the phrase "an old bull with shoes and a blanket," since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it in the Veda, this [understanding] is based on an injunction (*vidhi*). However, in the absence of such an injunction, the comprehension of a specific meaning that arises is impossible; therefore, that which is called such an understanding is an error (*bhrānti*).
Because of their co-utterance.
This is the error consisting in the apprehension of a relation when there is no apprehension of the distinction [between the objects].
Here, this alone must be investigated:
How is it that in the world conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is dependent upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
[If you say] because it is understood through another means of valid cognition,
that is incorrect, because even that which has never been experienced before (*apūrva*) is cognized.
Otherwise, the statement would be purposeless;
for a statement is employed to make known to the listener a meaning not yet understood.
Now, if it is argued that this is because the mere fitness for connection [of words] is already apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:]...
This is the same in the Veda; for instance,
in the statement "he buys with a red [cow]," there is a relation of conjunction (*saṃsarga*).
It is not [the case that] "one should sacrifice with a ruddy one-year-old cow";

likewise, it is established by the very power of the compatibility determined through other means of knowledge that the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) is the object of the injunction (niyoga), and not the meaning of words denoting substance or quality.
Now, if the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) were not apprehended from a single word, then the mere intention to express that word's meaning alone would be purposeless.
Therefore, since the establishment of a specific intention to speak does not occur with respect to word-meanings that are unconnected, words employed with such an intention become interconnected.
And that [connection] is established by another means of valid cognition;
even so, it would be based on the speaker's intention, because there is a conjunction of those things intended by him.
It is not based on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because that [other means] is neither its establisher nor its motivator.
As for the claim that there is an intention to speak regarding what is established by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
let it be so;
however, its connection [with the object] is of no use.
For indeed, [in that case] there is no utility for the relation [of words];
and likewise, even in the speech of a deceiver, there is a cognition of a relation.
As for the claim that there is no connection when there is contradiction—
let it be so;
however, it does not follow from that that there is no connection.
Even in the case of contradiction, there is no lack of connection [between the cognition and its object], because it is perceived.
Yet, even though it is perceived, it is sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, some speech is false.
Some [utterances] are meaningless, such as "ten pomegranates" and so forth; some are true.
Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the false and the meaningless.
Now, when a person, having perceived an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), desires to speak of it and communicates it to another,
the meaning of that speech is precisely the perception by means of another *pramāṇa*.
That [intention] alone is the motivator for the connection of word-meanings;
in the absence of that motivator, there can be no establishment of the connection of word-meanings in the Veda.
Let it not exist.
Only a specific meaning is the motivator [of linguistic usage].
Now, if it is argued that because the capacity of words is understood from common worldly usage, there can be no relation [between words] due to the absence of a worldly motivator,
then [this objection] would apply even in the case of a sentence containing a prescription (vidhi).
Now, in the world, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) applies only to the general fact of association,
not to its specific details,
because both cognition and linguistic usage are established by that general fact alone.
The comprehension of a qualified object is established even without perception by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, in the world, the truthfulness of a connection [between word and object] is understood through other means of valid cognition;

for even a previously unknown connection for a listener attains truthfulness by way of inferring the speaker's [reliability as a] means of valid cognition, whereas in the absence of that, it lacks truthfulness, as is the case with the words of the Buddha and others.
Therefore, in the world, a connection [between words] is said to be based on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Let that be so;
however, in the Veda, because there is no admixture with other means of valid cognition and because the meaning is understood independently, it is based on the word alone.
Let this matter rest;
let it be as it is in the world.
However, this is what is being questioned:
How indeed could there be dependence on injunction? If it were otherwise, [the injunction] would be in vain.
This same [objection] applies equally to the rule regarding the meaning of another word (anyapadārtha):
since it is understood as a qualified object, the meaning of another word is also employed [as the locus of the operation].
If it is argued that this [word] must be meaningful because there is no evidence for its being meaningless, then why would the injunction not be likewise? Or else, there would be another word.
When an object is already established by another means of valid cognition, an injunction is not applied to it;
for that object, being cognized as something not otherwise accessible, would necessarily imply its own proof.
An object is not a thing established as it is [by its own nature] such that it could be the subject of a restatement;
for if the knowledge of the relationship [between word and object] were denied, there would be no activity by one who is unlearned.
Otherwise, one would overstep one’s own duty (*svadharma*) for the sake of another’s accomplishment.
A prescription (*vidhi*) does not directly convey a relation in its general form or its specific instance;
rather, it implies it.
Otherwise, the mere injunction (niyoga) would be without an object and thus purposeless. This same [critique] applies equally to other word-meanings as well;
for they too, when isolated and failing to attain connection with other word-meanings, are purposeless because there is no comprehension of a new meaning (apūrva-artha).
Furthermore, in the world, word-meanings are not cognized as being restricted solely to their own essential forms by means of words;
rather, they are employed for the purpose of conveying qualified meanings,
since it is in this way that linguistic usage is possible.
And thus, for each individual word-meaning, there is an implication of a relation.
It might be argued:
"In common worldly usage, let there be no purposelessness for those words employed with conscious intent; therefore, they must have the relation as their meaning."
But there is no evidence for the Veda lacking purposeful meaning;
therefore, let it be that other word-meanings are indeed purposeless.
This is not sound.

Otherwise, meaning would be rendered purposeless, and it would be impossible to apprehend a specific meaning, as there would be the undesirable consequence of anyone being able to apprehend any meaning whatsoever.
Therefore, from common usage, it is understood that words possess the capacity to convey their own meanings only when employed in conjunction with one another.
Consequently, even in the case of the Veda, there would be the implication of a mere syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*).
Or, if other word-meanings were to be purposeless, why would that not apply to the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) as well? Now, if it is thought:
Other words are employed when an object is already established by another means of valid cognition;
they culminate in the restatement of that object as it has been understood.
For instance:

An object being restated (anūdyamāna) is not capable of implying a new (apūrva) meaning because it is merely a restatement according to how it was already understood. However, an injunctive word (*vidhāyaka-śabda*), whose object is a meaning not otherwise cognizable, is able to imply a new meaning when that meaning is being established as a valid cognition, since it could not otherwise be possible [otherwise].
Therefore, in the Veda, the connection with the new (*apūrva-saṃsarga*) is based on injunction.

That is incorrect; for if the meaning of the injunction were not the object of any other means of valid cognition, then the knowledge of its relationship [to the result] would be impossible, and thus it would have to be denied.

And thus, because it would not depend on the knowledge of a relationship [between word and meaning], even one who has not mastered the language would act; furthermore, the requirement of depending on the knowledge of a relationship, which is a property of individual words (*pada*), would be set aside, and its independence, which is a property of the sentence (*vākya*), would have to be accepted.
Furthermore, if its dependence on a relationship were not denied,
it would necessarily result in its having as its object that which is already established by another means of valid cognition;
and in that case, there would be no distinction [between this and other means of knowledge].
Even for one who maintains that the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] is known through the word itself, [it remains the case that... [KKS_104] MBs_2.78.
Indeed, there is no fault of mutual dependence, for that [cognition] is not self-cognized;
it is understood by another [means], namely through the comprehension of the word and indicated by its subsequent activity.
In that case, the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] is easily accomplished, as it is with other categories of objects.
As for the one who thinks:

"The knowledge of the relationship does not pertain to the object of an injunction (*vidhi*) when that object is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," [that view is incorrect].
Rather, it is established by the word itself;
nor is there the fault of mutual dependence—
once [the object] is established from the word, there is the cognition of the relationship.
And since the establishment [of meaning] from a word is preceded by the knowledge of the relationship [between word and object],
it is not said that [the meaning] is cognized directly from the word itself; rather, it is understood by another elder from the word employed by an [earlier] elder.

And from the understanding of that [word], by means of the activity of that elder, it is inferred: "Surely some object that is a cause for activity has been apprehended by this elder from this word, since he, upon hearing it, has engaged in activity."

Just as, upon seeing the bringing of an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth when one hears "Bring the cow," one infers that cognition [of the word-meaning] and thereby grasps the relationship [between word and object],
if that [cognition] were thus inferable, how could it be the exclusive domain of the word?
Since that [cognition] also has words as its precursor, it is the exclusive domain of inference;
why then is the understanding of words not also preceded by inference? MBs 2.81.
It cannot be established that these two have no beginning, like the seed and the sprout;
for everyone, inference from sound stands before them.
The word is a restatement of that [object] as being possessed of another category;
one who understands it through inference does not understand what has already been understood from the word.
In another cognizer, cognition is not produced by a restatement of another's cognition;
moreover, the meaning of a word would be something non-worldly, being merely the cause for activity.
It cannot be conceptualized even through worldly accomplishment.
If the prescriptive meaning, established as a qualification of the specific cognition inferred from activity, were the object of the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning],
then it would not have verbal testimony as its sole means of valid cognition.
Now, if it is argued that inference is preceded by verbal testimony,
then verbal cognition would likewise be preceded by inference, and thus [verbal cognition] would have inference as its sole object.
Indeed, it is not possible to establish a priority between these two, such as one does for the seed and the sprout.
Because that which is understood through verbal testimony is [reached] via inference,
and that which is inferred is understood through verbal testimony once the linguistic connection (*saṃgati*) is known;
moreover, for all cognizers, understanding from verbal testimony is preceded by inference, and thus for them, verbal testimony is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*).
For instance, every cognizer who understands from a word understands what has been inferred and whose connection [with the word] is known;
however, one who is performing an inference does not infer what was already understood through a word.

[Objection: Is it not the case that only what is understood through verbal testimony is inferred? [Response: True; however, this is by means of this particular cognizer. And the cognition belonging to one person does not serve as a restatement for the cognition of another.
Furthermore, since the understanding of the relationship [between word and object] occurs merely through the cause of activity (*pravṛtti*), the meaning of a word would have to be that alone.
Moreover, it is impossible even to postulate something non-worldly (*alaukika*),
because activity is established even by means of worldly [objects].
It might be argued:
"In the case of Vedic activities, because that [empirical basis] is impossible, there is the postulation of something non-worldly.
This is not so.
For a word whose capacity is understood from worldly usage is also a means of communication in the Veda.

In that regard, since the relationship [between word and meaning] is known in worldly activity within the worldly sphere, its comprehension must likewise occur in the Veda. Or, if it were impossible [to understand it there], the Veda would be false.

Now, since the causes of activity are manifold and because of their variability, they cannot be the meaning of the word; rather, it is the universal (sāmānya) that serves as the cause of activity which constitutes the meaning of the word.
In that regard, since worldly qualifiers are impossible in the Veda, another non-worldly (alaukika) qualification is understood.

Even so, that universal which is the meaning of the word in the Veda is established in the world; thus, its status as a restatement (anuvāda) does not cease, just as in the case of other word-meanings.

Even that specific distinction is the object of a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference due to the impossibility of other [possibilities]; thus, it is not the case that it is not the domain of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is even a residual inference possible for the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*).
Now, if it is thought:
Just as worldly linguistic usage is beginningless, so too is Vedic usage.

In that regard, since there is no cause for engagement in Vedic activities other than worldly causes of engagement, the knowledge of the relationship between the Vedic prescriptive injunctions and their objects constitutes the cause of engagement for those following the Vedas. Furthermore, these injunctions are not themselves inferable.
Because its existence is inferred from the occurrence of the cognition thereof,
and its establishment occurs precisely through the power of that cognition;
and since that cognition arises from the word, there is no other means of valid knowledge [for it].
Nor is it correct to say that only worldly [means] can be the means for achieving the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhana*).
For worldly capacity to achieve the highest good is understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In that case, because the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is observed [in such contexts], and because the meaning of words is determined in accordance with that [usage], the fact of being cognizable by other means of valid cognition also enters into the meaning of the word.
To this it is replied: Let it be granted that the correspondence between word and meaning proceeds solely from Vedic usage;
nevertheless, its status as an object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not thereby excluded.
To explain: at the time of knowing the word's capacity for a non-worldly cause of activity, would that [cause] have been cognized or not?
If it has been cognized, [then...]
Since the relationship between the word and its object is known at that very moment, it must necessarily be said to be known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If, however, it has not been cognized [by that other means], how can there be knowledge of the relationship regarding it?
For when two related entities are themselves unapprehended, their relation—which depends upon them—cannot be apprehended.
As for the one who thinks:
"The relation of a word is indeed its potency (śakti)," [that too is untenable].
And that [cognition] does not exist in the object, because the object is already established; rather,
cognition is its effect.
And that [word] is inferred from its activity;
it is precisely therein that the relationship, characterized by capacity, is cognized.
He should be asked this:
Is efficacy grasped in the mere condition, or in a specific condition that serves as the cause for engagement?
If it is in the mere condition, [then...]

Whatever might be understood from that [scripture] would then [refer to] a specific causal condition for activity distinct from worldly ones; since that [condition] is inferred through both the occurrence [of activity] and its exclusion [in other cases], it follows that it falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For there are two possible courses for a qualifier:
it either functions as a subordinate factor in the cognition of a qualified object by being drawn in through memory, as in "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke"; or...
Or, it may be an object of a means of valid cognition that apprehends a specific quality,
such as "the cow is white";
and in both cases, it is the domain of another means of valid cognition.
Because the word has not yet apprehended its relationship [to its object],
if it were drawn from memory, another means of valid cognition would have to be sought;
even in the second alternative, because it is inferred through the inference of a qualified cognition.
Now, in the case of inference, validity consists precisely in the cognition itself;
however, the qualifier therein is merely an object of that cognition,
and it serves as a factor for the cognition of the qualified object only to that extent.
The cognition of the qualifier, however, arises from an inferential cognition,
just as when the validity of a qualified object is inferred from the word of a person, the establishment of the object follows from that very means of valid cognition.
For in that case, the object serves as a qualifier of the speaker’s knowledge merely by being apprehended.
This is not tenable,
because cognition is included within the categories of memory, valid cognition, doubt, error, and conceptual construction;
among these, the cognition of the extraordinary qualifier is not memory.
Prior to its apprehension,
there is no doubt, because of the absence of contact with two alternatives.
It is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because that would entail the same consequence for the causal conditions (*pravṛttihetupratyaya*) as well.
Likewise, it is not an error (*viparyāsa*); for if it were in accordance with reality (*yathārthatva*), how could that cognition apprehending such a state be devoid of an object (*arthaśūnya*)?
By process of elimination, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And it is well said that another person is made to understand by means of another's cognition.
Now, if this is thought:
One does not understand another through another's knowledge;
rather, one understands through one's own knowledge alone by virtue of the capacity of that other's knowledge.
Now, it must be stated: what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that person's own knowledge?
It is not, first of all, verbal [cognition],
because the definition [of verbal cognition] is "the cognition of an object arising from the cognition of a word";
nor does that [cognition] arise from the cognition of the word.
From what, then, [is it known]? From the knowledge arising from the word, which has been inferred.
Now, if that [word] possesses validity, the existence of the cause for action is established.
And its validity arises from being produced by words free from defects;
therefore, the validity of the word is said to reside therein,
because the ascertainment of the object depends upon it.
That too is incorrect,
because the definition of verbal cognition is "knowledge of an object arising from a word.
Even the speech of a person is not a means of valid knowledge with respect to the object.
However, regarding the qualification of cognition,
two possibilities for a qualifier have been stated;
since recollection is impossible in this case, it is only while being itself cognized that it serves as a factor for the cognition of the qualified object.
Otherwise, one would have to seek another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the object;
nor is the object established by the speaker's knowledge alone, for it has been stated that one person does not apprehend another through [cognition of] another's mind.
As for what was stated—
that the establishment of an object depends upon the speaker’s cognition—

that is so because, if that cognition is false or impossible, the perception of the object is also sublated due to the sublation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and conversely, if that cognition is not sublated, the object is not sublated either.
But it is not that the meaning is not the object of the word;
otherwise, the very point that a person's word is dependent on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object and thus requires corroboration would not hold.
For that which is not the object of something cannot be either dependent upon or independent of it.
And thus it has been said: "The establishment of validity, however, occurs because of the possibility of the speaker's cognition being the cause [of the statement]";
here, "establishment" (sthāpana) means non-sublation (abādha), not validity itself.
And that [validity] belongs to the sentence because of the possibility of the speaker's cognition being its cause, but not to the speaker's cognition itself;
furthermore, there is a connection between the word and its object.
But not by means of knowledge; for it has been stated thus:
"The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate."
The inclusion of the word "object" here [is intended to show that] "the word does not touch the object;
the connection of the word is with cognition alone."
This is for the purpose of refuting those who hold such a view.
Therefore, the relationship between word and object is simply their mutual fitness (*yogyatā*). And that [fitness] cannot be apprehended when the object has not been cognized.
It has been stated that when something is already cognized, it becomes the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This does not apply to mere cognition in general;
for a cognition that possesses an object must be included within either memory or a means of valid cognition.
If [the statement] is meaningless, with what could it have a connection?
And if that [object] were made the object of a cognition even other than verbal cognition— even one consisting of non-valid knowledge—
then who could prevent the suspicion that this might also be the domain of non-verbal cognition, thereby opening the door to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Furthermore, the fact of being cognizable by another means of knowledge does not enter into the meaning of a word; for the meaning of a word is established neither by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone nor by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.
Indeed, when there is another factor that serves as the motivator (*prayojaka*), if the word is not employed in its absence, it is understood that this other factor is also a motivator of that word.
Just as when other causes are present, that whose absence prevents the effect from occurring is also understood to be a cause;

and here, since we observe the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth when there is an intention to express a cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), yet we do not observe them even when that [highest good] is accessible through other means of knowledge despite its presence, the status of being a cause of the highest good is, for now, the meaning of the word.

Although there is perception when it is accessible through another means of valid cognition, and non-perception when that is absent, this is not because its status as a cause of the highest good lacks accessibility through other means of valid cognition.
In that case, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful: since there is no non-application when both are absent, on what basis is this non-application grounded?

In this regard, because it has been determined that the capacity to be a means to the highest good (śreyaḥsādhanatā) is the operative factor, it is understood that in its absence, [the non-application] is grounded in that very absence.
Since positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are established by that alone, there is no evidence for anything else being the meaning of the word.

Otherwise, even properties such as existence (sattva) would enter into the meaning of the word "śiṃśapā," because [the word] is used when those [properties] are present and is not used when they are absent.

Now, since the property of being a *śiṃśapā* (a kind of tree) is the meaning of the word, it is precisely because of the absence of that [property] that there is no application [of the word] when existence (*sattā*) and so forth are absent;
and because of its presence, the application is justified. Thus, one does not postulate a capacity (*sāmarthya*) for those [higher categories like existence].
This is exactly the same in the present case as well.

Now, if it is argued that [the Veda] lacks authority because the status of being a cause of the highest good (*śreyas*) falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because that [status] is impossible in the case of the Veda—
that is incorrect. For it is not the case that something which is the object of a particular means of valid cognition in one instance must be false in another instance as well.
For that which is near is the object of the external senses, whereas that which is distant is to be understood through scripture and inference.
Likewise, in the case of sacrifices and the like, whose fruits occur at a remote time, the status of being a means to the highest good will be understood through the Veda.
Nor is that which is cognizable by one means of valid cognition sublated by the non-apprehension of it through another means of valid cognition,
because the operation of the means of valid cognition occurs according to the fixed determination of their respective objects.
If, however, it were within the domain of another means of valid cognition, its invalidity would follow from contradiction with that other means.
Because no immediate fruit is perceived;
however, with respect to the meaning of the word as its object, there is no contradiction with that [immediacy].
This would be so if there were a contradiction.

And that [is not the case], for it has been stated: "For the immediate transgression (ānantarya) is not enjoined. Now, let it be granted that there is no injunction regarding the immediate transgression; [nevertheless...]
Furthermore, let it not be that the meaning of a word is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If the referent of a word is in every respect already established by another means of valid knowledge, then it must be accepted exactly as it has been so established.
Otherwise, that [status] would not be established;
yet its establishment as the cause of immediate excellence is precisely what constitutes that status.
That is not so.
The accomplishment of a result immediately following an action is not necessarily determined by the action itself,
since this is seen to be otherwise in the case of agriculture, medicinal herbs, drinking potions, and so forth; furthermore,
even in the case of sacrifices and the like, an intermediate effect is established through the force of valid means of knowledge.
Moreover, when the qualified [object] is established, the qualification—namely, the mere fact of being a cause of the highest good—is also established;
and that much alone constitutes the meaning of the word.
Nor is there any contradiction with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding that extent.
Thus, since there is no fault even in this worldly cause for activity, the postulation of a non-worldly [cause] is futile;
for it, like pleasure and so forth, is an object of inference. To explain: [KKS 110]—
Pleasure and the like, which are to be inferred from the serenity of the face and other such signs, are inferred along with those very signs themselves;
however, no separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required for [the existence of] a sentient being.
Even when this view is held—
The meaning of a person’s speech is simply the speaker’s cognition.
Since that cognition cannot occur without an object, the object is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference.

Even in that case, the cognition which is the cause of the activity—being inferred from that activity—cannot exist without its object; thus, like the meaning of the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta*), its status as an object of inference does not cease.
Now, it might be argued that because a cognition derived from inference is established by means of words, it has words as its instrument of valid cognition (*śabdapramāṇaka*).
That is incorrect;

for the knowledge of the meaning of a trustworthy person’s statement is not established by the sense organs, and thus that object becomes one whose instrument of valid cognition for the listener is direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇaka*).
Therefore, it is rightly said:
"If that [dharma] is thus an object of inference, how can it have verbal expression as its sole domain?
Likewise:
"He cannot be conceptualized, because his existence is established even by worldly means."
Thus it is said.
Then, in the form of a means of valid cognition, it is manifested by its own word.
It is said that [the injunction] is both the prompter and independent with respect to another means of valid cognition (*pramā*).
Now, it might be argued: we do not say that the positive injunction would be in vain otherwise; rather, the connection [of the word] depends upon it.
However, it is expressed by its own word as being of the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, because it is a means of valid cognition, it implies an object of cognition (*prameya*) not previously known,
and it is independent of any other means of valid cognition.
For this [inference] does not depend on a prior establishment, as a word does, because it depends upon a relation;
nevertheless, if it were unestablished, the previously mentioned faults would apply, whereas if it is established, it is merely a restatement.
Let its authority reside wherever that of the Veda does; in this regard, however, it is useless.

Even so, if that [dharma], which is the very essence of valid cognition, is not established by another means of knowledge—[a fact] which would result in the non-occurrence of activity for the unlearned and the transgression of the dharma—it follows that if it is indeed established, then because it is merely a restatement of what is already known, it cannot imply a novel object (*apūrvārtha*).
Moreover, let it be the word itself that possesses authority in those cases where its authority is desired;
what is the use of this [inference]? But has it not already been said—
"Because it depends on the knowledge of the relationship between words, a [scriptural] statement is merely a restatement and is not capable of bringing about the understanding of a new object.
This is not sound; for if a word were merely a restatement, [it would follow that it could never convey anything new].

How could the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is itself being restated as that which is to be illuminated, convey a previously unknown object (*apūrvārtha*) in the manner it was already apprehended?
There is no apprehension of a means of knowledge devoid of contact with its object (*prameya*).
Therefore, that [means of knowledge] is understood precisely according to the object already apprehended.
And where is this [inference] a means of valid cognition regarding that object, when it does not apply to sacrifices and the like which have their own specific words?
Even in the absence of an injunction, the listener possesses a novel connection with worldly matters;
and if there is the capacity for the means to achieve a result, the word is not defective in that regard.
Since word-meanings are equal to other entities, the connection between them is not based on a requirement for an injunction; rather, they are manifested by their own respective words.
Therefore, because they participate in a relation by virtue of having forms capable of being related,
people employ co-utterance for the sake of a qualified meaning.
Therefore, a connection [of the injunction] with the non-existence of the act is not possible;
nor can the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the injunction be determined. To begin with, sacrifices and the like are not its objects of knowledge.
This is because they are the objects of words such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*). Nor is their relation (*saṃsarga*) beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for instance:
Even in worldly sentences that do not prescribe injunctions, such as "A son has been born to you, O Brāhmaṇa," a previously unknown relation is perceived by the listener.
Now, if it is argued that the object of knowledge (prameya) is the capacity to be a means for attaining a result;
It is said that for one who desires [an object], an injunction is not possible regarding the meaning of a verbal root when that meaning is not a means to satisfy desire;
for if it were not a means, it would not have been performed by the desirous woman.
But even that is incorrect.
For there is no fault whatsoever in the word in that regard,
by which one would have to bypass it and seek another means of valid cognition;
dependence upon another means of valid cognition has already been refuted.
However, the contradiction arising from the non-perception of an immediate result remains the same even if that [obligation] is understood through a *niyoga* (injunction).
Since "immediacy" is not an object of valid cognition (*apramāṇārtha*), its absence is equally applicable to the word as well.
Alternatively, the word is not defective in that regard with respect to its capacity to bring about the result.
But *niyoga* (the mandate) is indeed faulty;
for from it, the comprehension of the means for achieving human goals is not possible.
