This point is to be understood from the *Vidhiviveka* and the *Bhāvanāviveka*.

Therefore, since the meaning of an injunction is identical to other word-meanings in its dependence upon the knowledge of a relation, it cannot be stated with specificity that "the connection between word-meanings is based solely on that [injunction].

Rather, all word-meanings, having been understood from their respective words through their capacities as factors of action (*kāraka*) and so forth which are capable of being related, become connected through proximity.
Since the understanding of the operation of words is derived from worldly usage,
and in the world, words convey their own meanings through proximity for the sake of a specific composite meaning, rather than for the sake of conveying the mere individual meanings themselves.
And thus, connection (*saṃsarga*) is based solely on the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for all word-meanings.
For all of them are manifested by the words in their mere essential nature (*svarūpa*), without their forms being fully completed.
In this way, since an injunction (*vidhi*) is equal to other word-meanings, connection is not based specifically upon it.
Furthermore, since conjunction depends upon all constituent entities, in the absence of an injunction, conjunction is not possible.
Thus, an injunction is not to be resorted to even for the sake of conjunction.
Why is it not to be resorted to?
If it is argued that the cognition of the connection between word-meanings occurs only through the predominance of an injunction—
since the capacity of a word for that purpose is understood by inferring its causal condition through the observation of activity following another instigating statement—
this is not so, because the relationship is grasped even in a sentence that does not instigate action but rests solely on its own form.

When, with respect to one who requires fire, it is said— "The fire is in Caitra’s house"— referring to cooking utensils other than the fire that has been kept ready— then, having observed that the fire is brought from there by him, it is understood:
"Here, the existence of fire was cognized by this [person], and that [cognition] arose from this sentence";
nor is it possible to say—
From such sentences as "bring that from there" or "go there," conviction arises.

Since the accomplishment of activity from a sentence occurs through the cognition of the mere existence of fire, it cannot be assumed that the sentence possesses the capacity for an injunction (*niyojana*). Furthermore, since the application and cognition [of the sentence] are established through the connection with a general meaning, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for a connection with a specific [meaning]. Otherwise, as has been stated, the meaning of the Veda would be entirely without a basis in valid knowledge.
Now, it is argued that [the Veda] would be purposeless without knowledge of what ought to be done (kartavyatā).

There is no purpose for the employment of a sentence other than engagement or withdrawal; if it is argued that the injunction to understand is the same [as the former], then that alone is the purpose.
And if he were to offer this for that same purpose,
it would be consistent with what is required for the successful accomplishment of the authority over wisdom, action, and worship.
Well then, that statement does not terminate in its own form;
this is the same as a sentence that is completed and yet follows upon another sentence.
If there is an entry into ritual injunction (*niyoga*) for you now, it is otherwise in vain;
thus, the portion concerning the injunction for the realization of reality has been fully extracted.
Now, it might be thought:
knowledge of the mere nature of a thing, devoid of knowledge of what is to be done and lacking in engagement or withdrawal, is purposeless;
for the employment of speech is invariably prompted by engagement or withdrawal.
Moreover, there must be an injunction for the sake of purposefulness;
otherwise, it would be meaningless. To this, it is replied:
The same pointlessness applies even to the rule for practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*). For instance,
even in the case of "one should practice in this manner," there is no activity or cessation whatsoever that exceeds the mere cognition of its own nature.

Now, if the knowledge of the essential nature itself is the purpose, then that is equally applicable even to [a cognition] that rests solely upon that essential nature. Or, if it is a rule for realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*)—

It is purposeful by providing the objects for the wisdom and meditation required by the injunctions of qualification, such as "one should cultivate wisdom," "one should form a resolve," and "one should meditate [on the Self] as the Self."
Wisdom cannot be effective if it does not comprehend the true nature of its object; however,
even a statement that rests upon its own form is likewise meaningful,
for it possesses an even greater capacity for conveying that [nature].
But in that case, its status as resting upon its own intrinsic nature would be lost, since it has entered into a mandate (*niyoga*). Even so, it does not rest solely upon its own inherent mandate,
because it enters into another mandate.
Now, it might be thought: a sentence that has its purpose fulfilled in itself enters into syntactic unity with another sentence;
this is what is called a contextual connection (*prākaraṇika-sambandha*).
Otherwise, it would merely be a definition of a sentence.
This point is also the same:
even when entering into the sphere of an injunction (*niyoga*), the fact that [the word] rests upon its own essential form (*svarūpa*) is not lost.
Is it not the case that there is an entry into an injunction,
since otherwise [the statement] would be purposeless? Indeed, it is so.
First of all, the injunction for the realization of reality has been refuted on the grounds of its pointlessness,

since the comprehension of reality is established from that word even without an injunction. Now, it may be argued that the originative injunction is restricted to the comprehension of the form of the ritual action.
Just as is the method for the knowledge of reality, so should one abide in awakening.
And its engagement is considered to proceed from authority, like the authority for ritual action;
therefore, it consists of making the unknown known and instigating that which has not yet been engaged.
The wise declare that [the Veda] teaches injunction; this too is of the same nature.
In that case, the comprehension of the nature of the ritual action is not intended as the fruit of the injunction.
However, for that which depends on a task, there is a connection with the sentence stating the result;
here, the connection to the qualification (adhikāra) belongs to that which is not itself enjoined.

Reality is not an object for the entry into qualification regarding the realization of reality; for perception directed toward rice and such things does not possess the capacity for qualification [in this regard].

Furthermore, it is argued that the purpose of an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), is merely the comprehension of the form of the ritual action.
From that [injunction], there is no impulsion (pravṛtti),
because such impulsion is dependent upon an injunction of qualification (adhikāravidhi).
Likewise, the purpose of an injunction for the realization of reality is merely the realization of reality itself.
The engagement [of the agent] follows from the injunction of qualification—
such as "one should cultivate wisdom" and so forth—
and because there is a distinction between the injunction's purpose of engaging in activity and its purpose of comprehension.
Therefore, they state its two characteristics as "making known what was unknown" and "impelling one to act who has not yet acted.
This too is without substance.
For it is not merely the comprehension of the essential nature of the injunction pertaining to the origin that is intended as the result;
rather, it is its connection with the sentence of qualification (*adhikāra*). To explain:

When it is understood that an injunction is a means for achieving a human goal in general, and there arises a desire to know its specific nature, the connection with a qualification (*adhikāra*) is obtained.
Furthermore, the fruit of the injunction for the realization of reality (*tattva*) is not that same [human goal];
for the qualification belongs to the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is the object of meditation and so forth.
Because its nature is non-action, it is not the object of an injunction;
as for that which is its object— knowledge of reality—
it has no connection with [the notion of] entitlement (adhikāra).
It is like the perception of rice and so forth.
For the means of valid cognition that grasps the intrinsic nature of rice and so forth does not partake in being a constituent part of the ritual performance;
this is because those things already cognized are connected to the qualification [for the rite], just as in the case of garments made of wool and the like once they have been produced.
For activities such as carving or fashioning wood do not enter into the scope of that [ritual] authority.
Now, the procedure (vidhi) whose domain is the third mode of practice is set forth,
because it is connected by virtue of having the realization of reality (tattvāvabodha) as its object.
For the object of the second practice is not the object of the realization of reality, but rather the object of its cultivation.
Therefore, this verbal knowledge is prescribed as something else, accompanied by a means.
It is non-dual, having dissolved the grasping for the distinction between the grasper and the grasped.

For even this claim— that the reality of the self is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and thus cannot be the object of a cognition of sentence-meaning consisting of the connection of distinct referents— is fragile.
This is the manifestation of the non-dual self, free from the delusion of limitation;
it is the abiding in one's own nature, perfectly tranquil—that is the fruit, which is not the domain of ritual injunction.
For the activity of the prescriber is considered to consist in making known the means to achieve that [result];
indeed, the wise maintain that an injunction is simply the state of being a required means.
For [the process] beginning with determination does not arise from nothing, nor from mere verbal expression.
We do not say that the awakening to reality arising from words is what is enjoined.
However, it is that which has ceased to grasp the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and its object;

therefore, it is non-dual—either because of the absence of a second cognition of that same kind, or because of the absence of the duality of knower and known—and thus it is other than that [empirical state].

Since the means for the arising of this extraordinary state are not understood through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its prescription is given together with the means such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), reflection (*manana*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
For the reality of the Self is not the object of verbal cognition; for the means of valid knowledge known as verbal testimony consists of sentences,
and its object is of the nature of the relation between various word-meanings.
Because [the object] is cognized by following after that [cognition],

and how could the true nature of that cognition— which appears as a mere conflation of various objects— be the domain of the reality of the Self, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and untouched even by a trace of duality?
This too is without substance.

Since that realization of the reality of the Self— which is non-dual and devoid of even a trace of contact with duality— is the abiding in its own essential nature due to the absence of the delusion of limitation;
for it is through the turbidity of limitation that it appears in the form of the non-Self,
but there is no realization of reality other than that.
For the Śruti declares, "Truth, knowledge, infinite";
and the reality of the Self is free from all inauspiciousness such as sorrow,
because the Śruti speaks of it as being "free from evil" and so forth.
It is manifest as unsurpassed bliss;
"Brahman is consciousness and bliss";
"This is its supreme bliss."
For it is said in the scriptures: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss.

Thus, its essential state—due to the cessation of all worldly misfortune and the attainment of unsurpassed joy—is the fruit, which is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) characterized by perfect tranquility.
And it has been said:
"There is nothing higher than the attainment of one's own self.
Nor is it logical that one would not engage even in a human goal (puruṣārtha) if the means to it were unknown.
Since desire is the precursor of activity,
instruction regarding activity is sometimes given by way of that [desire], as in:
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma."
Likewise, it has been said: "For whatever one desires, that one does.
Moreover, if one does not engage in an action because the means are unknown, one must necessarily be prompted toward it by making the means known, with the fruit in view.
And since activity toward that [object] is established by that much alone, one need not assume an operation of an injunction there.
As it has been said:
"The desire for that is indicated by the purpose."
Therefore, the function of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists precisely in the means for achieving the result.
But surely, even with respect to that which possesses the result, there is an engagement based on the implication of the purpose; where, then, does the function of the injunction reside?
Regarding this state of being:
this is not essential, because, just as in the case of the generality of a means, it follows by implication.
There is activity,
and likewise even in the case of a general state of being;
for a means of proof that does not provide assistance is incapable [of its function].
If it is argued that [the agent] is to be impelled toward a specific instance of that [action],
then let it be the same regarding a specific means as well.
Moreover, an injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the state of being a sought-after means.

Because that [desire] is characterized by the instigation of what has not yet occurred, and because the property that is the cause of engagement is precisely what is denoted by the word "instigation" (*pravartanā*),
and because there is no other cause for engagement such as "desirability" (*iṣṭatā*) or "being a means to that" (*tatsādhanatā*).

Furthermore, since desirability (iṣṭatā) is determined by other means of valid cognition, one already knows for oneself, "This must be done by me"; thus, with respect to desirability, there is no such thing as inciting one who has not yet been prompted to act.

Since the fact that something is a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā) is not apprehended through any other means of knowledge and is accessible solely through verbal testimony, it cannot serve as the cause for the engagement of a person who has not yet acted without the word itself.
Therefore, being established by the authority of the word, it is designated as "injunction" (vidhi).
And for one who is about to act, the means to be performed is the cause of engagement.
It is not established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, for one who performs it, there is the injunction of its being a means (*sādhana*).
Consequently, from the injunctive word, it is understood that the performance has only the means as its object.
Is it not indeed determination, intention,
and the initial impulse?
Those who know injunction explain injunction as being merely the process of activity, devoid of the three times, and characterized by an unknown relationship between the action and its agent;
this, however, is not sound.
For it is precisely determination (*adhyavasāya*) and the like that are sought here as the cause;
and that [cause] is nothing other than the state of being a required means (*apekṣitopāyatā*).
Nor are those [determination and so forth] devoid of causes.
It might be argued: "The verbal expression of these is the cause [of their cognition]; and that is correct. But this is not so.
For these [entities] would arise from verbal designation (*abhidhāna*), not from actual production;
indeed, it has been explained in the *Vidhiviveka* that things such as jars are not causes for action merely by virtue of being cognized, and so forth.
Alternatively—

It is not by way of denotation; nor does determination and so forth arise from the word, because [the word] is a communicator [of meaning], which would entail the consequence that even one who has not learned the convention would act [upon it]. This and more has been stated in that very same place.
Alternatively,
it is that from which the determination arises: "This must be done by me."
Since the cognition "I am enjoined" arises, that injunction (*niyoga*) is a synonym for the word "prescription" (*vidhi*);
to this, it is replied:
precisely because it is the means to what is desired.
The determination that "it must be done" is [the nature of desire]. For it is said:
"In regard to the means to what is desired by the agent..."
In the world, there is the understanding that "this must be done";
but in its absence, however,
[the understanding is] "this must not be done."
Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), those two are understood with respect to that object; likewise, [one thinks],
"I am not appointed."
Thus,
the cognition "I am impelled" is the perception of the cause for one's own activity;
and that [cause] is nothing other than being the means to a desired end.
Indeed, it is not logical for that which has been observed to possess causal efficacy to be called "causeless" (ahetu) without reason;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for abandoning the worldly [reality] in favor of a supramundane conceptualization.
Why so? Not because of the designation.
Indeed, it has been stated that the denotation of a non-worldly object is not possible because its relation [to words] cannot be apprehended;
or rather, for from that [denotation] proceed the determination, the initiation, the performance, and the completion [of an action].
Because it is a means that is required;
for activity is undertaken only when that [means] exists, since no one engages in action merely from the command of anyone whatsoever.
It might be argued as follows:—
One engages in action because of the cognition "this must be done";
otherwise, what ought to be done would not have been performed.
And that is not the case, for the arising of the cognition that something "must be done" does not occur without a cause.
For that [attainment] has the acquisition of one's own purpose as its cause.
It might be argued:
"The cognition that something ought to be done arises from the word alone."
To this it is replied: not by way of denotation;
that is, the cognition of what is to be done does not arise from the word itself.
For *niyoga* is the meaning of the word;
it must be either a property of the instigator (*niyoktṛ*) or something independent.
However, "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*) is a property of the object (*viṣaya*).
Now, if one were to say that the duty regarding the object is an injunction (*niyoga*), then the state of being a required means would already be established;
for from an injunction alone, the status of something as "to be done" (*kartavyatā*) would follow.
Even so, verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition regarding that [obligation], because the word directly denotes the injunction (niyoga),
nor is it [known] through implication (artha).
Since one observes the application of an injunction even toward that which ought not to be done,
if it is argued that the status of the injunction as something to be performed is understood,
then the comprehension of the duty regarding the object follows from the accomplishment of that [injunction].
That is incorrect, because in the world, the status of being an effect is perceived with respect to the object.
For instance, when there is an injunction such as "The cow should be milked by you," if it has already been milked by another, one does not begin to milk it again.
Because the object is perceived as something to be accomplished, it must be brought to completion;
yet the injunction cannot be fulfilled by anyone other than the person concerned, since that other person is not the one enjoined.
In that case, there would be a further commencement of milking for the sake of fulfilling the injunction (*niyoga*).
This matter has been examined in detail in the *Vidhiviveka*; therefore, enough of this digression.
It might be argued as follows:
This knowledge is enjoined because it is the means to liberation;
for liberation is heard in scripture to be accomplished by knowledge:
"By means of knowledge they ascend there."
"By means of knowledge one attains immortality; he who, having known that Self, understands it, obtains all desires";
likewise, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him," and so forth.
And even though it is something to be accomplished, it does not have an end,
because it is to be understood through scripture as being non-recurrent—
as in the statement: "He does not return again."
For this is not accessible through reasoning,
such that its reality could be established by means of reasoning; rather,
for that which is accessible through scripture, its reality is established from scripture alone.
Alternatively, it is infinite because it is to be accomplished through infinite knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, even though consciousness is momentary, it is infinite by way of its continuity (*saṃtati*).
Regarding this, they say:
Liberation is not its fruit to be accomplished, nor is there any other liberation.
The cessation of ignorance is liberation; that [ignorance] is declared to be saṃsāra.
Knowledge itself is non-dual and peaceful; its cessation is so called.
But what is this liberation?
If it is the non-arising of future bodies, senses, and intellects— as in the statement, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless"— then...
Since this is seen [in scripture],
that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is not something to be accomplished.
Now, as for the attainment of Brahman:
And that [connection] between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman may be like that between Caitra and the village, on account of the scriptural texts concerning the path:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upwards by that, one attains immortality."
"In as much time as it takes to cast the mind, one goes to the sun; this indeed is the door to the world";
likewise, "They reach the light, from the light to the day," and so forth.
Or rather, it might be like the attainment of the juices of various flowers in honey, or of rivers in the ocean, characterized by non-distinction;
as it is said in the world: "Just as honey-makers produce honey."
As seen in the passage, "Just as, my dear, these rivers... [flow into the ocean], there is either the effect's attainment of the state of the cause, or...
"Thus, the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains supreme equality"—so says the Śruti.
Or [this state] is characterized by transformation into that very form, like a tiger in yoga:
"He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself."

This is because of such scriptural indications as "he attains Brahman," and because it is characterized by the recovery of one's own true nature through the removal of taints, just as in the case of a crystal.
Because of the scriptural statement: "Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form.
In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable.
Because of its omnipresence— as it is said: "Within that is all this," and "Eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent."
And because of non-difference,
since the teaching "That thou art" implies that through the knowledge of That, there is the knowledge of all.
Because it is established directly in this manner,
and because the word "Self" (ātman) is used everywhere to refer to the inner self (pratyagātman), [the text says]: "Now, he who [thinks] another..."
Thus, because of the refutation of the perception of difference;
and for this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable, as well as due to its being partless.
The first [alternative] is untenable because of the impossibility of non-distinction characterized by the mutual intermingling of parts, as expressed in the phrase "partless and actionless.
Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because an effect would then always be the cause.
Furthermore, if there were the destruction of the nature of the effect, it would follow that liberation consists in annihilation;
yet, in that regard, [the scripture states], "Through knowledge, one enjoys immortality."
Thus there is a contradiction,
because it would follow that [the self] is destroyed by knowledge alone;
and since the destruction of the self is undesirable, [liberation] would be fruitless.
Moreover, the primary relationship of cause and effect is negated in the passage concerning the "imperishable" (akṣara),
because the Śruti establishes the unreality of modifications by stating, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."
Nor is the fourth [alternative] possible, precisely because there is no difference, since consciousness, being of the nature of Brahman, is without distinction.

If it is argued that the absence of sorrow, delusion, and so forth is what distinguishes the conscious selves (*vijñānātman*), then in that case as well, if sorrow and the rest were identical with the conscious selves, they could not be eliminated. Alternatively, if they are merely attributes (*guṇa*) distinct from the self, subject to coming and going, and momentary;
And because they are momentary, they cease of their own accord; thus, no means for their destruction need be sought.
Nor, as has been stated, is anything required for the non-arising of future [moments].
Now, if it is argued that there is a specific power (*aiśvaryaviśeṣa*) in Brahman...

Liberation is the attainment of that [state] and the transformation into its nature, according to the Vedic revelation: "He becomes his own lord" (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*). That is incorrect, because it is impossible for there to be multiple lords.
Could the sovereignty of the individual selves (vijñānātman) be inferior to or equal to that of Brahman?
If it were inferior, there would be an attainment of the form of Brahman rather than self-sovereignty (svārājya). For instance:
The Supreme Lord, denoted by the word "Brahman," would be their overlord;
and thus there would be the rule of another king.
Furthermore, in that state, finitude is heard [in scripture].
"Now, those who know otherwise than this,

having other kings, come to have perishable worlds. This is also logically consistent, for in the world we observe the loss of sovereignty among those with inferior power due to the will of the Supreme Lord.
But the simultaneous non-arising of equality is certain:
if one [of them] is the sovereign lord of all and the ruler of everything, what could the other be doing to be a Lord?
And because of contradiction:
indeed, there is no reason for these [two] to possess a single cognition.
In that case, regarding a single object, if one follows the intention of the other while they hold contradictory intentions, then the latter lacks sovereignty.
There is no conformity with both [the Lord and the individual soul], because of contradiction;
if there is non-conformity with both, then both would lack sovereignty.
If it is argued that the cause for their agreement is the accomplishment of the task, as in the case of an assembly, [we reply:]...
If it is argued that [the Lord is not established] otherwise because He would be unestablished, then there would be a lack of sovereignty in each [individual].
Or, if sovereignty is asserted to exist successively in order to avoid contradiction, then there would be finitude.
Furthermore, because the creation of the world is impossible [for him], his sovereignty is not equal to that of Brahman;
for it is heard in scripture that he alone is the creator of the world,
and that liberation occurs at a time subsequent to creation through the worship of him.
Therefore, just as in the case of a crystal, the manifestation of its own nature through the removal of coloration and the like is the attainment of Brahman;
for the self of consciousness has Brahman as its true nature.
And thus it is said: "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form."
Because the application of its own term is untenable when another form is being produced.

If it is argued that this is tenable because of the non-difference or the relationship between that which is being produced and [the self], we say no; for the qualification would be meaningless, since everything that is being produced belongs to itself.

In this regard, just as a white cloth that was already white is said to have "become white" upon the removal of stains, so too, when the veil of delusion is removed and its true nature is manifested, it is said that "it is perfected in its own form."
Likewise, [it is said]: "Being Brahman itself, one attains Brahman.
Thus, because delusion is characterized by abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), it is not an effect, since the true nature exists even prior [to the delusion].
Because that which is adventitious lacks intrinsic nature,
nor is there any otherness [between them], since liberation is simply the removal of ignorance in the manner described.

Ignorance is saṃsāra; and knowledge itself is the cessation of ignorance. For if ignorance is non-apprehension, then it follows that the very existence of a thing is the exclusion of its non-existence.
Now, as for error (*viparyāsa*), even so, its cessation occurs only through the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which is its opposite.

For the cessation of the cognition of silver is not something other than the production of the cognition of mother-of-pearl; it is neither produced by that [cognition] nor accomplished by some other effort.
Because these two occur simultaneously and because no further effort is required,
the scripture declares the equality of time between the attainment of knowledge and the realization of Brahman:
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
Likewise: "He who knows Brahman as bliss fears not"; "Then he knew himself alone, thinking, 'I am Brahman.
Therefore, he became all this."
"In that state, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?"— thus it is known;
the knower does not fear.

What is the delusion? It is the [objection] "Look!"—since no sequence of priority and posteriority is heard there. As for the sequence that occurs in some cases, it is like [the expression]: "He sleeps having opened [his mouth]."
[Objection: But surely, if there is identity [between the pot and its destruction], simultaneity is also untenable.
[Reply: No, because even a single entity can be designated in terms of both existence and non-existence; for instance: "When the pot perishes, at that very time the shards are produced."
How, then, are the scriptural passages concerning the non-differentiation of the path, creation, dissolution, and lordship to be understood? To this they reply:
the scriptural passages concerning the path do not have as their object the knowledge of Brahman that is pure and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
For in those cases where Brahman—devoid of all adjuncts and characterized by being "not gross" and so forth—is to be meditated upon, [the path is taught].
In this regard, there are the scriptural passages: "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman," and "From him the vital breaths do not depart;
they are merged right here."

Thus, by means of the non-departure of the vital breaths, it is the very self consisting of consciousness (vijñānātman) that is said to arrive. For as long as there is no departure of that [breath], the self consisting of consciousness cannot exist as distinct from Brahman, which is its limiting adjunct (upādhi). However, in the passage "consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, whose form is light," [it is described differently].
Thus, that which possesses adjuncts is the object of worship; those [meditations] have that as their domain,
where this is heard:

"Furthermore, there are two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here; there is the lake Airammadīya, the Aśvattha tree named Somasavana, the city Aparājitā, and the golden hall built by the Lord for Brahman.
Likewise, there is the scriptural report of those who do not know Brahman attaining that state:

"And those who in the forest worship faith, truth, and austerity. However, the attainment of the Supreme Brahman is not possible for those who do not know Brahman, as it is said: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where all desires have vanished."
Neither sacrificial gifts nor ignorant ascetics go there.
Thus, because of the scriptural statement, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," how then is the scriptural teaching of non-returning to be understood?
On this point, some hold the following view:

by resorting to gradual liberation (*kramamukti*), having attained that [intermediate state] and there produced knowledge of reality free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi-tattvajñāna*), they reach the supreme state.
As it has been said:
"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified— they,
at the time of the final end, [attain] in the worlds of Brahman..."
Having attained the supreme nectar, they are all completely liberated.

"In the worlds of Brahmā" is a reference to the *kārya-brahmaloka* (the effected world of Brahmā), because the plural number is justified there through the multiplicity of its constituent parts. "The time of the ultimate end" refers to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), which is the termination of Brahmā’s own period of office.

In that [state], having become immortal by means of the supreme nectar— that is, having become immortal as the form of the Supreme Brahman— through the yoga of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yoga*), they [attain this] by means of the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the fruits of their own performed actions and through the yoga (*yoga*) of meditating that "all this,
including the agent and so forth, is Brahman. And thus says the Smṛti:
"When the time for the universal dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā at the end of the highest [cycle]."
Others, however, think as follows:

just as in the world of the moon, having dwelt there until the exhaustion of their merit, those who have experienced their enjoyments return while that world itself still persists; it is not so in the case of the world of Brahmā, from which there is no return while it persists.
Rather, their stay there lasts until the final dissolution of that world.
For at that dissolution, one does not return from it;
and thus non-return is heard in scripture:
"They do not return to this human whirlpool."
Thus,
"this" and "here" are qualifiers.
"He attains immortality"— here, immortality is relative, as in the expression "the gods are immortal. And likewise, there is a traditional recollection from the Purāṇas:
"Indeed, immortality is said to be that state which lasts until the dissolution of all beings.
As for the view held by some—
that even though Brahman is omnipresent, there is a distinction between its modified (vikṛta) and unmodified (avikṛta) states— [it is refuted as follows].
And from that follows a difference of location;
likewise, a difference of location for the unmodified Brahman is heard in scripture: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven."
Therefore, a specific path is appropriate for the attainment of Brahman, which is unchanging and has a fixed location;
this must be carefully considered.
First of all, this path does not belong to one in whom non-dual pure gnosis (*vidyā*) has not yet arisen.
It does not arise from hearing for one who already knows Brahman,
nor for one who possesses knowledge,
because upon the dawning of knowledge, all differentiation is destroyed.
Even the scriptural passage concerning the illustration of the river of honey refers to the absence of discriminative knowledge, and not to an actual state of non-distinction; likewise,
the scriptural passages regarding creation do not have creation as their primary purport.
What then? They have as their primary aim the realization of the single reality of the Self.
Therefore, the determination of their meaning is established solely in accordance with that [realization], and not in contradiction to it.
For it is said: "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known?
[The answer is: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
Thus, because of the commencement by way of oneness: "All this has that as its self;
that is the Truth, that is the Self."
Because of the concluding statement "That thou art," this single sentence is understood as being solely intent upon the realization of the reality of non-dual identity;
in that case, if another creation of principles such as fire and so forth were enjoined as being real, there would be a split in the sentence.

Therefore, just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* injunction, the statements such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper," which begin and conclude with the theme of non-repetition (*ajāmitva*), do not attain the status of separate injunctions due to the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); rather, because they serve that purpose, they are established as being for the sake of praise (*stuti*) in accordance with it—
so too do the scriptural texts concerning creation function as a means to [realize] oneness.
Nor can it be argued that the scriptural mention of oneness is intended for the purpose of establishing difference,
because there is an introduction and a conclusion regarding oneness throughout.
The meaning of a sentence is that with which one begins and that with which one concludes;
for the comprehension of difference yields no fruit,
whereas the comprehension of unity has both seen and heard fruits, such as the cessation of grief and so forth.

Because that [reality] is understood through the vision of the pure, singular Self— as heard in the scripture: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?"— [there is no delusion].
Furthermore, that which lacks a fruit serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to that which possesses a fruit,
and it serves as a means (*upāya*);
nor is this world rooted in non-existence.
What then? It has as its root a single, non-dual Being.
And because the effect is not distinct from its cause, this world is indeed one with Being, just like a jar or other such objects.
For jars and the like do not transcend oneness with clay in its form;
[one might object: "In that case, would this not be stating the primary relationship of cause and effect?
[We reply: This is not so, because it is merely a means for introducing [the concept of] oneness.
Indeed, it is not the causal relationship itself that is being established here, such that it would be understood in its primary sense exactly as the words suggest;
for it has been stated that [the relationship] is due to being a means to oneness.
And by this means, the person (puruṣa) is led to the realization of oneness;
yet that [oneness] is primary and opposed to the Pradhāna,

because the repeated scriptural declarations such as "one only, without a second" are intent upon the negation of all duality, and thus it cannot be said [that the person is identical with the Pradhāna].
There is unity in its nature as cause, and plurality in its nature as effect— ‘That is the Truth; That is the Self.’
And thus, because it is determined that the cause alone is real, and because elsewhere— in the passage "Indra [acts] through māyās"—
it is heard in scripture that difference is accessible only through māyā.
Furthermore, because the absence of difference is heard directly in the scriptural text,
"There is not even the slightest diversity here," and because the contradiction between difference and non-difference has already been described as logically untenable.
This is described without contradiction as being merely the material cause (*upādāna*) of the conceptual differentiation of difference,
just like the relationship between an original object and its reflection, or like letters, words, and sentences.
For indeed, reflections of various forms do not arise from the original object itself.
The conceptual differentiation of distinct reflections occurs solely by virtue of having the original object (*bimba*) as their material cause (*upādāna*).
For there are no entities that constitute reflections which are either separate from the original object or mutually exclusive of one another;
rather, the material cause of the original object is merely that which appears in various forms.
Likewise, there are no entities such as words, sentences, or contexts that exist apart from the phonemes,
because the conceptualization of them is based solely upon those phonemes; [it is held that] "words are produced from the phonemes."
It is said that "a sentence [arises] from words.
Moreover, even in a dream, creation is heard of in scripture:
"There are no chariots there, no draft animals, nor are there roads."
In that case, the statement "then he creates chariots, draft animals, and paths" would be similar,
because it is intended for another purpose.
It has been stated by [the Lord] himself that, because modifications are unreal— as in the passage, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name"— [this power] is not ultimately real.
Even in the scriptural texts concerning sovereignty, this is heard as the ripening of the knowledge of one's own qualities:—
"He becomes onefold; he becomes threefold"; "He obtains all desires";
"He becomes self-ruling"—thus [it is said].
But liberation is not so;
for that is caused solely by the knowledge of Brahman free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi-brahmavidyā*).
As for the scriptural mention in some places of "non-return" (*apunarāvṛtti*), [it refers to something else].
The explanation for that [liberated state] also has two possible courses; such is one view.
Others, however, think as follows:

because Brahman is the Self of all, the Lord of all, and the enjoyer of all enjoyments, and because the joys of the gods and others consist solely of the nature of that [Brahman’s] bliss, [the liberated soul] manifests in the form of Brahman.
"He attains all worlds and all desires;
he becomes his own ruler"—this proclamation of him is for the purpose of praising liberation, characterized by the manifestation of the nature of Brahman.
Now, one might object: if, by being the Self of all, he attains all desires, would he not also attain all sorrow, delusion, and so forth?
No, for those [attributes] are not the nature of Brahman, being superimposed by ignorance;
rather, knowledge, sovereignty, bliss, and enjoyment are the nature of Brahman, as in:
"Brahman is consciousness and bliss."
"There is no other seer but he";
"Other beings live on only a fraction of this very bliss";
"The Lord of all."
This is because of scriptural passages such as, "O Gārgī, under the command of this Imperishable (akṣara)... and so forth.
And thus, whatever lordship, whatever consciousness, and whatever bliss exists in all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—all those belong to Brahman;
it is therefore logical that he who has manifested the true nature of Brahman partakes of them.
The worlds and so forth, however, are superimposed by ignorance and are not the nature of Brahman;
how could they possibly affect the manifested essential nature of Brahman?

But surely, since the non-dual Brahman is devoid of the phenomenal world (prapañca), both consciousness and sovereignty are untenable due to the absence of an object of knowledge and the absence of anything to be ruled over.
In that regard, the scriptural statements "the omniscient one" and "the lord of all" are indeed to be reconciled.
This is not essential, because lordship is not constituted by that which is to be ruled, nor is knowership constituted by that which is to be known.

Rather, by means of his perfected nature as knowledge and his perfected power of lordship (*īśana-śakti*), he attains the object of knowledge and exercises command and governance over that which is to be ruled, just like light and heat. For indeed, by means of his perfected nature as light, the sun illuminates that which is to be illuminated.
But its nature as light does not depend upon that which is illuminated, nor is the burning power of fire dependent upon the fuel to be burned;
and thus, because the entire phenomenal world is manifested by that consciousness alone—
Its omniscience is established by such scriptural passages as, "By its light all this shines," and "There is no other seer but it.
Its status as the Lord of all is also established, because by its sovereignty, the various lords exercise their rule over those who are to be ruled.
And thus, by the statements "He is the lord of beings" and "He is the guardian of the world," the sovereignty of Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and the others is declared;
and the attainment of all desires follows from the fact that the bliss of the gods and others belongs to Him.
Desires are attained through the attainment of joy in desires, not by way of their own intrinsic nature.
Thus it is said: "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and delighting with women, or..."
Thus it should be described;
because of the enjoyment of bliss having that as its object, and not through union with women and the like.
As it is said, "He whose delight is in the Self, whose play is in the Self, whose consort is the Self";
for literal play with the Self or having the Self as a consort is not possible.
And because his very own knowledge and other qualities, which are actually undivided, appear as divided through conceptual construction within all beings.

Therefore, wherever there was no absolute limitation due to their excellence, the Blessed One, having declared those various beings as His own self on account of their proximity— beginning with "Among the sages, I am Vyāsa"— concluded [the enumeration] as follows:
"Whatever being possesses greatness";
likewise, "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer," and so forth.
Because the vision of all beings and so forth is based upon that consciousness;
others, however, say:
"Whatever designation there may be regarding the Supreme, which rests upon name and form, all of that is for the purpose of meditative contemplation."
As in the passages, "That person who is in the sun" and "He has golden hair and beard," and so forth;
for there can be no confinement to a specific location for the Supreme Being, who is established in His own majesty.
And for one who has transcended all distinctions, there is the possession of a distinguished form; moreover, this is supreme,
because of the scriptural teaching on the arising from all evils.
"He has risen above all evils"—
thus meditation is enjoined in that manner;
likewise, it should be understood from the fact of his omniscience as well.
Thus, the manifestation of that very nature of Brahman as the Self is its attainment; that is liberation, and it is indeed knowledge itself. Therefore, liberation is not something to be produced.
Nor is it sufficient to say that [liberation] is not something other than knowledge.
Now, it might be thought: "Let liberation not be something to be accomplished."
However, the destruction of the causes of bondage is what is to be accomplished;
the means for accomplishing that would be the vision of the self (ātmadarśana).
And it is heard that its fruit is the destruction of the karmas which are the causes of bondage.
"And his actions perish when that which is both high and low is seen";
likewise, "Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed. By the word "evil" (pāpman), merit (puṇya) is also included.
Because it has a faulty result;
and elsewhere, having begun with, "Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds [cross it]," [KKS 129]...
Because of the concluding statement, "All evils turn back from here," and because the attainment of security does not occur without the destruction of those [evils],
it must necessarily be performed.
Nor is there a destruction of karma that has not yet yielded its fruit,
because expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), when enjoined in connection with specific faults, have the destruction of those very faults as their result.
Therefore, just as through expiatory rites, the destruction of the causes of bondage is accomplished by means of knowledge (vidyā).
And that itself is liberation,
because the root *muc* has the sense of "severing from bondage";
and thus, there is no fault of having an end.
Because even an effect that has been destroyed is not itself annihilated;
regarding this, it is said:
"Even the destruction of the causes of bondage does not [occur] for us by means of expiation and the like."
When all ignorance has dissolved, nothing remains to be severed.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of bondage, has come to an end within knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the destruction of the cause of bondage is not something to be accomplished by the vision of the Self (*ātman*);
for that [knowledge] arises precisely while effecting the dissolution of the entire empirical functioning of ignorance.
Furthermore, the differentiation of the experience of the fruits of karma has ignorance as its substrate (*upādāna*).
In that regard, when ignorance is uprooted without remainder, there is nothing further to be cut away.
For actions are superimposed by ignorance; thus, upon the destruction of that [ignorance], they are indeed destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*).
For one who perceives the non-dual reality of the Self, there is no possibility at all for its maturation [of karma],
because that [maturational process] is based upon the perception of duality;
and since the cessation of karma occurs precisely through the eradication of ignorance.
Therefore, actions are completely dissolved by doubt and error, which are treated as equivalent [to ignorance]:
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and one's karmas are exhausted when that Higher-and-Lower is seen."
But surely, if the exhaustion of karma is accepted in this way, liberation would occur immediately upon the vision of reality, without waiting for the fall of the body—as it is said:
"For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]."
Otherwise, the scriptural passage concerning the expectation of the fall of the body would be contradicted.

However, for one who understands from scripture that knowledge is the means for their destruction, it follows accordingly that for some there is destruction by knowledge, and for others by experience.
In this regard, since the statement "and his actions are exhausted" is made without qualification, there arises the contingency of the exhaustion of all actions;

however, because of the scriptural hearing that "for him, the delay is only so long [as he is not delivered from the body]," there is no exhaustion of those actions whose effects have already begun (ārabdhakārya) and whose enjoyment has already commenced, even after liberation.
It is understood that [merit] is exhausted by enjoyment alone;
for it is not tenable that one should wait for the fall of the body when all [merit] has been exhausted.
As it has been said:
"But only those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is their limit";
and "But having exhausted the others by experience, he attains [the Self].

For if ignorance were destroyed by knowledge, then because there would be no distinction once the worldly process of the ripening of karma has ceased, all [karma] would be destroyed, and one would be liberated immediately.
There is no fault at all;
for this scriptural passage does not state that liberation has the falling off of the body as its limit qualified by a long duration of time, but rather [states] its swiftness.
Just as someone, wishing to convey something very quickly regarding some task, might say: "It has been only this long for me since I bathed and ate," so too is this [case].
Otherwise, one could not have said "only so long" (tāvadeva);
rather, one would have said "for a long time" (ciram). However, from the expression "only so long," it is understood that the intent is brevity.
Therefore, liberation occurs very swiftly; there is nothing to wait for.
However, the waiting for the fall of the body does indeed occur there as a necessary consequence.
Alternatively, having restated the quality of being "long," the state of having the fall of the body as its limit is stated here;
otherwise, if both the length and the specific limit were being stated simultaneously, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
In that case, the meaning is as follows:
If it were for someone for a long time,
lasting until "I am liberated," then indeed,

in the former position, because the falling away of the body occurs immediately after the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the description of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady (*sthitaprajña*) would not be tenable.
"What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? and so forth.

The second [position] is also untenable, because since all things have perished, the state of being "long-standing" is impossible, and thus it is illogical to prescribe a specific temporal limit therein.
It is said in reply:
First of all, one whose wisdom is steady is not a perfected being (siddha) from whom all ignorance has fallen away;
rather, he must be a practitioner (sādhaka) who has attained a particular stage.
Nor do we say—
The separation from the body occurs immediately after the realization of Brahman;
however, one must wait for the exhaustion of the karma that has already begun to bear fruit through its experience.
In that regard, for some, liberation occurs at that very time.
For some, there is a certain degree of delay.

For example, when the fear arising from the superimposition of a snake upon a rope ceases upon seeing the true nature of reality, for some that fear and its resulting effects, such as trembling, cease at that very moment, while for others they persist for some length of time.
Due to that conditioning (*saṃskāra*),
even when all karma has been exhausted, the persistence of the body is maintained by the continued operation of the conditioning of the maturation currently being experienced;
it is like the rotation of a potter's wheel continuing even after the potter's activity has ceased.
Now, if even for one who knows Brahman the perception of distinctions such as the enjoyer and so forth persists,
it would persist even after the fall of the body;
in that case, liberation would not be certain even for the knower.
And thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement, "For so long only is it delayed.
Now, if it is argued that because ignorance has been eradicated, it does not persist;
That it should not exist even for a single moment—that is the very contradiction;
this is the rope with a noose at both ends.
It is said in reply:
Just as, even when fear has vanished and one has regained composure, trembling and so forth may continue to occur due to mere residual impressions (*saṃskāra*);
yet, despite the disappearance of fear, this persistence does not imply that it lasts for a long time.
Furthermore, such a residual impression does not produce an effect equal to that of its primary cause.
Nor is it permanent;
otherwise, there would be no cessation of trembling and so forth.
Furthermore, because the cause for the removal of fear is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), it does not require another cause for that cessation.
For from that very [ignorance] it gradually ceases, or it ceases by itself like the momentum of the rotation of a potter’s wheel;

thus, when ignorance has ceased and all karmas— both those whose effects have already begun and those whose effects have not yet begun— have been terminated, this Self appears as if it were an embodied enjoyer due to the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the maturation of karma that has already begun.
Even the wise man returns [to the world] as a mere appearance, but unlike the ignorant person, he is not possessed by deep-seated attachment;
such is this one of steady wisdom described: his desires have departed, he is content in the nature of the Self, and he regards sufferings as being merely like shadows.

Because he perceives reality, his mind is undisturbed by artificial things such as tigers and the like, as if they were not real; and because he has no attachment, he is free from longing for pleasures that are merely artificially charming.
Indeed, just as an ignorant person’s perception of objects such as women fashioned from clay or wood is devoid of attachment, being a mere reflection, so it is for him.
Likewise, for the wise person whose karma and ignorance have been destroyed, perception of objects occurs through their mere residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) as if by a mere shadow.
And thus, the scripture—“Just as a snake’s slough might lie dead and cast off upon an anthill, even so is this body”—demonstrates the wise person’s lack of attachment to the body;
for the residual impression does not produce a result equal to that of the primary cause, just like trembling and other such involuntary movements.
Nor does it persist for a long time, because a mental formation (saṃskāra) endures only for a short duration;
and likewise, no other cause is required for its cessation.
Because that [ignorance] also ceases either gradually through the very vision of reality,
or by itself,
this state is celebrated as "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti).
Furthermore, the exhaustion of the karmic impressions (*saṃskāra*) that have initiated the activity of the body is understood to occur only upon the fall of the body.

If those impressions were to persist, the fall of the body would not even take place; thus, it is impossible for the fruition (*vipāka*) of that karma to be seen even in the slightest degree after the body has fallen.
For the residual appearance of that fruition occurs only within the very body by which it was initiated.

However, for those [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun—that is, those whose activity has not been attained—they have ceased without leaving a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), because there is no such impression.
For it is only from the latent impression of a cause that has attained its activity that a trace of its effect persists.

Indeed, when fear has not attained its activity and no trembling or similar effects have been produced, there is certainly no persistence of trembling or the like resulting from a latent impression of that [fear].

Therefore, because those whose effects have not yet begun have not yet attained their functional manifestation, and because the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of those whose effects have begun is understood from the falling away of the body, liberation (*kaivalya*) is inevitable for the knower once this body has fallen. And in this regard,
the remainder of the effect arises either from the latent impression of the cause that has attained its functional manifestation, or from the latent impression of the effect itself.
Likewise, the persistence of trembling and so forth arises solely from the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of both; or else, fear arises from the residual impression of fear,
and from that, trembling and so forth [occur].
Alternatively, the persistence of trembling and so forth arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of trembling and so forth.
In every case, even when the cause has ceased, the persistence of a remnant of the effect occurs due to latent impressions.
Therefore, the maintenance of the body for the wise person also proceeds from the latent impressions of karma that have already attained their functional state, or from its maturation (*vipāka*).
This has also been stated in another tantra:
"He remains, maintaining the body like the whirling of a potter's wheel, by the force of residual impressions (saṃskāra).
As for those, however, who think—
It is argued that for karmas whose fruition has already begun, just as it is impossible to stop an arrow in flight or a spinning wheel, there can be no obstruction;
therefore, one must wait for their exhaustion through experience.
This is incorrect, for an arrow can indeed be obstructed by walls and other such barriers.
And [rites] for destruction through cutting and so forth,

as well as propitiatory rites (*śāntika*) intended for the exhaustion of karma whose ripening has been indicated by dreams and the like and is to be experienced in the present body— all these are for the sake of [altering] that very conditioning.
Therefore, stability arises from conditioning alone.
But surely, ignorance alone remains as the residual effect of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
In that case, how can there be the complete dissolution of all ignorance, or how can it be said that nothing remains to be severed? It is replied:
Seized by the counteragent— the vision of the pure, singular Self— they have indeed already dissolved as soon as they arose;
for, being incapable of action and not constituting bondage,
there is no need for any further cause for their cessation.
For one who directly experiences the truly pure self, the appearance of maturation—which does not touch that [self] and is incapable of acting as bondage—is utterly dissolved.
Just as for one experiencing the reality of a painting and the like, the appearance of a woman or other objects serves as no cause for passion and so forth;

likewise, for one knowing the stainless self, even if a contrary appearance such as blackness arises in relation to a sword or similar object, it is dissolved the moment it finds no room due to the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
And thus, because of that, one does not grieve over the self due to its impurity, nor does one rejoice in its brilliance;
for even though both appear, their manifestation is obstructed within the self by the vision of reality (tattvadarśana).
And thus, as it is said:
"The maintenance of the body would result either from karma or from residual impressions (saṃskāra); what is the distinction?
And what is the exhaustion of karma if its effect continues?"
For it is through the cessation of that [desire] that its destruction is understood.
Therefore, it is only logical that "having exhausted the others by means of experience, one attains [the state of Brahman]."
That too has been refuted:

for the ripening of karma touches the self only for the ignorant who possess sorrow and delight; but for the wise, because it does not touch them, it is a mere appearance, like the specific reflections produced by a jewel, a sword, a mirror, and so forth.
It is not a karmic maturation (vipāka), because it is neither something to be delighted in nor something to be hated;
and thus it is said: "Having encountered various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one neither rejoices nor feels aversion."
Thus it has been shown. Likewise:
"That in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees."

Even while one is seeing, the manifold world of the body and so forth is "night," because it is not touched by that [seeing], owing to its being equal to the unseen. Now, if the appearance of the manifold world, though arisen, is struck down by the knowledge of reality, it does not touch the Self.
It performs no action, nor is it bondage, since that [result] arises from the word alone; for what purpose, then, is meditation and so forth? It is said in reply:
Verbal knowledge has the nature of being indirect, whereas the manifestation of the phenomenal world has the nature of being direct perception;
therefore, because there is no contradiction between the two, the manifestation of the phenomenal world does not touch upon the Self.
It is not ineffective, nor is it non-binding,
just as in the case of a substance whose sweetness is determined by another means of valid cognition, yet which possesses the character of being perceived by direct perception.

The appearance of bitterness through the gateway of the senses does not persist as a mere appearance because it lacks contact with a real substance; likewise, that substance—though appearing as if ultimately bitter—is like an unperceived sweetness and leads to suffering.

However, for one who has directly realized the reality of the Self through meditation and other means, even if the appearance of phenomenal diversity exists, it does not touch the Self due to its opposition [to that realization].
Like Devadatta appearing as a lion:
although he appears through the superimposition "Devadatta is a lion," he does not actually touch that [lion-nature].
It is ineffective and not a cause of fear;
and the manifestation of the reality of the self is eternal.
In that case, there is no further possibility for error;
however, verbal cognition, being dependent on a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is momentary,
and therein there is once again the possibility of error.
For it is observed that even when one does not investigate the means of valid cognition, fear of a rope arises again through the delusion of a snake;
therefore, in this case as well, one should constantly maintain the verbal knowledge.
What else could this be but meditation (*upāsana*)?
Therefore, the severance of the cause of bondage is also knowledge itself; it is not something to be accomplished by that [knowledge].
The same should be said regarding the non-attachment to future sins.
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus"— this is because the distinction between agent and action is dissolved by knowledge.
Thus, there will be no assumption of multiple fruits for knowledge,
nor will there be a transformation of present-tense statements into injunctions regarding results.

Regarding what was stated—that Brahman is not the object of verbal cognition—it is replied here: "If Brahman were not accessible through verbal cognition, then an injunction for [the attainment of] cognition would be impossible. (MBs 2.108)
For the purpose of establishing a specific cognition, an unestablished object is not suitable;
a positive affirmation does not have its locus unrepresented, nor is mere cognition itself affirmed.
Indeed, it is not mere knowledge that is enjoined, but rather a specific object of knowledge;
and there can be no injunction with respect to that which is unestablished and undefined.
For it is not possible to direct [the mind] toward an object that is not established;
and the distinction of cognition is mediated by its object.
Furthermore, an unestablished object is incapable of defining its own specific characteristics.
Furthermore, the nature of the self is not established by anything other than verbal testimony;
and if it is not established even by verbal testimony, then—
given that no specific cognition mediated by that [testimony] is established— the object [of action] is untenable, and consequently, the injunction is untenable.
Moreover, he demonstrates that for those who maintain that there is an injunction regarding a specific knowledge, the very authority regarding the reality of the Self is lost:
"Whether the injunction is aimed at its own establishment, or else intent upon the accomplishment of an action, the realization of the non-dual reality of Brahman is rendered causeless. (MBs 2.110)
The understanding of this [mantra] derived from its ritual application (viniyoga) consists in its purpose of knowledge and action;
that which is not directed toward that [purpose] is not authoritative, like the cognition arising from an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Since injunction (*vidhi*) pertains to action, it is not capable of operating upon a substance;
rather, the establishment of that [substance] arises from its connection with existence (*sattā*), and thus [the opponent's position] is refuted.
The cognition of a qualified object is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but not with respect to the qualifier;
for even though the cognition is qualified, it is necessarily directed toward the [qualified] object itself.
It does not establish the existence [of the object] at all, because it occurs through superimposition (*samāropa*).

If, first of all, the status of being an "action to be accomplished" (*kāryatā*) were understood as belonging to the injunction (*niyoga*) alone, then that [injunction], having culminated in its own fulfillment, would cease together with the word.
Even if the understanding of what is to be done arises from the application (viniyoga) regarding an object, nevertheless, in the accomplishment of that object,
in either case, it does not touch upon the true nature of reality.
In that case, the realization of the non-dual reality of the Self would be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*).
It might be argued as follows:
"The Self which is free from evil, ageless..."
Thus, it might be argued that the reality of things is understood either through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of these words or otherwise;
but that is not so, because the passage has another purpose.
For that [instruction] does not terminate with the thought, "It is thus."

However, the culmination in "what ought to be done"— in the form "this must be understood in this way"— is not a means of valid cognition regarding the reality of the thing itself, because it is intent upon something else, like the knowledge arising from an explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning historical narratives.
Nor is the reality of the Self itself the object of an injunction.
Because that [injunction] has as its object that which is to be performed,
and because action is of such a nature,
it is impossible for there to be an operation toward a substance that is already established and not to be performed, even when the word for it is directly employed.

On the contrary, the establishment of the essential nature of a substance occurs through its persistence as an existence that is not touched by any of the three times— [the past, present, or future]— as in:
"Such a thing existed,
exists, [or will exist]."
"Or it will come to be.
Therefore, [the injunction] is defective in its establishment of its own nature (*svarūpa*),
for there is no comprehension of the existence of that which is to be enjoined even across the three times.
For when it is said, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the existence of the sacrifice as belonging to the past, the present, or the future is not understood.
[Objection: But surely it is understood as belonging to the future, because an injunction has the future as its object.
This is not so;
for that which is enjoined will not necessarily be performed, as this would entail the consequence of there being no fault in the non-performance of what has been enjoined.
But surely, the denotation of a qualified action is accepted as a means of valid cognition even with respect to the qualifiers—
just as in "one should sacrifice with soma.
Likewise, in the sentence "Devadatta’s son, wearing armlets and earrings, broad-chested, is studying," the entire collection of qualifiers is perceived along with the action of studying.
True;

a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that cognizes a qualified action is also a means of valid cognition for the qualifier, because of the nature of apprehension (*pratipatti*). For an apprehension, being itself cognized as qualified by a particular object, does not necessarily indicate the actual existence of that particular object.
Since it is possible even through the superimposition of an appearance of something as it is upon that which has become otherwise—
as in the case of the view of heaven and so forth as fire, as in "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire"—
here [the opponent] says:
Is it not the case that our cognition does not have a contrary object, because that would contradict direct experience?
And because it is unreliable, the cognition of silver is a memory of silver;
for it is certainly not logical that one thing should be perceived as another, since that would contradict the nature of perception itself.

How can one thing be the object when something else appears [in consciousness]? Furthermore, because there would be no reliability: if cognition deviates from the form of the object, there could be no ascertainment of that object from it.
Moreover, a cognition that does not conform to the form of its object would be non-objective and without an objective support (*anālambana*), and thus it would be entirely ungraspable;

for the mere cause of cognition, like the eyes and so forth, lacks an objective support. Consequently, because it would lack the nature of being a cognizer, the establishment of an object cannot occur from it even through dependence on something else.
What then is this "silver" when the eye is in contact with mother-of-pearl?
It is memory, arising from the perception of a common feature.
If that is so, how then does error arise?
It arises from the non-apprehension of the distinction between what is perceived and what is being remembered.
Thus, for those devoid of discrimination, this is a false conceit of apprehending non-difference when there is actually a non-apprehension of difference.
Just as at a distance, when the intervening space is not perceived, there arises the misconception of perceiving contact among trees and other objects;
therefore, this recollection of silver, devoid of discrimination, takes the form "I remember.
To this, it is replied:
For this [cognition] would not arise with respect to a fragment of mother-of-pearl at that time.
If it is argued that the activity [of cognition] occurs with respect to silver because of its proximity, [we reply: no, because of its non-proximity;
and if it is argued that this is due to the non-cognition of non-proximity, then from what source comes the restriction of activity?
Whatever occurs therein is caused by the proximity of those very [factors],
because elsewhere there is the apprehension of difference as well as the non-apprehension of distinction.
If the distinction in activity arises from a failure to discern due to similarity,
then one would act toward unseen objects such as clods of earth because of that lack of discernment.
If that cognition does not exist there, then it would not exist even in the case of a fragment of mother-of-pearl;
if, on the other hand, it does exist as having a contrary object, how can its manifestation be denied?
Because it is not seen, there is no engagement with it, just as with a fragment of mother-of-pearl;
for that form by which it is seen is not the cause of such engagement.
If [you argue that this occurs] due to the non-discrimination between what is seen and memory, then let this be examined here:
whether from the cognition of reality or from the non-cognition of reality, there is the perception of silver.
In the former case, activity occurs toward what is seen, while the cognition is held to have a contrary object;
in the latter case, there is no distinction between the seen and the unseen, and [the cognition] is not useful.
For those two are indeed employed for superimposition in one's own perception of yoga;
otherwise, there could be no visual error regarding what is unseen or unassociated [with the senses].
If a piece of mother-of-pearl in contact with the eye were perceived as "this is not silver," [then there would be no error].
Or likewise, if it were silver,
a person seeking silver would not proceed toward a fragment of mother-of-pearl with the desire to obtain it;
for him, [it would be] "silver."
Thus, because there is no such comprehension, it is like a clod of earth or similar objects;
nor does that activity occur with respect to remembered silver, because that [silver] is not present in that location.
For even when an object has been perceived, one does not act toward it with a desire for that which is absent from it.
This might be argued:
"Action occurs there because of the perception of silver and the non-perception of its absence."
That is not so, because the activity occurs only with respect to the piece of mother-of-pearl;
indeed, the activity there is based on its proximity.
Furthermore, because there is a cognition of mere silver and a lack of discrimination from memory, the activity would occur even elsewhere.
Because non-apprehension due to non-proximity is no different in that case as well.
Now, if it is thought:
"In the case of objects in other locations, which are understood through specific perception, there is no activity because of the apprehension of the distinction from silver," [we reply:]...

In the case of a fragment of mother-of-pearl, however, activity occurs because there is a perception of the mere white and lustrous form common to silver, and because there is a failure to grasp its distinction from the silver that appears in memory.
Even so, in the case of the world and other such things not previously perceived, activity would still occur due to the lack of determination that they are something other than that [silver].
Now, if it is argued that there is no cognition of silver in those cases, [the response follows:]...
Nor is it the case in the other instance either;
or else, one would have to admit that there is a distorted manifestation (viparītakhyāti) even when the object exists.
Or, if it is argued that because [the object] has not been seen, one does not act toward things that have not been seen—
One would not even act toward a mother-of-pearl shell [mistaken for silver].
But surely, that which has the form of silver is not what is apprehended by that [cognition].
Just as it does not exist for that which is not in contact with the eye, so too it does not exist for the conch-shell even when it is in contact.
If one should think:
Due to the distinction between what is being seen and what is being remembered, [the cognition] operates only when conjoined with the eye, and not in relation to anything else.
Even in that case, this must be investigated:

Is the cognition of non-difference due to the perception of proximity resulting from the absence of one who grasps distinction and one who creates distinction, and from that [cognition] follows activity;
or is it merely from the absence of the cognition of difference?
In the former case, there is error.
