In the subsequent [cognition], there is no distinction between the seen and the unseen, or between the associated and the non-associated, because the non-apprehension of difference is equal in both cases.
For there is no utility whatsoever for either sense-organ contact or perception in the apprehension [of that difference].
However, [superimposition] exists in the case of an unreal superimposition (*abhūtasamāropa*).
Indeed, a sensory superimposition is not possible in any way with respect to that which has not been apprehended or is not associated [with the senses].
If it is argued that what is remembered is distinct from direct perception because it arises solely from its own cognition, then from where [does such a distinction arise]?
Otherwise, there would be no discernment, since there would always be only the perception of the universal.
If one considers that error arises from the non-discrimination between two memories when one is recollecting another, and not from the observation of doubt; // MBs_2.125 //
Therefore, that [distinction] does not belong to either of the two, since a reversal is observed in both memory and perception;
for if it is argued that perception is distinguished from memory by its specific cognition, [we reply: if it is so defined, [it fails].
If this [self-cognition] does not exist, how could there be a single cognition when there is forgetfulness?
For one who remembers the previous form as being truly one, it would appear clearly even in the case of the moon. (MBs 2.127)
How can you have the delusion of duality due to the defect of cataracts and the like, or [the delusion] of one who,
desiring water, has fixed his mind upon a mother-of-pearl shell?
For a misconception would not occur, or it would have to occur in water [as well]. Furthermore, you must explain this:
is that which is being remembered distinguished from that which is being perceived by its own cognition alone, or not?
The very nature of recollective cognition (*smṛtijñāna*) is such that it manifests [its object] as distinct from the object to be cognized,
or else it rests solely upon its own nature.
In the former case, how could there be a non-discrimination between the two objects of recollection?
Is it because of being distinct from one's own cognition alone?
Even in the other case, there would be error when there is constant recollection; and in the perception of a universal, there is non-discrimination due to the recollection of something else.
And that is not so,
because doubt is also observed.
Now, if it is thought:
In the case of a single recollection, there is error due to non-discrimination;
in the case of multiple recollections, however, there is doubt.
"It is not due to non-distinction from a single [object];
that is incorrect,
for even when there is recollection of many [objects], error is observed."
And if, in the case of a perceptible object, that which is being remembered is distinguished from it by means of a cognition of its specific qualities—
and not by means of a cognition of itself— then,
in the absence of such a cognition of specific qualities, when both are being remembered, there would necessarily be doubt.
A single appearance is not a misconception;
rather, it is distinguished from its own cognition through memory,
and a distinction between memory and misconception is thus admitted.
In that case, even when there is recollection of multiple [alternatives], error is possible due to specific defects of the sense organs;
and this has been demonstrated:
even upon seeing a common property, when one sometimes recollects only one alternative, there is neither doubt nor error.
Because the defects are not nourished;
therefore, at that time, it is remembered and discerned through its own cognition alone,
not from the determination of specific features of the object of perception.
If this is so, from what source does the non-discrimination between the perceived and the remembered arise?

Furthermore, for one who remembers, the identity with the previous form is something entirely different; it is like the illusion of duality regarding the moon, not born from a failure to discriminate between the remembered and the present.
Nor can it be due to a failure to distinguish between the different functions of the cognitive and motor organs,
because those two are not perceptible and are merely being remembered; furthermore,
for one whose mind is fixed on mother-of-pearl, there would be no error when he seeks water out of thirst.
Or it is like the appearance of water [in a mirage],
because of the distinction between the remembered object and its own cognition;
nor is every error necessarily bound by similarity.
An illusion of yellow is seen in what is white, and an illusion of bitterness is seen in what is sweet;
for due to some slight similarity, there would be no one who does not experience error in that regard.

Therefore, due to the specific distribution of the capacities of the defects of the sense organs, there is a restriction regarding errors; however, when there is no apprehension [of the object], there is no restriction on error caused by the defect.

Furthermore, if error arises from the recollection of a similar object due to the perception of a similar one, how could there be an illusion of yellow in what is white, or a delusion of bitterness in what is sweet?
For such an error would occur even for one who does not employ the external sense organ, provided there is an internal sensation of bile.
Because it is invisible, like collyrium that has entered the eye or the blackness residing therein;
furthermore, if there were similarity in only some respect, there would be the undesirable consequence of error occurring in every possible way.
Therefore, the arising of error is determined by the specific capacity of the defects of the sense organs.
If the operation of the defect were merely non-apprehension, there would be no restriction on the occurrence of error due to defects such as jaundice (kāmalā) and the like;
for [error] is not caused by similarity, since error is observed even in the case of what is dissimilar.

Nor is there a failure to apprehend that [object] even in memory due to the recollection of specific qualities; furthermore, because of the particularity of place and time, what was remembered is not clearly distinguished.
Cognition that has apprehended various objects and is distinct from them is also called "recollection"; thus, cognition is stated to be something other than recollection itself.
Nor is that [recognition] established by a fruit distinct from the fruit of pride, in the absence of a fruit;
and when there is a distinction in memory, there is the delusion of recognition.
Furthermore, that which is not present would become known as being present;
thus, because it is a memory of something undistinguished from reality, it would possess a contrary object.
And because the mind is not impaired, there is no lack of presence or grasping;
for it has been stated that a defect is the cause for the non-grasping of the sense faculties.
It has also been stated here that there would be no restriction on the process of manifestation;
furthermore, under this hypothesis, it follows as a logical consequence that all cognitions would be false.
For no object is ever grasped by any cognition in its entirety;
likewise, for one who has not discerned the distinction [between subject and object], there occurs error, such as the appearance of two moons and the like.
Seeing that [the object] possesses continuity, whose own nature would it deny?
Now, if it is thought: "The remembered [object] is distinguished by its own cognition alone."
However, at times there, due to the non-apprehension of the specific difference as if it were present before the eyes, there arises non-discrimination (*aviveka*).
But when the specific difference is apprehended in that which is connected with the sense organ, even if only the universal is seen, there is no non-discrimination;
therefore, even when both alternatives are remembered, no doubt arises.
In a single recollection, there is neither doubt nor error;
likewise, even when there is recollection of two [objects], there would be no error.
Furthermore, in recollection, there is no grasping of distinctions.
Because of the recollection of specific qualities.
Now, if that which is being recollected is distinguished by way of a particular place and time, then there is no apprehension of a difference in place and time in that case.

That is not so; for that which is perceived at a particular place, as well as that which is understood through its distinctions of infinite space and time, is apprehended as distinct from the visible object when it is being remembered.
Nor is this because of the apprehension of distinctions in space and time, since it would otherwise be impossible to remember an infinite number [of instances].
And because there is no difference in location when it is perceived in that same place;
or, if it is argued that there is non-discrimination because it is not grasped as being remembered, whereas discrimination arises from the knowledge that it is being remembered,
and therefore one thinks "I remember."
Thus, cognitions of silver and the like, being devoid of [true] knowledge, are the causes of error.
In that case, memory is indeed complete; nothing of its own object has failed to be grasped by it.
Since that [cognition] itself distinguishes its own object from the visible, there is no lack of distinction between the perceived and the remembered;
for the cognition "I remember" is distinct from memory and serves to differentiate perception from recollection.
In this regard, the following must be considered:
Does memory distinguish its own object or not? If it does distinguish it,
then there is an absence of error.
Now, if memory does not distinguish its own object,
then it was said that there would be an error when there is a perception of a generality and a recollection of something else.
If it is argued that [memory] does distinguish because of the discernment "I do not remember," [we reply:]...
That [distinction] would belong to memory itself by virtue of its own lack of discernment;
for the distinction of a cognition, which is to be understood through its effect, must be inferred from a specific effect.
This would not be the case if the effect of memory were not distinct from the effect of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By what means could that [object] be understood as distinct?
For even when there is a distinction in memory, the delusion of recognition— "that is the very same"— is observed.
Thus, there is no lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) in perception;

for if both [the object and its qualifier] were modified through the discrimination of one, then, due to the lack of discrimination from what has been remembered, there would be an error of memory (*smṛtivibhrama*),
not an error of perception (*pratyakṣabhrama*).
Therefore, it is not due to "non-remembrance" (*pramoṣa*) that there is non-discrimination (*aviveka*).
Furthermore, if non-discrimination were the cognition of something absent as being present, it would follow that memory has a contrary object (*viparītārtha*).
Now, [it may be argued that] this [non-apprehension of non-proximity] occurs in the case of dream-cognition,
but not in the case of an error produced by the sense organs.
Because there is no impairment of the mind, and because non-apprehension is itself a cause of impairment,
it has been stated that there could not be such a restriction on the operation [of cognition].
Furthermore, if an object were actually apprehended, then due to the non-apprehension of some part of it, all cognitions would be erroneous in the case of delusion.
For no cognition whatsoever has an object in its entirety.

Moreover, even when there is discriminative knowledge, it is observed that one may still follow after [errors] such as a double moon or confusion regarding directions due to other means of valid cognition; thus, error is not merely non-apprehension.
Manifestation, which consists in the negation of what was previously expected, is possible only when there is an actual attainment [of the object].
Non-apprehension does not bring about attainment, nor does contrary cognition;
rather, it is the two appearances of silver and the object conjoined with the eye [that do so].
This is not understood as a negation of the object presented by that [perception];
nor does this cognition subvert non-apprehension itself.
For if all [objects] were obstructed by non-apprehension, such a birth would not occur;
this is a cognition of discernment (*viveka-vijñāna*), not a cognition that functions through the negation of what is present.
Speaking thus out of impudence, he denies his own cognition;
for such a discerning intellect does not exist either in succession or in simultaneity.
When there is the attainment of the cognition of identity, there can be no determination of difference,
as one recollects the silver while perceiving the object in contact with the eye.
Having failed to perceive the distinction from silver due to a general perception, one later understands it by discriminating; such is not the case in the initial perception of the universal.
In the absence of the recollection of both alternatives, doubt does not necessarily arise,
because there is no apprehension of their distinction due to the cognition of temporal proximity.

Because it appears as that [object], the apprehension would be of what is desired; otherwise, there would be a non-apprehension. In that case, the cause would be either a non-apprehension or an apprehension of proximity.
Devoid of the denial of the apprehension of difference and existing as a positive entity, error— when no contrary [apprehension] is admitted— is based on non-apprehension.
It has been stated that [the object] is to be known solely through verbal testimony; however, non-apprehension is the bondage of non-apprehension.
The cognition in the form of a negation of what was previously expected—namely, "this is not silver"—is not possible if there is no apprehension, because there would be no basis for the expectation.
Indeed, the non-apprehension of anything does not entail [an error],
for that is simply an absence. Rather,

it is a distorted manifestation (*viparītā khyāti*) that entails [the error] by presenting as present either the silver-ness of something nearby— which is not actually silver— or the presence of silver itself.
But surely, there are two cognitions of the silver and of the object composed of the eye; those two alone are the subsumers.
True.
But this comprehension of negation does not apply to those two things as they are presented [in the cognition].
For we do not perceive that it is "silver" alone, or merely the object conjoined with the eye, that is being negated in the judgment "this is not silver.
Rather, we perceive either the "silver-ness" of that which is conjoined with the eye, or the "eye-conjunction" of the silver.
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of these two cannot be the means of attainment,
precisely because it is a non-apprehension.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the object of negation, the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) must necessarily be accepted.
Nor is it the case that only the non-apprehension "this is not" is being precluded, for that would entail the consequence of such a form [of negation] applying to all cognitions.

Furthermore, if all cognitions were to arise through the sublation of non-apprehension, then this would be merely a cognition of distinction (*vivekajñāna*), and not a cognition in the form of a negation of what was previously supposed; thus, it conforms to the nature of the perception.
For when silver and a fragment of mother-of-pearl are perceived simultaneously as distinct, such a cognition does not occur; it occurs, however, when they are perceived sequentially.

If it is argued that such a cognition would occur when they are perceived as non-distinct, that is correct, because when two things are perceived as distinct, there is the negation of their non-distinction.
The apprehension of two distinct things is joined with the absence of [actual] attainment;
moreover, it sometimes happens that one who remembers silver—
One who perceives only the general features of an object in contact with the eye does not grasp its distinction from silver;
later, through the clarity of the eye, one realizes it.
And yet, at that time, there is no such cognition, because there is no grasping of non-discrimination.
[Objection: But if there is no error upon seeing a common feature, would there not be doubt?
And the determinative cognition that removes that [doubt] is exactly of this same nature.
This is not the essence [of doubt];
for indeed, when there is no recollection of two alternatives, there is no doubt even upon seeing a common property.
Nor is there a reversal;
for there is indeed the perception of mere luminous form standing before one,
while there is a memory of silver.
Nor is any otherness between the two apprehended,
nor is there oneness;
in that case, the knowledge of distinction is not of such a nature.
Because of the non-apprehension of their identity.
Now, if it is thought:
"Due to the non-apprehension of distinction and the perception of temporal proximity, silver appears as if it were in contact with the eye."
Or [it is] conjoined with the eye, like silver;
therefore, since there is contact (*prāpti*), the refutation is established.
In that case, you have accepted the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
For that [appearance] is not something other [than the object],
because it appears as such despite not having that nature;
it may well be caused by ignorance regarding reality.
For that [superimposition] does not arise when there is knowledge of reality,
due to their contradiction;
even in that case, the cause is simply the proximity [of the object].

However, the apprehension of distinction regarding that [non-existence] is a denial (*apavāda*). In the absence of such apprehension, that very non-apprehension is the cause, not the absence [of the object].

Furthermore, if one does not accept the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), then error would be based on non-apprehension; thus, to say that "non-apprehension is based on non-apprehension" is a most ill-spoken statement.
And since there is no second [object] in a dream, how could there be non-discrimination?

If that which was previously undiscriminated due to being remembered were thus discriminated, then—once the substratum has been apprehended—the apprehension of another property would constitute a sublation of the previous [apprehension], and the former would be a delusion.
Thus, whatever contradiction of experience [is alleged] is cited as one's own fault.
This silver is cognized as having the same form [as the shell] because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Since there is a cognition through coreferentiality in the form "this is white silver," the self-reproach [of contradiction] is attached to the other [position], for it contradicts experience;
this is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a distinction between two cognitions.
When it is being known, that lack of confidence is sublated by knowledge itself.
Incapacity [to prove a point] does not arise from deviation, because its effect is obtained;
however, if there is deviation regarding the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), the effect itself is not obtained.

For when there is a lack of confidence regarding an object known in a certain way—namely, the thought that it might otherwise be so—the arising of that very cognition which determines its true nature is blocked.
To explain: for the cessation of such lack of confidence, precisely that kind of cognition is required.
And that [cognition] certainly exists.
Nor is it logical to say that a cognition is an ineffective means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
because the function of a means of valid knowledge— ascertainment— is established by the very nature of cognition itself.
For validity consists in delimitation; however,
deviation and non-deviation are not the determining factors,
because even though smoke and the like are non-deviant, they would lack validity in the absence of that [delimitation].
Furthermore, even though the eye is subject to deviation regarding white, black, and other such objects, it possesses validity when that [object] is present.
Nor is deviation ever observed anywhere to be a cause of sublation or a destroyer of validity, as is the case with defects;
for the eye and other sense organs, despite being subject to deviation, function as valid means of cognition.
But is it not observed that deviation (vyabhicāra) subverts validity, as in the cases of "knowability" (prameyatva), "verticality" (ūrdhvatva), and so forth?
This is not sound. It is not because of deviation in those cases that there is invalidity; rather, [the reason for their being considered valid is different].
Rather, it is because there is an absence of the function of discernment;
and that absence [of the function] is due to the absence of a cause.
For the discernment of the signified (liṅgin) occurs through a mark (liṅga) that is non-deviant.
However, where non-deviation is not the cause [of validity], there is no dispute regarding its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) when there is determination, even if deviation occurs.
And in the case of the sense organs (*akṣa*), knowledge is likewise the cause of determination, unlike a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Furthermore, the arising of doubt does not undermine validity through deviation,
because when something has been correctly determined, the state of being twofold is no longer a cause for doubt;
people do not entertain doubt regarding a post that has already been ascertained as such by its verticality.
Knowledge, by its very arising, determines its object;
however, that which does not determine is not at all what is intended here. And thus, to say that there is non-determination precisely because of determination is a contradiction.
However, for one who seeks non-deviation for the sake of confidence in cognition, there is indeed no confidence;
because even regarding the cognition of non-deviation, there is a lack of confidence.
For that [cognition of non-deviation], being itself unestablished and deviant, cannot serve as a cause for confidence in itself or in other cognitions.
If [the object] were established by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress.
Moreover, if [the object] were not established through the form of the cognition itself, then in the absence of that [establishment], with what could the non-deviation of the cognition be grasped?
Furthermore, non-deviation is also stated to arise precisely from the nature of cognition itself, because that would be contradicted in the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
This being the case, that [cognition] alone is the establisher of the object.
Non-deviation is useless;
moreover, it has been stated that deviation does not undermine validity. Furthermore, even when there is non-apprehension, that which serves as the basis for the desired discrimination [is required].
When the opposite is observed, punishment is not to be repelled by [mere] threats.
Defects that do not cause an increase [in the potency] do not destroy the capacity for the effect;
therefore, there may be a distinction between grasping and non-grasping based on the presence or absence of those [defects].
For in the case of the opposite, an extreme impairment occurs,
both through the obstruction of the desired result and through the arising of its contrary.
Therefore, even here, a distinction must be made between its existence and non-existence;
otherwise, how could the suspicion that there is no apprehension when a fault is absent be removed?
For the existence of an effect is not necessarily tied to the presence of its cause;
thus, the effect would have to be perceived directly or else inferred by means of a logical reason.

In the opposite case, the absence of the fruit is logical due to the absence of the cause. Furthermore, the means for discernment and the presence or absence of defects are not restricted by force regarding grasping and non-grasping.
In the case of error, the causes of error are harmful.
This is because it would excessively obstruct the desired effect and because of the occurrence of contrary results.
Furthermore, even when the sense organs and other factors are unimpaired, there is no cessation of the suspicion that perception might not occur;
for even when the cause is present, the effect does not necessarily follow.
And there would be a reversal:
the non-perception of the direct object would have to be inferred by means of a cause;
whereas from the effect, one infers the causal state of the cause.
However, due to the absence of defects, the non-existence of an effect that would result from error is a valid inference,
because an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause. [Otherwise] there would be the consequence of [cognition] being without an object, just as in the case of the projection of another form.
In this way, even in the case of non-apprehension, [the fault] would apply to you simply because of the non-communication of its own nature;
or, if it were equally the case that something else does communicate its nature, then it would not be so in that instance.
For if it were likewise for another in that very case, and if it remained so there, then such a state would exist everywhere; and it would be the same even in your apprehension of it.
Just as in that case, because it is signless, the state of being signless is established in right knowledge;
so too, even regarding apprehension, that state is determined in its non-apprehension.
The status of other [factors] as mere instrumental causes is not distinguished from that of cognition alone;
furthermore, there is a loss of their status as objective supports (*ālambana*), just as in the case of the appearance of another form, even when something conjoined with the eye is perceived,
because the failure to impart its own nature (*svarūpānarpaṇa*) is equal in both cases.
Now, [if it is argued that] because a certain universal form possesses its own aspect—

namely, that some objects conjoined with the eye are grasped in their own form— then even if some [aspects] are not grasped, there is no lack of a common objective support (*ālambana*); this is the same [as our position].
Even when other forms appear, some of its own forms still manifest;
for if non-apprehension were the case, one would not accept that what is in contact with the eye constitutes the objective support (*ālambana*),
and the opponent likewise does not desire the opposite.
For it has been said thus:
"Therefore, that cognition which apprehends as otherwise what exists otherwise is a cognition without an objective basis, and it has non-existence as its object."

Now, if the opposite were the case, since that which is conjoined with the eye serves as an object, there would be a suspicion that other things might also lack the status of being objects; this would apply equally even to non-perception.

Just as it is observed that in erroneous cognition there is independence from the intrinsic nature of the thing conjoined with the eye, so too—in virtue of the commonality of being a cognition—it is suspected that in correct cognition as well, [there may be independence], even though [the object] is conjoined with the eye.
An object is not perceived in its complete form;
therefore, it becomes an objectless [cognition] and serves as the cause for a similar recollection.

If it is argued that because there is no apprehension [of an object] when there is no perception, why is it not suspected that even in cases of apprehension there is no objective basis (*anālambanatā*)?
If you say "because there is an absence of defects," that is equally true in the opposite case as well.
Nor is there a lack of an objective basis (nirālambanatva) when the object of cognition is otherwise;
for the eye is not perceived as an object even in other ways.
And the meaning of "objective basis" (ālambana-artha) is the capacity of the mother-of-pearl to function as silver in conventional usage.
For indeed, one who desires silver takes up that [shell];

for even in the case of a jar, its being the objective support (*ālambana*) of its own cognition is nothing other than its fitness for conventional usage (*vyavahārayogyatā*), since cognition does not possess the form of the object.

In that case, the mother-of-pearl is not apprehended in its own form by the cognition of silver, because the practical activity based upon it does not occur; however, it is apprehended in the form of silver, because the practical activity of grasping it, which is based upon that [form], does occur there.
Even regarding an injunction whose focus is action, someone says that for the sake of establishing the nature of the thing itself:
"Just as the purpose of threshing, sprinkling, and so forth is established as being for the sake of the substance. (MBs 2.161)
Knowledge is for the sake of the substance [of the object] by its very nature, and likewise for the self by virtue of being an action;
even if this were so, how can the establishment of the desired form be considered possible?
The word is established as the effect of that cognition which has its object;
what other meaning could there be for the object of cognition than the manifestation of its own form? MBs 2.163.
The postulation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is not tenable when the seen is possible;
therefore, just as from the injunction regarding sprinkling and so forth, it is understood that [the result pertains] to the rice grains.
The unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskṛti*) is likewise the form of the injunction for knowledge with respect to the self;
just as threshing, sprinkling, and so forth, serve the purpose of the substance by their very nature,
since the substance is designated as the object (*karman*) by means of the accusative case.

Likewise, knowledge also exists for the sake of another by its very nature; and because it is designated as an object (*karman*) of the self, it exists for the sake of that [self]. Therefore, even the injunction whose object is knowledge touches upon the nature of the self.
It does not terminate in mere knowledge,
because since knowledge has the self as its object, the self-nature is implied by the very injunction of knowledge through the understanding that it is something to be accomplished.
This might be argued:
Granted that knowledge is intended for the sake of the self;
however, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated for the realization of the self whose nature is free from evil and so forth.
For the scripture (*śabda*) culminates in the necessity of performing such knowledge of the self.
"One should produce knowledge with reference to the Self as being of such a nature," but not [the thought] "the Self is of such a nature."
To this it is replied:
for it is not logical that something which produces no effect at all should be enjoined as being for the sake of that [result];
and in the case of cognition, there is no other fruit in respect to the object than the awareness of its own form.
For when that [visible result] is seen, there is no postulation of another unseen [result].

In this regard, just as from the injunction of sprinkling itself— namely, "he sprinkles the rice"— there is the understanding of an unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) in the rice, even though it is the object of the act of sprinkling.

Otherwise, the necessity of performing the sprinkling for the sake of the rice would not be logical; for in that case, if one were to do nothing at all, the sprinkling could not be considered performed for that purpose. Thus, it is from the injunction itself that the existence of an invisible refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) is established, just as in the case of the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
Otherwise, it would not be logical for one who desires heaven to understand that the sacrifice is something to be performed, if the sacrifice were not a means to heaven;
and if one is enjoined toward what is not a means, then the person desiring heaven is not truly enjoined.

Even if an action is performed, it is not truly "performed" by one who desires heaven; thus, from an injunction whose object is an action, there arises a verbal comprehension of the relationship between the end and the means.
Likewise, from an injunction whose object is knowledge, there arises the realization of the nature of the Self.
For an injunction to know directed toward such a Self is not tenable.
If it is argued that the self, though not of that nature, is perceived by that cognition,
this has already been answered, because [the cognition] illuminates even that which is formless.
Otherwise, the fruit of that practice would not be the manifestation of knowledge;
for while dissolution is to be averted, distraction is not so, since it is as pleasant [as the former].
Furthermore, there would be no distinction between the distraction of a householder and mere non-apprehension;
for indeed, if there were no appearance of form, one would have to postulate the fruit of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
The visible fruit seen in the manifestation of form is characterized by its accomplishment;
it is not merely from the sight [of the object] that the purpose is seen, for that [accomplishment] follows upon the human goal.
And there is no difference in its nature between the appearances of form and the formless,
just as it is in the reality revealed by knowledge, which is empty of conceptual proliferation.
The abandonment of suffering, karma, and afflictions would likewise occur even in the case of what is unreal;
and this would be logical here, because it does not contradict perception and other means of valid cognition.
And since they would be non-figurative in meaning because they are the objects of action,
this much is understood from the rule regarding the knowledge of the self's purpose:
that it is illuminated by knowledge.
It is apprehended and rendered fit for conventional usage;
and that manifestation is perceived in its own essential nature.
And by way of another form—
that is, as having the nature of silver— this has been established regarding the mother-of-pearl.
This is not merely a case of non-apprehension;
rather, it is the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti).
Since both possibilities exist there, on what basis is this [the latter] established?
The realization of reality must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, the appearance of that [reality] in what is not that would not occur, and the injunction for the knowledge of the Self would not be fruitful.
That [negation] indeed has the purpose of dissolving what is not the self-nature;
for it is observed that the comprehension of a reality occurs through the dissolution of what is not its self-nature.
And if the Self were not manifested in the form of the manifold proliferation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), [then negation would be unnecessary].
What is to be dissolved? Now, it may be thought:
this ignorance is of two kinds—the obscuring and the distracting.
In the states of dreaming and waking, it is the cause of distraction;
in deep sleep, it is characterized by dissolution and acts as a veil. Among these, the cessation of the veiling ignorance is the fruit of the injunction for knowledge.
But that is not the case;
for a person does not seek the cessation of obscuring ignorance in the same way they seek the cessation of distraction,
since the latter consists of manifold sufferings.

Furthermore, since liberation (*laya*) is described in the Śruti as being repeatedly characterized by bliss due to the cessation of various sufferings, it would instead have to be sought after. Moreover, for one who does not accept [the existence of] cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*), there could be no differentiation of ignorance (*avidyā*),
because it would be nothing more than mere non-apprehension across all three states.
Therefore, non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension are two forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) existing in a relationship of cause and effect.
Both exist in the states of dreaming and waking, while that characterized by causal non-apprehension exists in deep sleep; thus, the classification of ignorance is logically established.
As it has been said:
"The Viśva and Taijasa are considered to be bound by both cause and effect;
the Prājña is bound by the cause alone; but these two [bondages] do not apply in the fourth state (turya)."
Is it not the case that this distinction is otherwise— namely, by way of non-apprehension and correct apprehension?
For in deep sleep, the veiling [power] is characterized by non-apprehension.
The incorrect apprehension of the other two [aspects] is as follows:
for when an undivided, partless entity is apprehended, because its state of being as such is not apprehended, it appears as if distinct.
This is not sound.

For if that [non-apprehension] consists merely in the incorrect apprehension of an object, or in the dullness of cognition, or in its apprehending it in some particular form rather than in its entirety; [then it does not prove the non-existence of the object].
In that regard, when an object is distant or subtle, cognition is unsharp and constitutes a cognition of a general property (*sāmānyajñāna*).
Yet, this is not ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, since no cognition whatsoever grasps an object in its entirety, it does not follow that all cognitions are false.
Even if non-difference is not grasped, even if difference persists, and even if difference is not perceived, there is nothing that needs to be removed by knowledge (*vidyā*).
Indeed, the non-apprehension of non-difference is not something to be removed;
for it does not commit any fault whatsoever.

But difference is the locus of manifold suffering; furthermore, the apprehension of what is not distinct as having a distinct appearance for that which is non-distinct in essence is, then, the acceptance of the theory of erroneous cognition (*viparyayakhyāti*).
"It appears both non-different and different.
Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that it appears as something separate."
"But it appears as if separate.
What is the meaning of "as if"?
If it means that just as a separate entity appears while its non-dual nature remains unmanifest, so too the single reality of the Self (ātmatattva) appears while its oneness is not grasped.
It is stated that there is apprehension in one respect and non-apprehension in its entirety;
and regarding that, it was said:
"Now, as if it were manifest..."
But it does not manifest.
If it were to manifest, what would be the purpose of the analogy?
It would be the engagement in conventional discourse based upon that manifestation.
If conventional usage is based upon that [manifestation], then it follows that manifestation must exist— since an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause.
Now, it might be argued that the very non-apprehension of non-difference is what is mistakenly taken to be the apprehension of difference.
That is incorrect, because it is not admitted that non-apprehension—which is an absence—can be apprehended either in its own form or in the form of another.
Furthermore, if difference itself is not being manifested, how can there be a non-apprehension of it?

And if one abandons the conceit of difference regarding what is non-different, while simultaneously embracing the conceit of grasping at difference when there is no grasping at non-difference, what would have been avoided?
Therefore, it is well said:
"In the case of mere non-grasping, there would be no distinction between dissolution and distraction."
Indeed, if there were cognition in the form of a non-self, no fruit would be observed;
in that case, one would have to postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). But for the cognition in the form of a self, the observed fruit is the establishment of its own nature.
It is said:
it is not from the mere sight of anything whatsoever that a thing is considered to have a visible purpose; rather, it is when it touches upon the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
For by that, the injunction becomes free from expectancy.
Nor is there a difference in the human goal between the realization of reality and the non-realization thereof;
for just as one who realizes the pure, non-dual Self is not touched by sorrow even while remaining in such a state, [so too is the case for one who does not realize it].
Because there is nothing to be grieved for,
he does not accumulate a latent deposit of karma,
as there is no longer anything that remains to be done.
He does not crave anything nor does he hate anything,
because of the absence of objects;
thus, even while living, the wise one becomes liberated.
Likewise, even that which is not as it appears, one realizes as if it were directly present by means of the preceding cultivation of it as such;
thus, even an unreal object becomes the cause for conventional usage as if it were real due to the excellence of its cultivation.
And this alone is what is logical in this case.
Because there is no contradiction with perception and the other means of valid cognition, and because the injunctions for ritual action have as their object that which already exists;
for if the ultimate reality were the voidness of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), then perception and the other means of valid cognition would be sublated.
Furthermore, ritual injunctions would have as their domain objects established through conventional usage based on the appropriation of unreal conceptual constructions.
Therefore, it is only from a non-ultimate perspective that the injunction for the knowledge of the non-dual Self is appropriate.
If it is argued that the root *jñā* (to know) refers to the awakening to reality, [we reply] no, because of the qualifying terms such as "false" (*mithyā*) and so forth.

If it were the case that the self is not known [by the Upanishads], then it would not be so; for [the Upanishads] do not enjoin its nature. This is even more certain if it is established by another means of knowledge, or otherwise [if it were not].
Knowledge of that [object] is produced by means of a form imparted by words;
even though that [form] is not the actual reality, through it the cognition of the object is possible.
If it is thought that the verb "to know" (jānāti) in the phrase "He is to be desired to be known" (sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ) refers exclusively to the determination of reality;
Therefore, there would be no way to establish knowledge through such an unreal superimposition.
That is not so; for knowledge is qualified by its falsity and other attributes—as false knowledge, correct knowledge, and doubtful knowledge.
That would not be tenable if there were a restriction to that alone, because of tautology and contradiction.
This might be [objected]:
If one apprehends [an object] by way of what is not its true nature, that is not knowledge of its self;
it is merely knowledge of something else.
And yet, knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is what is prescribed.
Therefore, [it is argued that] the establishment of reality [occurs through this];
but that is not so.
Indeed, it is not merely this much.
"The self is to be known":
if this were an injunction for the cognition of its form,
that would not be the case, because it is untenable in either way.
If the nature of the self were established by another means of valid cognition, then that knowledge would not be something to be enjoined.
On the other hand, if it were not established,
it would be impossible [to know].

It might be argued as follows: "The knowledge of that [Self] whose nature is presented by such scriptural statements as 'free from evil, ageless, deathless' and 'all this is what this Self is' is enjoined."
And since that [result] can occur through that reality even when it is superimposed,
one does not necessarily perceive its existence as such from the injunction for knowledge of that kind.
Furthermore, if knowledge has a perceived object, it is obtained precisely from perception itself.
For one who desires to know the nature of the self, or for one who does not desire to know it, that [effort] is indeed in vain.
If the means to that [attainment] is not known, then let the injunction for that very [means] follow from it;
for injunctions such as threshing are not devoid of contact with the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
If this knowledge is established as being supramundane, then it cannot be brought about by an injunction,
because the function of an injunction is not for the purpose of establishing the nature [of an object].
And the sense of "what ought to be done" regarding a perceptible object is established from that very perception;
therefore, when an object of a non-worldly nature is communicated by means of a word, [it is established through that].
Since knowledge is the means for attaining the object of knowledge, a person is naturally inclined toward it;
however, if the means to that [knowledge] is not understood, he should be impelled toward it by an injunction.
Therefore, the entry into an injunction necessarily destroys its status as a means of valid cognition;
thus, that which has an already established object should not be relied upon by one who desires to understand the nature of reality.
And if the fruit of knowledge is already perceived, then since activity is established by that alone, an injunction is useless;
for one who desires to experience the nature of the Self [already knows it].
He exerts himself toward that knowledge by his own accord; however, for one who does not do so,
such effort is in vain, and thus he cannot be incited even by a hundred injunctions.
Now, it might be argued that because one lacks knowledge of the means, one does not engage in an action even when its result is visible,
and therefore it must be enjoined;
but that is a triviality.
Therefore, let that very means be prescribed by which he has not yet engaged due to ignorance;
for once there is knowledge, he will certainly engage because of the visible fruit.
It might be argued that even in cases such as threshing, where the result is perceptible, an injunction is observed.
True; however, it is not devoid of contact with the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
For even there, the result is the unseen merit of restriction (niyamādṛṣṭa), or else, through that medium, the accomplishment of the primary apūrva is itself indeed unseen.
Now, it might be thought:
"The knowledge of the non-dual Self has never been seen before and is extraordinary;
therefore, even though its fruit is immediate, it is prescribed as something to be performed."
To this it is replied: for what purpose is it enjoined?
It is for the sake of the comprehension of the essential nature of that which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition.
Or is it for the sake of performance?
In that regard, it is not for the sake of establishing the essential nature [of the act],
because an injunction has performance as its fruit and does not exist for the sake of performance itself.
Since that [realization] is established precisely because its object is directly perceived (*dṛṣṭārtha*),

it follows that when the reality of the Self— characterized by being free from evil and so forth— is understood through the word (*śabda*) regarding that which is beyond the world (*alaukika*), a person’s own inclination toward it occurs spontaneously, as the word serves as a means for experiencing it and leads to direct knowledge (*sākṣājjñāna*) of it;
therefore, a formal injunction (*vidhāna*) for that is redundant.
Just as when some wondrous object has been understood through scripture, there arises a spontaneous inclination toward its direct realization;
however, regarding the means to that [realization], since they are unknown, it is appropriate to prescribe them for the purpose of making known their status as means.

Thus, since an injunction (*niyoga*) is untenable with respect to knowledge, and since validity is impossible if an injunction were to result in the comprehension of the nature of a real entity, one who desires the realization of the established reality of the self must not admit that such [knowledge] enters into the scope of an injunction.
"...must be accepted.
Now, in order to refute the second method of practice, he says:
"For this very reason, there is no finality in the prescription of a continuum of consciousness."
In that case as well, as before, there would be no valid cognition consisting in the comprehension of the thing's own nature.

However, from a word established in its own essential nature, there arises an injunction for meditation based on what has been cognized through another statement; or else, even that [injunction] would be in vain.
Because the excellence of the cognition is observed through repeated practice,
therefore the Vedāntas possess the status of valid authority regarding that object which is not [previously] known.
As for the view that [one should] "perform the sacrifice," "cultivate discernment," and "meditate upon [the Self]"— these [injunctions], too, [are intended to lead to realization].
Even where the state of abiding in one's own essential nature alone is indicated,
as in "That thou art," there too [the sense is] "I am That."

Because it is intended that one should "hold the mind" in this manner, meditation (*dhyāna*)—defined as reflection other than hearing (*śravaṇa*), a continuous flow of cognition—is enjoined; like ritual action (*karman*), it has immortality as its fruit.
However, even that is not tenable for this very reason:

because it would result in the previously mentioned absence of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the realization of reality (*tattva-avagati*), or because the sentence would be focused on something else.
But if it is maintained that, based on another statement established in reality, there is an injunction for the practice of a continuous flow of cognition directed toward that object,
let it be so; there is no fault whatsoever.
And likewise, by stating "having known, one should practice wisdom," it shows that the knowledge of the reality of the Self is already established;
furthermore, that [injunction] would be entirely useless,
because its purpose has already been attained.
For reflection upon each [of these] has as its fruit direct realization; it has a visible purpose, and no fruit other than that is expected.
Indeed, it was explained previously that immortality is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature.
And it is observed in the world that the practice of knowledge is the cause for the clarity of right knowledge;
for through a particular kind of cultivation, one may even experience what is unreal, so how much more so what is real?

But the statement, "He should perform that rite," does not enjoin the contemplation of the reality of the Self as transcending all particularities, which has that state [of liberation] as its fruit; rather,
it enjoins meditation upon forms such as the mind-made (manomaya) and the vital-breath-bodied (prāṇaśarīra), which have adjuncts of name and form, and which have sovereignty as their fruit.
Or rather, the fruit is direct realization attained through a gradual process;
thus, the statement "the wise man, having known that very [Self]" is not an injunction for the performance of wisdom.
Because the exclusion of others is explicitly heard in the phrase "that very [one]," it is understood that the intention lies in negation;
just as in the sentence "the cloth becomes red," the sentence's purpose is directed toward the quality of redness.
Here, non-differentiation is established following the prior distinction of the principles (tattvas) such as space and the rest.
In that context, when the application of discernment (*prajñākaraṇa*) arises in the same manner,
it is enjoined: "that very [thing]."
And likewise, in the first half [of that same passage]:
"The stainless, supreme Self is beyond space, unborn, great, and eternal";
thus the reality of the Self is shown to be superior to space and the other elements.
Since there is the possibility of applying the same [interpretation] regarding the formation of the term *prajñā*, the phrase "that very [one]" (*tameva*) is stated in order to exclude that.
Otherwise, the word "only" (*eva*) would have no purpose.
And that which is to be turned away would not be understood;
thus, it is elaborated upon by the subsequent [text]:
"One should not meditate on many words."
Thus, there is syntactic unity;
otherwise, the sentence would be split.
Furthermore, since meditation does not apply to mere sound—because that [meditation] is preceded by the word—it follows that this [meditation] has as its object only the meaning of the word.
Thus, from the hearing of the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) in the text "One should meditate [on the Self] as indeed the Self," there is an injunction regarding that meaning;
so too in the case of "It is to be contemplated" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*).
Since it begins with "But for the sake of one's own self" and concludes with "All this is what this self is," the entire passage is a single statement whose purport is the true nature of the Self.
Included within that [context],
the injunctions "He is to be seen, He is to be heard, He is to be meditated upon" are not separate injunctions, even though they are formed with gerundive suffixes (*kṛtyapratyaya*).

Since the potential suffix (kṛtyapratyaya) is remembered to have other meanings as well, such as praise, [passages] like "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in secret" occurring within the Upāṃśuyāja section are for the purpose of praise.
However, the sentence "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; thou art That" culminates in an existing reality (bhūta).
In this regard, the conceptual construction is: "One should maintain the thought, 'I am.'"

Therefore, since all three types of knowledge cannot be objects of an injunction, and since the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence occurs even without an injunction, the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to an already existing reality is established by virtue of their being independent due to their non-human origin.

And likewise, in the sūtra "But that [Brahman], because of the harmony [of the texts]" (Tat tu samanvayāt), Brahman—which is distinguished from dharma characterized by injunction by the word "but" (tu)—is stated to be known through harmony (samanvaya).
For harmony is the connection or application of the meanings of words; therefore, Brahman is understood from that, not from injunction—this is the meaning.
But has not the authority of the Veda with respect to its objective matter been described without distinction— as in "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ)?
The meaning is that the subject matter of the Veda is characterized by injunction.
This is not sound.
For if this were the case, the investigation into the meaning of the Veda would already presuppose its established authority, just like the subsequent definitions [of the means of knowledge].
In that case, it would be illogical to establish its authority immediately thereafter.
And [it is said]: "The definition of the means of valid cognition has been established.
Furthermore, there would be no disagreement regarding the fact that the purpose of the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) is to denote what is to be done (kārya).
That [objection] will be refuted later on; moreover, much more could be said on this matter, so enough of this digression.
Just as cognition that is free from the interference of other human beings attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object,
so too does that which has arisen from a scripture not authored by a person, because it is independent with respect to what is established (*siddha*).
Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on Appointment (niyoga).
The Fourth Section: Accomplishment (Siddhi)
Thus far, an effort has been made to refute those who, under the guise of discussing the authority of the duty of practice (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*), have asserted its lack of authority;
now, however, an effort is being made to refute those who assert that there is no authority at all.
Regarding this, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

Indeed, since the meaning of a sentence consists of related word-meanings, if it does not attain the status of a word-meaning, there would be no sentence-meaning; for if it were a word-meaning, it would require another means of knowledge.
First of all, words such as "Brahman" or "Inner Controller" (antaryāmin) are not themselves a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa),
because they function as causes for cognition only when preceded by a known relationship [between word and object].
Nor is the sentence [itself] such a means.
For that [word] is not a direct denoter [of the sentence meaning]; rather, its comprehension occurs by way of the meanings of the individual words,
because there is no cognition of what is not a word-meaning.
For these [words], through their association in a relationship of primary and subordinate status, convey a single word-meaning as qualified by other word-meanings.
In that case, the sentence-meaning is simply the word-meaning itself as thus qualified.
Furthermore, the status of being a word-meaning does not belong to things that have not been apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It has been stated that [the meaning] depends upon the knowledge of the relationship [between word and object]. In that regard, if it were not the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*), it would not be the object of a sentence; for those [words], the sentence would be non-informative.
If they were [already] established as categories of existence (*padārtha*), they would be merely repetitive because they are understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, concerning those sentences accepted as authoritative regarding objects such as Brahman—which are absolutely unperceived before—do words denoting them exist or not?

If they do not exist, then those [objects] could neither be conjoined with nor distinguished from others; thus, they would not be objects of knowledge (*prameya*), like a clod of earth or similar things.

But even if they do exist, they could not be communicated by those who have already apprehended the relationship [between word and meaning]; and those not so apprehended are not causes for the comprehension of a specific sentence-meaning.
In this regard, it is just as in the case of the command: "Let the cuckoo be brought from the forest."
Thus, just as there is a capacity for conveying meaning in the cognition of the referent of the word "cuckoo," so it is with those [words] as well.
Therefore, the understanding of a previously unknown (apūrva) entity does not arise from *codanā*;
for that [injunction] indeed authorizes a person toward actions through prescriptions and prohibitions.
However, their acceptance by the elders of the threefold [Veda] is due to their utility for recitation (*japa*);
as for the *upaniṣads*, they are the *vedāntas*, because of their application (*viniyoga*) therein.

To this it is replied: Once the status of being a category (padārtha) has been established in a general sense, the specific [category] that was previously unknown can be demonstrated through its unique qualities, just as is done in the world. MBs 4.2.
Just as in the world, when one hears that "in a particular island there are birds with such-and-such names, having feet made of emerald, beaks made of ruby,

and wings made of gold and silver," the general category of "bird"— already apprehended through another means of knowledge— when conjoined with a unique set of attributes not shared by others, acquires a specific form that was previously unapprehended by any other means of knowledge.
And it is cognized by means of a sentence in its specific form, which has not been apprehended through other means of knowledge—

for indeed, the object of knowledge for every sentence is exclusively that specific aspect not yet apprehended; thus, [the sentence] "from which indeed these beings are born" [establishes] either the generality of the cause or the generality of Being.
Thus,

through the connection with and the differentiation from the meanings of such words as "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short," it attains a specific form not apprehended by other means of knowledge and becomes the object of cognition for the sentence.

Thus, because the understanding of the unprecedented meaning (apūrva-artha) occurs precisely through the connection with word-meanings already established in common worldly usage, there is neither a lack of intelligibility nor is it a mere restatement (anuvādaka).
Or rather, since the nature of Brahman is established as that which is known by all cognition, the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is taught by means of words. (MBs 4.3)

It is held that [Brahman], whose nature is such that all conceptual proliferation has dissolved, is not an object of any other means of knowledge; thus, its basis is solely the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
Alternatively, Brahman is not entirely unknown in the world, because it is cognizable through all means of knowledge,
and because there is nothing to be known apart from Brahman.
And because particular cognitions conform to a universal form,
and because it is established that the true Brahman remains as that which is left over when differences are withdrawn.
"Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth"—from this illustration [it follows].
What, then, is conveyed by the word?
The absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*):
therein, both the referent of "conceptual proliferation" is established, and its negation is also established.
The realization of that absence [of duality] arises from the conjunction of those two [means].
However, its being based solely on sacred tradition (āmnāya) is stated because perception and the other means of knowledge are permeated by ignorance (avidyā).

"Because [the Self] is not made an object through a form in which all distinctions have subsided, and because the subsidence of distinctions is to be understood from the sacred tradition (āmnāya). But the opponent objects:
"Surely, if it is focused on an existing entity (bhūta), the consequence follows that it would not be a human goal (apuruṣārtha)."

Indeed, that statement which does not incite a person toward the accomplishment of any benefit, nor turn him away from the accomplishment of harm, but merely describes an already established fact, is devoid of human purpose (*apuruṣārtha*).
Furthermore, because they do not serve a human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*), they lack authority like the ravings of a madman;
and such is generally the case with the Vedāntas.
To this it is replied:
And it is not the case that the scope of the means of valid cognition is restricted solely to this human goal.

"For they declare even equanimity (*upekṣā*) to be the fruit of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya*). It is inferred that this half-verse ought to be here; however, it is not seen in the manuscript collections (*mātṛkā*).
Furthermore, due to ignorance, the living being appears as one who grieves and suffers.
And the cessation of that [process] is itself considered the human goal, which consists in consciousness when some object has been known by men who possess curiosity. (MBs 4.7)
The arising of knowledge for those who are distressed is accepted as a human goal;
and just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth, which are fixed upon their respective forms, there is no lack of being a human goal.
And why should its being grounded in activity be prevented in this case?
If it is argued that the knowable object possesses human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) there [in the Vedas], it is the same here as well.
The goal of human endeavor is itself Brahman—tranquil and free from old age and other such afflictions;
therefore, it is taught to the disciple by means of the instruction, "That thou art."
If it is held that perception and the other means of knowledge are auxiliary to the activity of another,
then in this case as well, let them be accepted as auxiliaries to the activity of direct realization.
It is not necessarily the case that the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Indeed, the acquisition of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful are not the only fruits of a means of valid cognition;
for those who know the means of valid cognition declare even equanimity (*upekṣā*) to be a fruit of a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, being for the sake of human purpose is not the definition of a means of valid cognition;
rather, it is being the cause of valid cognition.
Therefore, validity is not negated by the absence of a human purpose.

Moreover, such notions as "I am sorrowful," "I am suffering," or "my wealth and so forth have perished" constitute the false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), whose true nature is pure Brahman;
and the knowledge of the reality of the self as Brahman— which is pure bliss and luminosity— consists in the cessation of that [false knowledge].
That [liberation] is a human goal (puruṣārtha) by its very nature, because it consists in the cessation of the undesirable and the manifestation of the desirable.

And although its persistence follows from the residual impression (saṃskāra), nevertheless, for the wise person who continues to contemplate the knowledge derived from scripture, it does not occur as before; rather, it ceases once and for all.
And it is observed that the very arising of knowledge constitutes the human goal in certain cases—for instance, among those agitated by curiosity regarding an unknown object.
For nothing further is sought beyond the knowledge of that object.
Nor is there a rule that the human goal must exclusively consist of an object for engagement or withdrawal.

For the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, do not have as their sole purpose the instigation or cessation of activity, as they have established entities as their objects; yet, they do not forfeit their status as human goals.
If it is thought:
"For an established entity known through perception and other means, such as water and so forth, is the human goal,
because it provides assistance [to the person];"
Consequently, even though perception and the other means of knowledge are grounded in objective reality (*bhūta*), they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

Here too, Brahman itself—the object of knowledge through scripture—is the *puruṣārtha*, because it is supremely serene due to the cessation of various miseries such as old age and because it is the manifestation of supreme bliss.
For this very reason, in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the Śruti teaches [Brahman] as non-different from the person for whom instruction is intended, by means of Śvetaketu.
For that [instruction] is non-different from that which is to be instructed;
and being perceived as distinct, it would not be the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).

However, when there is knowledge of identity with reality (*tattva*), such being the case through the cessation of all inauspiciousness in the world and the attainment of the state of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), the complete goal of human endeavor is achieved.
If it is thought that even perception and the other means of knowledge are indeed limbs of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*),
because activity— characterized by rejection, acquisition, and so forth— occurs only when an object has been cognized, and because such activity is rooted in those [means of knowledge];
Such a status as being a factor for engagement exists here as well,
because it is accepted that one engages in order to effect direct realization once Brahman has been known through the word.
This [work], with the brilliance of logic flashing forth through its skill in discerning the reality of Vedānta,
obstructs the path to liberation by piercing the dense, beginningless darkness and instantly washing away even the thick mire of the fallacious reasoning of worldly sectarians.
The *Brahmasiddhi*, which has explained and uprooted all [opposing views], is for the sake of the unsurpassed bliss of Śiva.
[Thus ends the *Brahmasiddhi*, the work of Maṇḍanamiśra.]
